You are building an application component to collect user-behavior data and stream it into BigQuery. You plan to use the BigQuery Storage Write API. You must ensure that data arriving in BigQuery contains no duplicates. You want to achieve this by using the simplest operational approach. What should you do?

options.text: Create a write stream in the default type.
Create a write stream in the committed type.
Configure a Kafka cluster. Use a primary universally unique identifier (UUID) for duplicate messages.
Configure a Pub/Sub topic. Use Cloud Functions to subscribe to the topic and remove any duplicates.

questions.explanation:
An application-created committed write stream, used with stream offsets, provides exactly-once write semantics in the BigQuery Storage Write API. The default stream provides only at-least-once semantics and can produce duplicates; external Kafka or Pub/Sub deduplication adds unnecessary operational complexity.

**Learn more:** [Stream data using the Storage Write API](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/write-api-streaming) · [BigQuery Storage Write API best practices](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/write-api-best-practices)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has users and groups configured in an external identity provider (IdP). You want to use that same external IdP to let all employees access the Google Cloud console. You also want to personalize sign-in by showing each user's name and photo when they access the Google Cloud console. What should you do?

options.text: Configure workforce identity federation with the external IdP, and set up attribute mapping.
Configure a service account for each individual by using the user name and photo, and grant permissions for each user to impersonate their respective service accounts.
Configure workload identity federation to get the external IdP tokens, and use these tokens to sign in to the Google Cloud console.
Create a Google group that includes organization email IDs for all users. Ask users to use the same name, work email ID, and password to register and sign in.

questions.explanation:
Workforce Identity Federation enables workforce users from an external IdP to use SSO for Google Cloud access. Attribute mapping can populate `google.display_name` and `google.profile_photo`, which set the signed-in user's name and profile image in the Google Cloud console.

**Learn more:** [Workforce Identity Federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workforce-identity-federation) · [Set up user access to the console (federated)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workforce-console-sso)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an ecommerce company. The company is migrating multiple applications to Google Cloud, and you are helping migrate one of them. The application is currently deployed on a VM with no OS dependencies. You created a Dockerfile and used it to upload a new image to Artifact Registry. You want to minimize infrastructure and operational complexity. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the image to Cloud Run.
Deploy the image to a GKE Autopilot cluster.
Deploy the image to a GKE Standard cluster.
Deploy the image to a Compute Engine instance.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform for deploying container images. It abstracts infrastructure management and does not require creating or operating a Kubernetes cluster or virtual machine, making it the lowest-operational-complexity choice for a containerized application with no OS dependencies.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [Deployment options and resource model](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/resource-model)

questions.question: To store application state and fulfill HipLocal’s stated business requirements, which database service should it migrate to?

options.text: Cloud Spanner
Cloud Datastore
Cloud Memorystore as a cache
Separate Cloud SQL clusters for each region

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed, globally distributed relational database that provides strong transactional consistency, automatic synchronous replication, and horizontal scalability. These capabilities support consistent application state across regions, increasing concurrent-user demand, high availability, and reduced infrastructure-management overhead. [Google Cloud Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs)\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs)

options.text: Install Service Mesh in your GKE cluster. Configure Service Mesh user authentication to integrate the service hosted on GKE by using an OpenID Connect-compliant identity provider. Expose the application externally by using an Istio Ingress Gateway. Use VPC firewall rules to restrict Ingress traffic to the Ingress gateway.

You are building an ecommerce application that stores customer, order, and inventory data in relational tables within Cloud Spanner. A recent load test shows that Spanner performance is not scaling linearly as expected. Which of the following is causing this?

options.text: The use of 64-bit numeric types for 32-bit numbers.
The use of the STRING data type for arbitrary-precision values.
The use of Version 1 UUIDs as primary keys that increase monotonically.
The use of LIKE instead of STARTS_WITH keyword for parameterized SQL queries.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner range-shards data by primary key. Version 1 UUIDs contain a timestamp in their high-order bits, causing newly inserted primary-key values to cluster in the same range. The resulting write hotspot overloads a split and limits throughput, so performance does not scale linearly.

**Learn more:** [Schemas overview | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-and-data-model) · [Schema design best practices | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-design)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You configured your Compute Engine instance group to autoscale based on overall CPU utilization. However, your application's response latency rises sharply before the cluster has completed adding instances. You want to deliver a more consistent latency experience to end users by modifying the instance group autoscaler configuration.  
  
Which two configuration changes should you make? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add the label ג€AUTOSCALEג€ to the instance group template.
Decrease the cool-down period for instances added to the group.
Increase the target CPU usage for the instance group autoscaler.
Decrease the target CPU usage for the instance group autoscaler.
Remove the health-check for individual VMs in the instance group.

questions.explanation:
A lower CPU utilization target makes a Compute Engine managed instance group scale out before the existing instances are as heavily loaded, preserving capacity headroom and helping prevent latency spikes. The initialization (formerly cool-down) period controls how long the autoscaler ignores utilization data from newly created VMs during scale-out; reducing an unnecessarily long period allows those instances to contribute to autoscaling decisions sooner.

**Learn more:** [Scaling based on CPU utilization | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler/scaling-cpu) · [Autoscaling groups of instances | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a mobile application that lets users create and manage to-do lists. Your application must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Store and synchronize data across different mobile devices.  
- Support offline access.  
- Deliver real-time updates on every user's device.  
  
You need to implement a database solution while minimizing operational effort. Which approach should you use?

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. Implement a data model to store to-do list information. Create indexes for the most heavily and frequently used queries.
Create a Bigtable instance. Design a database schema to avoid hotspots when writing data. Use a Bigtable change stream to capture data changes.
Use Firestore as the database. Configure Firestore offline persistence to cache a copy of the Firestore data. Listen to document changes to update applications whenever there are document changes.
Implement a SQLite database on each user's device. Use a scheduled job to synchronize each device database with a copy stored in Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Firestore is a managed mobile-oriented database that synchronizes data across client applications. Its offline persistence caches actively used data, permits reads, writes, listeners, and queries while offline, and synchronizes local changes after reconnection. Real-time listeners deliver updated snapshots whenever the watched documents or query results change.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Firestore overview](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/index.html) · [Access data offline](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/manage-data/enable-offline)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a resource-sharing policy for applications used by different teams in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. You must ensure that every application can obtain the resources required to run. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Specify the resource limits and requests in the object specifications.
Create a namespace for each team, and attach resource quotas to each namespace.
Create a LimitRange to specify the default compute resource requirements for each namespace.
Create a Kubernetes service account (KSA) for each application, and assign each KSA to the namespace.
Use the Anthos Policy Controller to enforce label annotations on all namespaces. Use taints and tolerations to allow resource sharing for namespaces.

questions.explanation:
Resource quotas manage the CPU, memory, and object resources that a namespace can consume, preventing one tenant from using more than its assigned share of a shared cluster. A LimitRange can set default compute resource requests and limits for resources in a namespace, so workloads without explicit values still have defined scheduling requirements. Together, per-team namespaces with ResourceQuotas and namespace LimitRanges provide controlled, predictable resource sharing.

**Learn more:** [Cluster multi-tenancy | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/multitenancy-overview) · [Resource Quotas | Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application stores customer content in a Cloud Storage bucket, and every object is encrypted with that customer's encryption key. Each Cloud Storage object key is entered into your application by the customer. You find that the application receives an HTTP 4xx error while reading an object from Cloud Storage. What could cause this error?

options.text: You attempted the read operation on the object with the customer's base64-encoded key.
You attempted the read operation without the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of the encryption key.
You entered the same encryption algorithm specified by the customer when attempting the read operation.
You attempted the read operation on the object with the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of the customer's key.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage customer-supplied encryption-key requests made through the REST APIs must include the `AES256` algorithm, the Base64-encoded AES-256 key, and the Base64-encoded SHA-256 hash of that key. A read request that omits the required SHA-256 hash is invalid and can return an HTTP 400 error.

**Learn more:** [Customer-supplied encryption keys | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption/customer-supplied-keys)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],This architecture diagram shows a system streaming data from thousands of devices. You want to ingest the data into a pipeline, store it, and analyze it by using SQL statements. Which Google Cloud services should be used for steps 1, 2, 3, and 4?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783708349475-ikhdy7cl.png)

options.text: 1. App Engine2. Pub/Sub3. BigQuery4. Firestore
1. Dataflow2. Pub/Sub3. Firestore4. BigQuery
1. Pub/Sub2. Dataflow3. BigQuery4. Firestore
1. Pub/Sub2. Dataflow3. Firestore4. BigQuery

questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub ingests and distributes streaming device events, and Dataflow provides managed stream and batch data-processing pipelines. Firestore is suitable for transactional application data, whereas BigQuery is the analytical data warehouse used for SQL queries. This produces the service sequence Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Firestore, and BigQuery.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/overview) · [Stream from Pub/Sub to BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/tutorials/dataflow-stream-to-bigquery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a microservices application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application will receive daily updates. You anticipate deploying a large number of distinct containers that will run on the Linux operating system (OS). You want to be alerted to any known OS vulnerabilities in the new containers. You want to follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gcloud CLI to call Container Analysis to scan new container images. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.
Enable Container Analysis, and upload new container images to Artifact Registry. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.
Enable Container Analysis, and upload new container images to Artifact Registry. Review the critical vulnerability results before each deployment.
Use the Container Analysis REST API to call Container Analysis to scan new container images. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.

questions.explanation:
Container Analysis automatic scanning is designed for container images pushed to Artifact Registry. After the scanning API is enabled, each new image pushed to Artifact Registry is scanned for supported OS-package vulnerabilities, and the vulnerability metadata is continuously updated as new vulnerability information becomes available. This avoids manual, per-image on-demand scans and preserves visibility into vulnerabilities at every severity.

**Learn more:** [Container scanning overview | Artifact Analysis | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/container-scanning-overview) · [Enable or disable automatic scanning | Artifact Analysis | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/enable-automatic-scanning)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company stores its source code in a Cloud Source Repositories repository. The company wants to build and test its code on every source-code commit to the repository and requires a managed solution with minimal operational overhead.  
  
Which method should it use?

options.text: Use Cloud Build with a trigger configured for each source code commit.
Use Jenkins deployed via the Google Cloud Platform Marketplace, configured to watch for source code commits.
Use a Compute Engine virtual machine instance with an open source continuous integration tool, configured to watch for source code commits.
Use a source code commit trigger to push a message to a Cloud Pub/Sub topic that triggers an App Engine service to build the source code.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build provides managed CI and can use a build trigger to automatically run a build when code is pushed to Cloud Source Repositories. This avoids operating Jenkins, virtual machines, or custom event-processing services.

**Learn more:** [Automating builds with Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/source-repositories/docs/integrating-with-cloud-build) · [Cloud Build triggers](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/triggers)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to re-architect a monolithic application so it follows a microservices model. You want to do this efficiently while minimizing the business impact of the change.  
  
Which approach should you use?

options.text: Deploy the application to Compute Engine and turn on autoscaling.
Replace the application's features with appropriate microservices in phases.
Refactor the monolithic application with appropriate microservices in a single effort and deploy it.
Build a new application with the appropriate microservices separate from the monolith and replace it when it is complete.

questions.explanation:
A phased replacement of features with appropriately scoped microservices enables incremental migration while the monolith continues to provide the remaining functionality. This strangler-fig approach reduces disruption and risk compared with a single large refactor or a complete replacement delivered only at the end. Google Cloud recommends moving services incrementally and iteratively rather than treating the change as a big-bang project.

**Learn more:** [Re-Architecting to Cloud Native](https://cloud.google.com/resources/rearchitecting-to-cloud-native)

Your company has deployed a new API to the App Engine Standard environment. During testing, the API is not functioning as expected. You want to monitor the application over time to diagnose the issue within the application code, without redeploying the application.  
  
Which tool should you use?

options.text: Stackdriver Trace
Stackdriver Monitoring
Stackdriver Debug Snapshots
Stackdriver Debug Logpoints

questions.explanation:
Stackdriver Debug Logpoints dynamically add log statements to a running application without rebuilding or redeploying it. They can record code-level values and behavior as the selected execution path runs, supporting diagnosis over time.\

Your company has deployed a new API to the App Engine Standard environment. During testing, the API is not functioning as expected. You want to monitor the application over time to diagnose the issue within the application code, without redeploying the application.  
  
Which tool should you use?

options.text: Your user account does not have privileges to interact with the cluster using kubectl.
Your Cloud Shell external IP address is not part of the authorized networks of the cluster.
The Cloud Shell is not part of the same VPC as the GKE cluster.
A VPC firewall is blocking access to the cluster’s endpoint.

questions.explanation:
GKE control-plane authorized networks restrict access to an IP-based public endpoint by source IP address. If Cloud Shell’s outgoing external IP address is not included in the cluster’s authorized-network CIDR ranges, requests to the Kubernetes control plane cannot connect and can time out. IAM or Kubernetes RBAC authorization failures would instead occur after connectivity is established and return an authorization-related error.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot the kubectl command-line tool | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/kubectl) · [About network isolation in GKE | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/network-isolation)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a Node.js-based mobile news-feed application that stores data on Google Cloud. You need to choose the application's database. You want the database to provide out-of-the-box zonal resiliency, low-latency responses, ACID compliance, an optional middle tier, semi-structured data storage, and client libraries that tolerate network partitions and support offline mode. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Firestore and use the Firestore client library in the app.
Configure Bigtable and use the Bigtable client in the app.
Configure Cloud SQL and use the Google Client Library for Cloud SQL in the app.
Configure BigQuery and use the BigQuery REST API in the app.

questions.explanation:
Firestore is a flexible document database with nested, semi-structured data, ACID properties for writes, transaction support, and strongly consistent queries. A regional Firestore location replicates data across multiple zones, while multi-region locations further improve availability. Firestore supports direct mobile and web SDK access without an intermediary server, as well as Node.js server client libraries when a middle tier is needed. Its mobile and web SDKs cache active data, allow reads and writes while offline, and synchronize changes after connectivity returns.

**Learn more:** [Firestore overview](https://cloud.google.com/firestore/docs/overview) · [Firestore locations](https://cloud.google.com/firestore/docs/locations)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using the latest stable release of Python 3 to build an API that stores data in a Cloud SQL database. You must perform CRUD operations on the production database securely and reliably with minimal effort. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Use Cloud Composer to manage the connection to the Cloud SQL database from your Python application.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the composer.worker permission.
1. Use the Cloud SQL API to connect to the Cloud SQL database from your Python application.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the cloudsql.instances.login permission.

1. Use the Cloud SQL connector library for Python to connect to the Cloud SQL database through a Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the cloudsql.instances.connect permission.
1. Use the Cloud SQL emulator to connect to the Cloud SQL database from Cloud Shell2. Grant an IAM role to the user that includes the cloudsql.instances.login permission.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud SQL Python Connector provides secure, IAM-authorized connectivity for Python applications while avoiding manual IP allowlisting and certificate management. A service account used for this connectivity must have a role containing the `cloudsql.instances.connect` permission, such as Cloud SQL Client.

**Learn more:** [Connect using Cloud SQL Language Connectors](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/connect-connectors) · [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/sql-proxy)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a microservice-based application that will run on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Some services must access different Google Cloud APIs. How should you configure authentication for these services in the cluster according to Google-recommended best practices? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use the service account attached to the GKE node.
Enable Workload Identity in the cluster via the gcloud command-line tool.
Access the Google service account keys from a secret management service.
Store the Google service account keys in a central secret management service.
Use gcloud to bind the Kubernetes service account and the Google service account using roles/iam.workloadIdentity.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended mechanism for workloads to access Google Cloud APIs because it provides distinct, fine-grained IAM identities without service-account key files. Enable it on the GKE cluster, then bind each Kubernetes service account to the appropriate Google service account using the `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` role.

**Learn more:** [Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity) · [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You operate a system that runs on stateless Compute Engine VMs and Cloud Run instances. Cloud Run is connected to a VPC, and its ingress setting is configured as **Internal**. You want to schedule tasks on Cloud Run. You create a service account and grant it the `roles/run.invoker` Identity and Access Management (IAM) role. When you create a schedule and test it, Cloud Logging returns a `403 Permission Denied` error. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the service account the roles/run.developer IAM role.
Configure a cron job on the Compute Engine VMs to trigger Cloud Run on schedule.
Change the Cloud Run ingress setting to 'Internal and Cloud Load Balancing.'
Use Cloud Scheduler with Pub/Sub to invoke Cloud Run.

questions.explanation:
`roles/run.invoker` is sufficient for authenticated invocation, but internal ingress also restricts the network path that may reach the Cloud Run service. Pub/Sub push subscriptions are recognized as internal Google Cloud traffic for a Cloud Run service with internal ingress, and Pub/Sub can authenticate the push request using a service account granted the Cloud Run Invoker role. Cloud Scheduler can therefore publish to Pub/Sub, which invokes the service without exposing it through an external load balancer.

**Learn more:** [Private networking and Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/private-networking) · [Restrict network endpoint ingress for Cloud Run services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/ingress)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application team is building an ecommerce application. The team has created new functionality that depends on a third-party service. That third-party service will be deployed in several days, but its reliability has not been confirmed. You need to select a deployment strategy for the ecommerce application that avoids disruption and can be rolled back quickly if problems are found. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the new functionality by using an A/B deployment strategy.
Deploy the new functionality to all users by using a blue/green deployment strategy.
Use a feature flag to enable the new functionality to users on demand. Gradually enable the new functionality to more users.
Gradually roll out the new functionality by using a rolling updates deployment strategy. Start with a small subset of users and increase the number of users over time.

questions.explanation:
A feature flag decouples deployment of the code from release of the functionality. The feature can remain disabled initially, be enabled for a small group of users, and be progressively enabled for more users only after the third-party service proves reliable. If issues occur, disabling the flag immediately removes access to the functionality without requiring a full application rollback.

**Learn more:** [App Lifecycle Manager feature flags overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/saas-runtime/docs/flags/flags-overview) · [Use gradual feature rollouts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/saas-runtime/docs/flags/flags-gradual-rollout)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must redesign audit-event ingestion from your authentication service so it can accommodate a substantial traffic increase. Currently, the audit service and authentication system run on the same Compute Engine virtual machine. You plan to use these Google Cloud tools in the new architecture:  
  
- Multiple Compute Engine machines, each running an authentication-service instance  
- Multiple Compute Engine machines, each running an audit-service instance  
- Pub/Sub to send events from the authentication services  
  
How should the topics and subscriptions be configured to ensure the system handles a high message volume and scales efficiently?

options.text: Create one Pub/Sub topic. Create one pull subscription to allow the audit services to share the messages.
Create one Pub/Sub topic. Create one pull subscription per audit service instance to allow the services to share the messages.
Create one Pub/Sub topic. Create one push subscription with the endpoint pointing to a load balancer in front of the audit services.
Create one Pub/Sub topic per authentication service. Create one pull subscription per topic to be used by one audit service.
Create one Pub/Sub topic per authentication service. Create one push subscription per topic, with the endpoint pointing to one audit service.

questions.explanation:
A single Pub/Sub topic can accept events from all authentication-service instances. Multiple audit-service instances can pull from the same pull subscription, with Pub/Sub distributing a subset of messages to each instance; this provides load-balanced consumption without duplicating every event to every audit worker. Pull subscriptions are suited to high-volume, throughput-critical processing.

**Learn more:** [Pub/Sub subscription types](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscriber) · [Pub/Sub service overview](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/pubsub-basics)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s development teams want to use Cloud Build in their projects to build and push Docker images to Container Registry. The operations team requires that all Docker images be published to a centralized, securely managed Docker registry operated by the operations team.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Container Registry to create a registry in each development team's project. Configure the Cloud Build build to push the Docker image to the project's registry. Grant the operations team access to each development team's registry.

Create a separate project for the operations team that has Container Registry configured. Assign appropriate permissions to the Cloud Build service account in each developer team's project to allow access to the operation team's registry.

Create a separate project for the operations team that has Container Registry configured. Create a Service Account for each development team and assign the appropriate permissions to allow it access to the operations team's registry. Store the service account key file in the source code repository and use it to authenticate against the operations team's registry.

Create a separate project for the operations team that has the open source Docker Registry deployed on a Compute Engine virtual machine instance. Create a username and password for each development team. Store the username and password in the source code repository and use it to authenticate against the operations team's Docker registry.

questions.explanation:
A registry in a dedicated operations project centralizes image management. The Cloud Build service account from each development project can be granted the appropriate write permissions on the registry’s backing storage in the operations project, enabling cross-project image pushes without distributing or storing long-lived credentials. Container Registry uses Cloud Storage roles for access control, including write access to existing registry hosts.

**Learn more:** [Changes for Docker — Artifact Registry documentation](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/transition/changes-docker) · [Configure access for the default Cloud Build service account](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/securing-builds/configure-access-for-cloud-build-service-account)

Your production application has recently experienced reliability problems, and you are uncertain how it will behave if an unexpected failure occurs. You want to evaluate the application's resilience. What should you do?

options.text: Write end-to-end tests to determine how different microservices interact. Validate that all tests pass.
Perform chaos engineering by intentionally introducing failures into the system. Observe how the application behaves, and ensure that it is able to recover from a failure.
Test individual units of code for a critical portion of the application's code. Ensure that unit tests are part of the Cloud Build pipeline.
Perform load testing of the application, and use JMeter for the critical endpoints of the application. Ensure that the application performs as expected under a heavy load.

questions.explanation:

Three teams are developing an ecommerce application in the same Google Cloud project. Team A will build a set of RESTful APIs that expose core application functionality. Team B and Team C will call those APIs from downstream processes running in Cloud Run services. You need to propose an API-exposure solution that maximizes security and minimizes management overhead for all three teams. How should you design this solution?

options.text: 1. Team A uses service accounts to authorize Cloud API Gateway. Team B and Team C each create a service account, export their service account's key, and store each key in a separate secret in Secret Manager.2. Team B and Team C use this service account key to create an OAuth token to access the APIs.

1. Team A uses Apigee hybrid to create an API key and shares that key with Team B and Team C.2. Team B and Team C store the API key in a secret in Secret Manager, and use this API key to access the API endpoint.

1. Team A uses an API key to authorize Cloud API Gateway and shares the key with Team B and Team C.2. Team B and Team C store the API key in a secret in Secret Manager, and use this API key to access the API endpoint.

1. Team A uses service accounts to authorize Cloud API Gateway. Team B and Team C each create a service account that has access to the APIs.2. Team B and Team C access the APIs in the Cloud Run service running their processes by using the service accounts attached to their service.

questions.explanation:
Service-account-based authentication is suited to microservice communication, and Cloud Run services can use their attached service identities rather than distributing shared credentials. Assigning each calling service account access to the APIs provides distinct, manageable identities while avoiding exported service-account keys and shared API keys. API keys are primarily used to identify a Google Cloud project for quota, billing, and monitoring, not as the preferred mechanism for securing service-to-service access.

**Learn more:** [Choosing an Authentication Method | API Gateway](https://cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/authentication-method) · [Authenticating service-to-service | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/authenticating/service-to-service)

A government regulation has recently been enacted that affects your application. To meet compliance requirements, you must now send a duplicate of specified application logs from your application’s project to a project restricted to the security team. What should you do?

options.text: Create user-defined log buckets in the security team’s project. Configure a Cloud Logging sink to route your application’s logs to log buckets in the security team’s project.
Create a job that copies the logs from the _Required log bucket into the security team’s log bucket in their project.
Modify the _Default log bucket sink rules to reroute the logs into the security team’s log bucket.
Create a job that copies the System Event logs from the _Required log bucket into the security team’s log bucket in their project.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging sinks can route selected log entries from a source project to a log bucket in a different project. A user-defined log bucket in the security team’s project, combined with a sink in the application project that filters for the required logs, maintains the original logging while storing the required duplicate in the restricted project.

**Learn more:** [Route log entries | Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview) · [Route logs to supported destinations | Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Cloud Build to build a Docker image. You need to update the build so that it executes unit and integration tests. If a failure occurs, you want Build History to clearly show the stage where the build failed.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Add RUN commands in the Dockerfile to execute unit and integration tests.
Create a Cloud Build build config file with a single build step to compile unit and integration tests.
Create a Cloud Build build config file that will spawn a separate cloud build pipeline for unit and integration tests.
Create a Cloud Build build config file with separate cloud builder steps to compile and execute unit and integration tests.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build executes a build as a sequence of build steps and records an individual status for each step. Separate builder steps for compiling and running unit and integration tests make the failing stage visible in Build History, rather than combining all test activity into the Docker image build or one undifferentiated step.

**Learn more:** [View build results](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/view-build-results?hl=en) · [Configuring the order of build steps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/configuring-builds/configure-build-step-order)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a Python application to Cloud Run by using Cloud Source Repositories and Cloud Build. The Cloud Build pipeline is shown below:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783709004295-sj1b1np5.png)  
  
You want to optimize deployment time and avoid unnecessary steps. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the step that pushes the container to Artifact Registry.
Deploy a new Docker registry in a VPC, and use Cloud Build worker pools inside the VPC to run the build pipeline.
Store image artifacts in a Cloud Storage bucket in the same region as the Cloud Run instance.
Add the --cache-from argument to the Docker build step in your build config file.

questions.explanation:
Docker image layers can be reused across builds by specifying a previously built image as the cache source with `--cache-from`. This reduces rebuilding of unchanged layers and speeds subsequent Docker builds. The image must still be pushed to Artifact Registry because Cloud Run deploys the container image from that registry. [Best practices for speeding up builds](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/speeding-up-builds)

**Learn more:** [Best practices for speeding up builds | Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/speeding-up-builds)

You plan to use A/B testing to determine, in a randomized manner, the new algorithm’s effect on sales. How should you test this feature?

options.text: Split traffic between versions using weights.
Enable the new recommendation feature flag on a single instance.
Mirror traffic to the new version of your application.
Use HTTP header-based routing.

Google Cloud documents weight-based traffic splitting as a traffic-management capability for global external Application Load Balancers and identifies A/B testing as a typical use case.

You are building a web application that runs on a Compute Engine instance and writes a file to each user's Google Drive. You need to configure the application to authenticate with the Google Drive API. What should you do?

options.text: Use an OAuth Client ID that uses the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope to obtain an access token for each user.
Use an OAuth Client ID with delegated domain-wide authority.
Use the App Engine service account and https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope to generate a signed JSON Web Token (JWT).
Use the App Engine service account with delegated domain-wide authority.

questions.explanation:
OAuth 2.0 user authorization is required to access an individual user's Google Drive. The `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file` scope permits an app to see, edit, create, and delete the specific Drive files it uses. Domain-wide delegation instead requires a Google Workspace administrator and applies to users within that Workspace domain, while service accounts alone do not access users' Google Workspace data.

**Learn more:** [Choose Google Drive API scopes](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/api-specific-auth) · [Learn about authentication and authorization](https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/auth-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for deploying a new API. The API will have three distinct URL paths:  
  
- https://yourcompany.com/students  
- https://yourcompany.com/teachers  
- https://yourcompany.com/classes  
  
You must configure each API URL path to invoke a different function in your code. What should you do?

options.text: Create one Cloud Function as a backend service exposed using an HTTPS load balancer.
Create three Cloud Functions exposed directly.
Create one Cloud Function exposed directly.
Create three Cloud Functions as three backend services exposed using an HTTPS load balancer.

questions.explanation:
An HTTPS Application Load Balancer uses a URL map and path rules to send requests for distinct paths to specific backend services. Each backend service can target a separate serverless Cloud Function, allowing `/students`, `/teachers`, and `/classes` to invoke different functions while sharing the same custom HTTPS domain.

**Learn more:** [Serverless network endpoint groups overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/negs/serverless-neg-concepts?hl=en) · [Use URL maps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/url-map)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new web application with Cloud Run and committing code to Cloud Source Repositories. You want to deploy new code as efficiently as possible. You have already created a Cloud Build YAML file that builds a container and runs the following command: `gcloud run deploy`. What should you do next?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub topic to be notified when code is pushed to the repository. Create a Pub/Sub trigger that runs the build file when an event is published to the topic.
Create a build trigger that runs the build file in response to a repository code being pushed to the development branch.
Create a webhook build trigger that runs the build file in response to HTTP POST calls to the webhook URL.
Create a Cron job that runs the following command every 24 hours: gcloud builds submit.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Build trigger configured for pushes to the development branch automatically invokes the build configuration whenever new code is committed. The build can build the container and run `gcloud run deploy`, providing continuous deployment directly from Cloud Source Repositories.

**Learn more:** [Automating builds with Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/source-repositories/docs/integrating-with-cloud-build) · [Create and manage build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a containerized application on Google Kubernetes Engine, with container images stored in Container Registry. Your team follows CI/CD practices. You must prevent containers that have known critical vulnerabilities from being deployed. What should you do?

options.text: • Use Web Security Scanner to automatically crawl your application• Review your application logs for scan results, and provide an attestation that the container is free of known critical vulnerabilities• Use Binary Authorization to implement a policy that forces the attestation to be provided before the container is deployed

• Use Web Security Scanner to automatically crawl your application• Review the scan results in the scan details page in the Cloud Console, and provide an attestation that the container is free of known critical vulnerabilities• Use Binary Authorization to implement a policy that forces the attestation to be provided before the container is deployed

• Enable the Container Scanning API to perform vulnerability scanning• Review vulnerability reporting in Container Registry in the Cloud Console, and provide an attestation that the container is free of known critical vulnerabilities• Use Binary Authorization to implement a policy that forces the attestation to be provided before the container is deployed

• Enable the Container Scanning API to perform vulnerability scanning• Programmatically review vulnerability reporting through the Container Scanning API, and provide an attestation that the container is free of known critical vulnerabilities• Use Binary Authorization to implement a policy that forces the attestation to be provided before the container is deployed

questions.explanation:
Container Analysis vulnerability scanning provides vulnerability findings for container images, and its API enables a CI/CD pipeline to evaluate those findings programmatically. The pipeline can issue an attestation only for an image with no known critical vulnerabilities. A Binary Authorization policy can require that attestation before GKE allows deployment, thereby blocking noncompliant images.

**Learn more:** [Container scanning overview | Artifact Analysis](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/container-scanning-overview) · [Attestations overview | Binary Authorization](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations)

You are building a new mobile game that will be deployed on GKE and Cloud Run as a collection of microservices. At present, there are no forecasts for the game’s user volume.  
  
You need to store these data types:  
  
- Data type 1: leaderboard data  
- Data type 2: player profiles, chats, and news feed  
- Data type 3: player clickstream data for BI  
  
You must identify a data-storage solution that is easy to use, cost-effective, scalable, and supports offline caching on the user’s device. Which data storage option should you select for the different data types?

options.text: • Data type 1: Memorystore• Data type 2: Firestore• Data type 3: BigQuery
• Data type 1: Memorystore• Data type 2: Spanner• Data type 3: Bigtable
• Data type 1: Firestore• Data type 2: Cloud SQL• Data type 3: BigQuery
• Data type 1: Firestore• Data type 2: Firestore• Data type 3: BigQuery

questions.explanation:
Memorystore for Redis provides low-latency in-memory storage and Redis sorted sets for maintaining game leaderboards. Firestore supports mobile-client offline persistence, caching actively used data on the device and synchronizing local changes after reconnection, which suits player profiles, chats, and news feeds. BigQuery is optimized for large-scale analytical queries, making it suitable for BI analysis of clickstream data.

**Learn more:** [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview) · [Enable offline data — Firestore in Native mode](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/manage-data/enable-offline)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a social media company. The company operates its social media website on-premises and uses MySQL as the backend for storing user profiles and user posts. Your company plans to migrate to Google Cloud, and your team will migrate user profile information to Firestore. You are responsible for designing the Firestore collections. What should you do?

options.text: Create one root collection for user profiles, and create one root collection for user posts.
Create one root collection for user profiles, and create one subcollection for each user's posts.
Create one root collection for user profiles, and store each user's post as a nested list in the user profile document.
Create one root collection for user posts, and create one subcollection for each user's profile.

questions.explanation:
User posts are a potentially large, growing set of records that naturally belong to an individual user profile. Cloud Firestore subcollections associate a collection with a specific document and are the scalable structure for this type of hierarchical data; storing all posts as a nested list would cause the profile document to grow. [Choose a data structure | Firestore](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/manage-data/structure-data?hl=en)

**Learn more:** [Choose a data structure | Firestore](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/manage-data/structure-data?hl=en) · [Cloud Firestore Data model](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/data-model)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application hosted on Google Cloud that uses a MySQL relational database schema. The application will generate a high volume of database reads and writes and will need backups and continuing capacity planning. Your team lacks time to fully manage the database but can handle minor administrative tasks. How should the database be hosted?

options.text: Configure Cloud SQL to host the database, and import the schema into Cloud SQL.
Deploy MySQL from the Google Cloud Marketplace to the database using a client, and import the schema.
Configure Bigtable to host the database, and import the data into Bigtable.
Configure Cloud Spanner to host the database, and import the schema into Cloud Spanner.
Configure Firestore to host the database, and import the data into Firestore.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL is a fully managed relational database service. It supports MySQL schemas while reducing database-administration work, and provides managed backup and capacity capabilities appropriate for an application with substantial read and write activity.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/introduction) · [Cloud SQL backups overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backups)

You recently migrated a monolithic application to Google Cloud by decomposing it into microservices. One microservice is deployed with Cloud Functions. While modernizing the application, you make a backward-incompatible change to the service API. You must support both existing callers that use the original API and new callers that use the new API. What should you do?

options.text: Leave the original Cloud Function as-is and deploy a second Cloud Function with the new API. Use a load balancer to distribute calls between the versions.
Leave the original Cloud Function as-is and deploy a second Cloud Function that includes only the changed API. Calls are automatically routed to the correct function.
Leave the original Cloud Function as-is and deploy a second Cloud Function with the new API. Use Cloud Endpoints to provide an API gateway that exposes a versioned API.
Re-deploy the Cloud Function after making code changes to support the new API. Requests for both versions of the API are fulfilled based on a version identifier included in the call.

questions.explanation:
For backward-incompatible API changes, separate major API versions should be served concurrently so callers can select the version they use while migrating. Cloud Endpoints can expose versioned API paths and manage multiple major versions concurrently, routing each versioned request to its appropriate implementation. [Versioning an API | Cloud Endpoints](https://cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/versioning-an-api)

**Learn more:** [Versioning an API | Cloud Endpoints](https://cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/versioning-an-api)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your development team is responsible for maintaining a legacy .NET application. The application receives occasional changes and was recently updated. Your objective is to ensure that it produces consistent results as it progresses through the CI/CD pipeline from one environment to another. You want to minimize deployment cost while ensuring that external factors and dependencies among hosting environments do not cause issues. Containers have not yet been approved in your organization. What should you do?

options.text: Rewrite the application using .NET Core, and deploy to Cloud Run. Use revisions to separate the environments.
Use Cloud Build to deploy the application as a new Compute Engine image for each build. Use this image in each environment.
Deploy the application using MS Web Deploy, and make sure to always use the latest, patched MS Windows Server base image in Compute Engine.
Use Cloud Build to package the application, and deploy to a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Use namespaces to separate the environments.

questions.explanation:
A custom Compute Engine VM image can include the application, its configuration, and all required dependencies, so the identical immutable artifact can be promoted through every environment. This avoids configuration drift and reliance on separately provisioned hosting dependencies, while retaining a Windows-compatible deployment model for a legacy .NET application. Google Cloud describes this CI/CD approach as image baking: install the application on a VM, create a custom VM image, and reference that image in an instance template.

**Learn more:** [Deploying .NET apps on Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dotnet/docs/deploy-dotnet-applications)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a public web application on Cloud Run and expose the Cloud Run service directly through its public IP address. You are now conducting a load test to confirm that the application remains resilient under high traffic loads. You observe that the application performs as expected under light traffic. However, when you generate heavy loads, the web server becomes slow and returns error messages. How should you troubleshoot this problem?

options.text: Check the network traffic to Cloud Run in Cloud Monitoring to validate whether a traffic spike occurred. If necessary, enable traffic splitting on the Cloud Run instance to route some of the traffic to a previous instance revision.
Check the min-instances value for your Cloud Run service. If necessary, increase the min-instances value to match the maximum number of virtual users in your load test.

Check whether Cloud Armor is detecting distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks and is blocking traffic before the traffic is routed to your Cloud Run service. If necessary, disable any Cloud Armor policies in your project.
Check whether the Cloud Run service has scaled to a number of instances that equals the max-instances value. If necessary, increase the max-instances value.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run normally adds instances as request load increases, but a configured maximum-instance limit can prevent further scale-out. Once all permitted instances are busy, new inbound requests may wait for an available instance and fail if capacity does not become available. Checking the instance-count metric and increasing `max-instances` when the service is at that limit addresses this capacity constraint.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot Cloud Run issues](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/troubleshooting?hl=en) · [About maximum instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances-limits)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a mix of packaged and internally developed applications hosted on a Linux Compute Engine instance. These applications write text log records to local files. You want the logs to be sent to Cloud Logging. What should you do?

options.text: Pipe the content of the files to the Linux Syslog daemon.
Install a Google version of fluentd on the Compute Engine instance.
Install a Google version of collectd on the Compute Engine instance.
Using cron, schedule a job to copy the log files to Cloud Storage once a day.

questions.explanation:
The Google Cloud Logging agent, `google-fluentd`, is a Google-packaged Fluentd log collector for Compute Engine. It can read log records from local files and send them to Cloud Logging. `collectd` is for metrics collection, while copying files to Cloud Storage does not write them to Cloud Logging.

**Learn more:** [About the Logging agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging) · [Configure the Logging agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/configuration)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Cloud Run to host a web application. You need to securely retrieve the application project ID and the region in which the application is running, then display this information to users. You want the most performant approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use HTTP requests to query the available metadata server at the http://metadata.google.internal/ endpoint with the Metadata-Flavor: Google header.

In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Project Dashboard and gather configuration details. Navigate to the Cloud Run “Variables & Secrets” tab, and add the desired environment variables in Key:Value format.
In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Project Dashboard and gather configuration details. Write the application configuration information to Cloud Run's in-memory container filesystem.
Make an API call to the Cloud Asset Inventory API from the application and format the request to include instance metadata.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run’s instance metadata server supplies runtime details including the project ID and region. Accessing `http://metadata.google.internal/` with the `Metadata-Flavor: Google` header retrieves this information directly from within the running container, without requiring a separate Google Cloud API call or manually maintained configuration.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run container runtime contract — instance metadata server](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/container-contract#metadata-server)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a large organization deploying a web application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The DevOps team has created a CI/CD pipeline that uses Cloud Deploy to deploy the application to Dev, Test, and Prod GKE clusters. After Cloud Deploy successfully deploys the application to the Dev cluster, you want it to be automatically promoted to the Test cluster. How should you configure this process according to Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: 1. Create a Cloud Build trigger that listens for SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the clouddeploy-operations topic.2. Configure Cloud Build to include a step that promotes the application to the Test cluster.

1. Create a Cloud Function that calls the Google Cloud Deploy API to promote the application to the Test cluster.2. Configure this function to be triggered by SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the cloud-builds topic.

1. Create a Cloud Function that calls the Google Cloud Deploy API to promote the application to the Test cluster.2. Configure this function to be triggered by SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the clouddeploy-operations topic.

1. Create a Cloud Build pipeline that uses the gke-deploy builder.2. Create a Cloud Build trigger that listens for SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the cloud-builds topic.3. Configure this pipeline to run a deployment step to the Test cluster.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deploy publishes successful deployment and rollout operation notifications to the `clouddeploy-operations` Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Function subscribed to that topic can use the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release, which creates the rollout for the next target in the delivery pipeline progression.

**Learn more:** [Integrating Cloud Deploy with other systems](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/integrating) · [Using Cloud Deploy notifications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/subscribe-deploy-notifications)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to migrate a standalone Java application that runs on an on-premises Linux virtual machine (VM) to Google Cloud cost-effectively. You choose not to use a lift-and-shift approach; instead, you plan to modernize the application by converting it into a container. How should you complete this task?

options.text: Use Migrate for Anthos to migrate the VM to your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster as a container.
Export the VM as a raw disk and import it as an image. Create a Compute Engine instance from the Imported image.
Use Migrate for Compute Engine to migrate the VM to a Compute Engine instance, and use Cloud Build to convert it to a container.
Use Jib to build a Docker image from your source code, and upload it to Artifact Registry. Deploy the application in a GKE cluster, and test the application.

questions.explanation:
Jib builds a container image directly from Java source and build metadata, making it suitable for containerizing a standalone Java application. The image can be stored in Artifact Registry and deployed to GKE, which runs containerized workloads. VM migration or importing a VM disk retains the VM-based deployment model rather than modernizing the application into a container.

**Learn more:** [Introducing Jib — build Java Docker images better](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/application-development/introducing-jib-build-java-docker-images-better) · [Deploying to Google Kubernetes Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/integrate-gke)

questions.question:
You are operating an App Engine application that you inherited. You want to determine whether the application uses insecure binaries or is susceptible to XSS attacks.  
  
Which service should you use?

options.text: Cloud Amor
Stackdriver Debugger
Cloud Security Scanner
Stackdriver Error Reporting

questions.explanation:
Cloud Security Scanner identifies common security vulnerabilities in App Engine web applications, including cross-site scripting (XSS) and outdated or insecure libraries.\
\
**Learn more:** [Overview of Web Security Scanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-web-security-scanner-overview?hl=en) · [Implement shift-left security](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/implement-shift-left-security)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
You are operating an App Engine application that you inherited. You want to determine whether the application uses insecure binaries or is susceptible to XSS attacks.  
  
Which service should you use?

options.text: The folder structure inside the bucket and object paths have changed.
The permissions of the service account’s predefined role have changed.
The service account key has been rotated but not updated on the application server.
The Interconnect link from the on-premises data center to Google Cloud is experiencing a temporary outage.

questions.explanation:
A 403 Permission Denied response specifically indicates the caller was authenticated successfully but lacks sufficient IAM permissions on the resource; an invalid or rotated-out key instead fails authentication itself, which Cloud Storage surfaces as a 401 Unauthorized (invalid/expired credential), not a 403. Since the request in this scenario returns 403, the more consistent cause is that the permissions granted by the service account's predefined role were changed, not a stale key.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage troubleshooting](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/troubleshooting) · [JSON API status codes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/status-codes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a Java web server that must interact with Google Cloud services through the Google Cloud API on a user's behalf. Users need to authenticate to the Google Cloud API with their Google Cloud identities. Which workflow should your web application implement?

options.text: 1. When a user arrives at your application, prompt them for their Google username and password.2. Store an SHA password hash in your application's database along with the user's username.3. The application authenticates to the Google Cloud API using HTTPs requests with the user's username and password hash in the Authorization request header.

1. When a user arrives at your application, prompt them for their Google username and password.2. Forward the user's username and password in an HTTPS request to the Google Cloud authorization server, and request an access token.3. The Google server validates the user's credentials and returns an access token to the application.4. The application uses the access token to call the Google Cloud API.

1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to a Google Cloud consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account.2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server.3. The Google server returns the authorization code to the user, which is stored in the browser's cookies.4. The user authenticates to the Google Cloud API using the authorization code in the cookie.

1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to a Google Cloud consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account.2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server.3. The application requests a Google Server to exchange the authorization code with an access token.4. The Google server responds with the access token that is used by the application to call the Google Cloud API.

questions.explanation:
Google web-server applications use the OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow for user-delegated API access: redirect the user to Google to authenticate and grant the requested scopes, receive the authorization code at the application’s redirect endpoint, exchange that code with Google’s authorization server for an access token, and use the token to call the API. User passwords must not be collected or forwarded by the application, and an authorization code is not used directly as an API credential.

**Learn more:** [Using OAuth 2.0 for Web Server Applications](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server) · [Using OAuth 2.0 to Access Google APIs](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2)

Your application is built as a custom machine image. You have multiple distinct deployments of that machine image. Each deployment is a separate managed instance group with its own template. Each deployment needs a unique set of configuration values. You want to supply these unique values to every deployment while using the same custom machine image across all deployments. You want to use built-in Compute Engine features.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Place the unique configuration values in the persistent disk.
Place the unique configuration values in a Cloud Bigtable table.
Place the unique configuration values in the instance template startup script.
Place the unique configuration values in the instance template instance metadata.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine instance templates support custom instance metadata, and a managed instance group creates its VMs from its associated template. Setting deployment-specific configuration as metadata in each template preserves one shared custom image while making the appropriate values available to that deployment’s instances.

**Learn more:** [Create instance templates](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-templates/create-instance-templates?hl=en) · [Use startup scripts on Linux VMs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/startup-scripts/linux)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an ecommerce application that processes customer purchases, which customers can later cancel or modify. You find that order volumes vary greatly and that the backend order-processing system can handle only one request at a time. You want to provide seamless customer performance regardless of usage volume. Customer order-update requests must be processed in the order in which they were created. What should you do?

options.text: Send the purchase and change requests over WebSockets to the backend.
Send the purchase and change requests as REST requests to the backend.
Use a Pub/Sub subscriber in pull mode and use a data store to manage ordering.
Use a Pub/Sub subscriber in push mode and use a data store to manage ordering.

questions.explanation:
A Pub/Sub pull subscriber decouples incoming customer traffic from the single-request backend and lets that backend control the rate at which it receives work. Pub/Sub pull subscriptions provide subscriber-controlled flow control, and ordered processing requires tracking the related order state so updates can be applied sequentially. This accommodates traffic spikes without sending concurrent requests to the backend.

**Learn more:** [Choose a subscription type](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscriber) · [Order messages](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/ordering)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: You are deploying applications on Compute Engine. One of your Compute Engine instances did not launch. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Determine whether your file system is corrupted.
Access Compute Engine as a different SSH user.
Troubleshoot firewall rules or routes on an instance.
Check whether your instance boot disk is completely full.
Check whether network traffic to or from your instance is being dropped.

questions.explanation:
A VM cannot complete its boot process when its boot disk is completely full or when the disk’s file system is corrupted or otherwise invalid. Compute Engine startup troubleshooting specifically recommends verifying available boot-disk space and validating the disk file system for launch failures.\
\
**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting VM startup](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/vm-startup)

questions.question: You are deploying applications on Compute Engine. One of your Compute Engine instances did not launch. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Get the entity with an ancestor query.
Get and put the entity in a transaction.
Use a strongly consistent transactional database.
Don't return the account entity from the function.

questions.explanation:
A balance increment is a read-modify-write operation that must be atomic. Performing the entity lookup and update in a Cloud Datastore transaction provides serializable isolation and prevents concurrent requests from silently overwriting each other’s balance changes. [Cloud Datastore transactions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/concepts/transactions)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Datastore transactions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/concepts/transactions)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a financial institution who uses Cloud Shell to interact with Google Cloud services. User data is presently stored on an ephemeral disk; however, a newly enacted regulation requires that sensitive information no longer be stored on an ephemeral disk. You need to implement a new storage solution for the user data while minimizing code changes. Where should you store the user data?

options.text: Store user data on a Cloud Shell home disk, and log in at least every 120 days to prevent its deletion.
Store user data on a persistent disk in a Compute Engine instance.
Store user data in a Cloud Storage bucket.
Store user data in BigQuery tables.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Shell’s persistent home disk can be deleted after 120 days of inactivity. For sensitive data that must be retained long term, Google Cloud recommends a different solution on Cloud Storage. Cloud Storage provides durable persistent object storage without requiring a move to a Compute Engine-hosted disk or a BigQuery data-model change.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Shell quotas and limits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/shell/docs/quotas-limits)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is configuring a build pipeline for an application that will run in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). For security reasons, you want only images created by the pipeline to be deployed to your GKE cluster. Which combination of Google Cloud services should you use?

options.text: Cloud Build, Cloud Storage, and Binary Authorization
Google Cloud Deploy, Cloud Storage, and Google Cloud Armor
Google Cloud Deploy, Artifact Registry, and Google Cloud Armor
Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, and Binary Authorization

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can build container images and generate attestations, Artifact Registry securely stores those images, and Binary Authorization can enforce a GKE policy requiring the `built-by-cloud-build` attestation. This permits deployment only of images built by Cloud Build.

**Learn more:** [Securing image deployments to Cloud Run and Google Kubernetes Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/securing-builds/secure-deployments-to-run-gke) · [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an application that follows a microservices architecture. You plan to deploy the application both in the cloud and on-premises. You want to ensure that the application can scale up on demand while using managed services as much as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy open source Istio in a multi-cluster deployment on multiple Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters managed by Anthos.
Create a GKE cluster in each environment with Anthos, and use Cloud Run for Anthos to deploy your application to each cluster.
Install a GKE cluster in each environment with Anthos, and use Cloud Build to create a Deployment for your application in each cluster.
Create a GKE cluster in the cloud and install open-source Kubernetes on-premises. Use an external load balancer service to distribute traffic across the two environments.

questions.explanation:
Anthos enables consistent managed Kubernetes clusters across cloud and on-premises environments. Cloud Run for Anthos provides a serverless microservices deployment model on those clusters, including demand-driven autoscaling and reduced infrastructure-management overhead. This meets the hybrid deployment, scalability, and managed-services requirements.

**Learn more:** [Anthos simplifies application modernization with managed service mesh and serverless for your hybrid cloud](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/hybrid-cloud/anthos-simplifies-application-modernization-with-managed-service-mesh-and-serverless-for-your-hybrid-cloud) · [What’s new in Cloud Run for Anthos](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/serverless/new-features-in-cloud-run-for-anthos-ga)

Your team is building an ecommerce platform for your company. Users will sign in to the website and add products to their shopping cart. Users will be logged out automatically after 30 minutes of inactivity. When they sign in again, their shopping cart must be retained.  
  
How should users’ session and shopping-cart information be stored while following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Store the session information in Pub/Sub, and store the shopping cart information in Cloud SQL.
Store the shopping cart information in a file on Cloud Storage where the filename is the SESSION ID.
Store the session and shopping cart information in a MySQL database running on multiple Compute Engine instances.
Store the session information in Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached, and store the shopping cart information in Firestore.

questions.explanation:
Short-lived session state is well suited to the low-latency managed in-memory stores provided by Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached. A shopping cart that must survive logout and a subsequent login requires durable persistence; Firestore is a managed, persistent, distributed, transactional document database. This separates ephemeral session data from persistent cart data while avoiding self-managed database infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Caching data with Memorystore](https://docs.cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/using-memorystore) · [Handling sessions with Firestore](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nodejs/getting-started/session-handling-with-firestore)
