Use signed URLs to upload files.

Assign the IAM service account to the cluster’s node pool. Encrypt the IAM service account key file by using a symmetric block cipher, and store the encrypted file on a persistent volume. Store the encryption key in Secret Manager.

You are a developer building an internal payroll-processing application. You are creating a component that lets an employee submit a timesheet, which triggers several actions:  
  
- An email is sent to the employee and manager to notify them that the timesheet was submitted.  
- A timesheet is sent to payroll processing through the vendor's API.  
- A timesheet is sent to the data warehouse for headcount planning.  
  
These actions do not depend on one another and may finish in any order. Additional actions are under consideration and will be implemented by different development teams. Each team will implement error handling specific to its own action. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud Function for each step that calls the corresponding downstream system to complete the required action.
Create a Pub/Sub topic for each step. Create a subscription for each downstream development team to subscribe to their step's topic.
Create a Pub/Sub topic for timesheet submissions. Create a subscription for each downstream development team to subscribe to the topic.
Create a timesheet microservice deployed to Google Kubernetes Engine. The microservice calls each downstream step and waits for a successful response before calling the next step.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Pub/Sub is an asynchronous messaging service that decouples event producers from processing services. Publishing each timesheet-submitted event to one topic and creating one subscription per downstream team gives every subscriber its own copy of the event, allowing independent processing, retries, and error handling. Additional consumers can be added by attaching subscriptions without changing the timesheet-submission component.

**Learn more:** [Publish message overview | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/publish-message-overview) · [Subscription overview | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscription-overview)

Your API backend is deployed across multiple cloud providers. You want to produce reports on your API's network latency.  
  
Which two steps should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Zipkin collector to gather data.
Use Fluentd agent to gather data.
Use Stackdriver Trace to generate reports.
Use Stackdriver Debugger to generate report.
Use Stackdriver Profiler to generate report.

questions.explanation:
A Zipkin collector gathers distributed trace data, including timing information across API services. Stackdriver Trace, now called Cloud Trace, collects and displays application latency data and supports its analysis, so it can generate latency reports from that tracing data.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Trace overview](https://cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview) · [Trace labels](https://cloud.google.com/trace/docs/trace-labels)

Which two steps should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add the users to their projects, assign the relevant roles to the users, and then provide the users with each relevant Project ID.
Add the users to their projects, assign the relevant roles to the users, and then provide the users with each relevant Project Number.
Create groups, add the users to their groups, assign the relevant roles to the groups, and then provide the users with each relevant Project ID.
Create groups, add the users to their groups, assign the relevant roles to the groups, and then provide the users with each relevant Project Number.

questions.explanation:
Assigning IAM roles to Google Groups centralizes access administration and makes onboarding, offboarding, and team membership changes more efficient than assigning identical roles to individual users. The Google Cloud CLI uses the project ID as the project setting for local configurations, for example `gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID`; a project number is not the standard value for that setting.

**Learn more:** [gcloud config set](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/config/set) · [Recommended user groups and IAM roles](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/security-best-practices-catalog/recommended-iam-groups?hl=en)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your infrastructure team uses Terraform Cloud and manages Google Cloud resources with Terraform configuration files. You want to set up an infrastructure-as-code pipeline that authenticates to Google Cloud APIs. You want to use the most secure approach while minimizing configuration changes. How should you configure authentication?

options.text: Use Terraform on GKE. Create a Kubernetes service account to execute the Terraform code. Use workload identity federation to authenticate as the Google service account.
Install Terraform on a Compute Engine VM. Configure the VM by using a service account that has the required permissions to manage the Google Cloud resources.
Configure Terraform Cloud to use workload identity federation to authenticate to the Google Cloud APIs.

Create a service account that has the required permissions to manage the Google Cloud resources, and import the service account key to Terraform Cloud. Use this service account to authenticate to the Google Cloud APIs.

questions.explanation:
Terraform Cloud can provide an OIDC token that identifies its workspace and environment. Workload Identity Federation lets Google Cloud exchange that external identity for short-lived credentials, avoiding the security risk of importing and managing a long-lived service-account key. Google Cloud specifically documents enabling Workload Identity Federation for HCP Terraform workspaces.

**Learn more:** [Configure Workload Identity Federation with deployment pipelines](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-deployment-pipelines) · [Authentication for Terraform](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/authentication)

questions.question: You are operating an inherited web application on Google Kubernetes Engine. You want to find out whether the application uses libraries with known vulnerabilities or has XSS vulnerabilities. Which service should you use?

Debugger

options.text: The final step uses a Cloud Run instance name that does not match the container name. Update the deployment step so that the Cloud Run instance name matches the container name, and rerun the pipeline.
The Docker container image has not been pushed to Artifact Registry. Add a step to the pipeline to push the application container image to Artifact Registry, and rerun the pipeline.
Cloud Run does not allow unauthenticated invocations. Remove the --allow-unauthenticated parameter to enforce authentication on the application, and rerun the pipeline.
Unit tests in the pipeline are failing. Update the application code so that all unit tests pass, and rerun the pipeline.

questions.explanation:
A Docker build creates the tagged image only in the Cloud Build worker unless the configuration also pushes it or declares it in the `images` field. Cloud Run must be able to retrieve the referenced image from Artifact Registry, so the pipeline must push the application image to Artifact Registry before running `gcloud run deploy`.

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are preparing a compliance report on vulnerability metadata for a particular set of images identified by Artifact Analysis. Metadata for images scanned more than 30 days ago is absent from the compliance report. You must access vulnerability metadata for these older images. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub subscription to pull from Artifact Analysis topics.
Check Artifact Analysis storage buckets in Cloud Storage.
Push or pull the images from Artifact Registry.
Check Cloud Trace logs for Artifact Analysis findings.

questions.explanation:
Artifact Analysis stops updating vulnerability metadata after an image has not been pulled for 30 days. Pulling or pushing the image through Artifact Registry reactivates the monitoring window and enables refreshed vulnerability metadata to be produced. [Enable or disable automatic scanning](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/enable-automatic-scanning)

**Learn more:** [Enable or disable automatic scanning | Artifact Analysis](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/enable-automatic-scanning) · [Investigate vulnerabilities | Artifact Analysis](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/investigate-vulnerabilities)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s development teams want to use different open-source operating systems in their Docker builds. When images are created in published containers in your company’s environment, they must be scanned for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). The scanning process must not affect software-development agility. You want to use managed services where possible. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the Vulnerability scanning setting in the Container Registry.
Create a Cloud Function that is triggered on a code check-in and scan the code for CVEs.
Disallow the use of non-commercially supported base images in your development environment.
Use Cloud Monitoring to review the output of Cloud Build to determine whether a vulnerable version has been used.

questions.explanation:
Registry-integrated vulnerability scanning provides managed, automatic vulnerability analysis of container images when they are published, identifying CVEs in supported OS and language packages without requiring developers to build or maintain custom scanning automation. Google Cloud documents this capability as automatic scanning for images pushed to its container artifact registry.

**Learn more:** [Container scanning overview — Artifact Analysis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/container-scanning-overview) · [Transition from Container Registry — Artifact Registry](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/transition/transition-from-gcr)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You built a JavaScript web application that must access the Google Drive API and receive users’ permission to store files in their Google Drives. You need to choose an authorization approach for the application. What should you do?

options.text: Create an API key.
Create a SAML token.
Create a service account.
Create an OAuth Client ID.

questions.explanation:
Delegated access to a user's Google Drive requires OAuth 2.0 user authorization and the applicable Drive scope. A JavaScript web application must be registered with Google using an OAuth client ID so it can request consent and obtain access tokens on the user's behalf. API keys do not grant access to private user data, while service accounts authenticate an application identity rather than obtaining individual users' consent.

**Learn more:** [Using OAuth 2.0 to Access Google APIs](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2) · [OAuth 2.0 for Client-side Web Applications](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/javascript-implicit-flow)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a containerized application to GKE. You have configured a Cloud Build build pipeline that builds a Java application and pushes the application container image to Artifact Registry. Your build pipeline runs multiple sequential steps that reference Docker container images with identical layers.  
  
You observe that the Cloud Build pipeline runs take longer than expected to finish. How should you optimize the Docker image build process?

options.text: Add the --squash parameter to the Docker build steps to combine newly built layers into a single layer.
Configure Cloud Build to use a private pool in your VPC for pipeline executions.
Specify the cached image by adding the --cache-from argument in your build config file with the image as a cache source.
Store container artifacts on Cloud Storage. Configure Cloud CDN on the Cloud Storage bucket to enable caching on edge locations.

questions.explanation:
A previously built Docker image can be used as a cache source with `--cache-from`, allowing Docker to reuse unchanged stacked layers and rebuild only from the first changed layer onward. Cloud Build documents this as the simplest way to speed subsequent Docker image builds.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for speeding up builds | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/speeding-up-builds)

Using Cloud Build, execute a Terraform script to deploy a new Cloud Run revision in the existing Google Cloud project. Use traffic splitting to send traffic to your test environment.
Using Cloud Build, execute gcloud commands to create a new Google Cloud project and a Cloud Run instance of your application in the Google Cloud project.
Using Cloud Build, execute gcloud commands to deploy a new Cloud Run revision in the existing Google Cloud project. Use traffic splitting to send traffic to your test environment.

questions.explanation:
A fresh Google Cloud project isolates test resources from production. Terraform defines the project and Cloud Run infrastructure declaratively and reproducibly, while Cloud Build automates applying that configuration. Google Cloud recommends creating a fresh project or folder for each test when isolation from production is required, and Terraform supports repeatable test and production environments.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for testing Terraform on Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/testing) · [Infrastructure as Code on Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/iac-overview)

HipLocal wants to increase the resilience of its MySQL deployment while continuing to meet its business and technical requirements.  
  
Which configuration should it select?

options.text: Use the current single instance MySQL on Compute Engine and several read-only MySQL servers on Compute Engine.
Use the current single instance MySQL on Compute Engine, and replicate the data to Cloud SQL in an external master configuration.
Replace the current single instance MySQL instance with Cloud SQL, and configure high availability.
Replace the current single instance MySQL instance with Cloud SQL, and Google provides redundancy without further configuration.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL is a fully managed MySQL service that reduces database administration. Configuring it for high availability creates a regional deployment with redundant capacity across zones and automatic failover, protecting the database from zonal and instance failures. High availability is an explicit configuration; a standard Cloud SQL instance is otherwise zonal and does not automatically recover from a zonal outage.

**Learn more:** [Availability in Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/availability) · [Configure high availability for Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-ha)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an external-facing application on GKE that offers users a streaming API. You want to provide two subscription tiers, “basic” and “premium,” based on how many API requests each client application may make per day. You want to design the application architecture to provide user subscription tiers while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to an Apigee proxy.2. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.3. Configure a Quota policy in Apigee for API keys based on the subscription tier.

1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to an Apigee proxy.2. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.3. Configure a SpikeArrest policy in Apigee for API keys based on the subscription tier.
1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to two new projects, each with a separate Application Load Balancer.2. Configure the quota

1. Deploy the application to two GKE clusters, one for each subscription tier. Configure each cluster to have a separate Ingress.2. Configure each cluster as a backend to an Apigee proxy.3. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.4. Configure separate rate limits for client applications based on the subscription tier.

questions.explanation:
Apigee’s Quota policy enforces consumption limits for identifiable client applications over intervals such as a day. API keys identify the client application, allowing quota settings to vary by subscription tier. SpikeArrest is intended to protect a backend from short-term traffic surges, not to enforce daily subscription entitlements.

**Learn more:** [Apigee Quota policy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/policies/quota-policy) · [Apigee rate limiting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/develop/rate-limiting)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to deploy hundreds of microservices in your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. How should communication between the GKE microservices be secured by using a managed service?

options.text: Use global HTTP(S) Load Balancing with managed SSL certificates to protect your services
Deploy open source Istio in your GKE cluster, and enable mTLS in your Service Mesh
Install cert-manager on GKE to automatically renew the SSL certificates.
Install Anthos Service Mesh, and enable mTLS in your Service Mesh.

questions.explanation:
Anthos Service Mesh—now called Cloud Service Mesh—is Google Cloud’s managed, Istio-based service mesh. It can enforce mutual TLS (mTLS) for service-to-service traffic, providing mesh-wide encryption and workload authentication without requiring each microservice to implement it. Open-source Istio is not the managed offering.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Service Mesh by example: mTLS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/tutorials/mtls) · [Provision managed Cloud Service Mesh on a GKE cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/managed/install-anthos-service-mesh-console)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running on Cloud Run that handles a high volume of traffic. You need to deploy a new version of the application. You want the deployment process to reduce the risk of downtime while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Run emulator to test changes locally before deploying the new version of the application to the production Cloud Run service.

Use Cloud Build to create a pipeline, and configure a test stage before the deployment stage. When all tests pass, deploy the application to Cloud Run, and direct 100% of users to this new version of the application. Roll back if any issues are detected.

Use Cloud Load Balancing to route a percentage of production traffic to a separate Cloud Run service running the new version of the application. If performance meets expectations, gradually increase the percentage of users until the new Cloud Run service reaches 100%.

Use traffic splitting to have a small percentage of users test out new features on the new revision of the application on the production Cloud Run service. If performance meets expectations, gradually increase the percentage of users until it reaches 100%.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run supports gradual rollouts through traffic splitting between revisions of the same service. Routing a small share of production traffic to a new revision, validating its performance, and progressively increasing that share reduces the impact of faults while retaining the existing revision for rollback.

**Learn more:** [Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

You recently deployed an Apigee API proxy for your organization in two regions. Each region is configured with a separate backend that hosts the API. You need to configure Apigee so that traffic is routed to the appropriate local-region backend. What should you do?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783712144966-iktmalj6.png)

options.text: Create a TargetEndpoint with a weighted load balancing algorithm. Configure the API proxy to use the same weights for each region's backend.

Configure a regional internal Application Load Balancer in each region, and use health checks to verify that each backend is active. Create a DNS A record that contains the IP addresses of both regions' load balancers. Configure a Targetserver for each region that uses this DNS name.

Configure a global external Application Load Balancer and configure each region’s backend with a different regional backend service. Each region communicates to this single global external Application Load Balancer as its TargetServer.
Configure a TargetServer for each region's backend host names. Configure the API proxy to choose the TargetServer based on the system.region.name flow variable.

questions.explanation:
`system.region.name` identifies the data-center region in which an Apigee proxy is running. Using it to select between TargetServers whose host names correspond to the two regional backends ensures that each runtime region sends requests to its local backend.

**Learn more:** [Apigee flow variables reference](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/variables-reference) · [Understanding routes in Apigee](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/fundamentals/understanding-routes)

Your company has a BigQuery dataset called "Master" that stores employee travel and expense information. The information is arranged by employee department, so employees must be able to view only the information for their own department. You want to apply a security framework that enforces this requirement with the fewest steps.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate dataset for each department. Create a view with an appropriate WHERE clause to select records from a particular dataset for the specific department. Authorize this view to access records from your Master dataset. Give employees the permission to this department-specific dataset.

Create a separate dataset for each department. Create a data pipeline for each department to copy appropriate information from the Master dataset to the specific dataset for the department. Give employees the permission to this department-specific dataset.
Create a dataset named Master dataset. Create a separate view for each department in the Master dataset. Give employees access to the specific view for their department.
Create a dataset named Master dataset. Create a separate table for each department in the Master dataset. Give employees access to the specific table for their department.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery authorized views let specific users or groups query a defined subset of data without receiving access to the underlying source dataset. A department-specific view with a `WHERE` filter, authorized to read the Master dataset and shared through a department dataset, restricts each department to its own rows without duplicating the data.

**Learn more:** [Authorized views | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/authorized-views) · [Create an authorized view | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/create-authorized-views)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The web application is deployed on the corporate intranet, and you need to migrate it to Google Cloud. It must be available only to company employees and remain accessible while they travel. You need to ensure the web application's security and accessibility while minimizing application changes. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the application to check authentication credentials for each HTTP(S) request to the application.
Configure Identity-Aware Proxy to allow employees to access the application through its public IP address.

Configure a Compute Engine instance that requests users to log in to their corporate account. Change the web application DNS to point to the proxy Compute Engine instance. After authenticating, the Compute Engine instance forwards requests to and from the web application.

Configure a Compute Engine instance that requests users to log in to their corporate account. Change the web application DNS to point to the proxy Compute Engine instance. After authenticating, the Compute Engine issues an HTTP redirect to a public IP address hosting the web application.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy centrally authenticates users and authorizes access to HTTPS applications using IAM, so access can be limited to company employees without changing the application to implement authentication or deploying a custom proxy. It supports identity-based application access without requiring users to connect through a VPN.

**Learn more:** [Identity-Aware Proxy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview) · [Identity-Aware Proxy documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team builds services that run on Google Cloud. You want to process messages sent to a Pub/Sub topic and then store them. Every message must be processed exactly once to prevent duplicate data and data conflicts. You need the cheapest and simplest solution. What should you do?

options.text: Process the messages with a Dataproc job, and write the output to storage.
Process the messages with a Dataflow streaming pipeline using Apache Beam's PubSubIO package, and write the output to storage.
Process the messages with a Cloud Function, and write the results to a BigQuery location where you can run a job to deduplicate the data.
Retrieve the messages with a Dataflow streaming pipeline, store them in Cloud Bigtable, and use another Dataflow streaming pipeline to deduplicate messages.

questions.explanation:
Dataflow streaming pipelines use exactly-once processing by default. When Pub/Sub is the source, Apache Beam's PubsubIO integration uses Pub/Sub message identities and Dataflow deduplication mechanisms to support exactly-once message processing. This avoids the cost and operational complexity of storing records and running a separate deduplication pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Exactly-once in Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/exactly-once) · [Read from Pub/Sub to Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-with-cloud-pubsub)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application with App Engine and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Before deploying new application versions to the development environment shared by other developers, you want to test the application code locally.  
  
You need to configure your App Engine local development environment to test the application while ensuring that all traffic to Cloud SQL instances remains encrypted and is authenticated to Cloud IAM and PostgreSQL. What should you do before you start the local development server?

options.text: Install PostgreSQL on your local workstation. Run a local PostgreSQL database on your workstation. Configure the application to connect to a PostgreSQL instance on localhost.

Download and install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to your local development environment. Configure the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to connect to the Cloud SQL instance and run the proxy. Configure the application to connect to a PostgreSQL instance on localhost.

Deploy a Compute Engine instance, and install HAProxy on the instance. Configure Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on the instance, and use the instance’s service account to authenticate to Cloud SQL. Configure the application to connect to the Compute Engine instance's IP address.

Configure your local development server to connect to the private IP address of the Cloud SQL instance. Encrypt database entries with a cryptographic library before submitting them to the database. Store the decryption key as an environment variable in App Engine.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy runs locally, authenticates to Google Cloud with IAM credentials, and creates an authorized TLS-encrypted connection to the Cloud SQL instance. The local application connects through the proxy’s localhost endpoint using the normal PostgreSQL protocol, while the proxy securely forwards traffic to Cloud SQL.

**Learn more:** [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/sql-proxy) · [Connect using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/connect-auth-proxy?hl=en)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application is managed by a managed instance group. You need to share a large read-only data set across every instance in the managed instance group. You want to ensure that every instance starts quickly and can access the data set through its filesystem with very low latency. You also want to minimize the solution’s total cost.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Move the data to a Cloud Storage bucket, and mount the bucket on the filesystem using Cloud Storage FUSE.
Move the data to a Cloud Storage bucket, and copy the data to the boot disk of the instance via a startup script.
Move the data to a Compute Engine persistent disk, and attach the disk in read-only mode to multiple Compute Engine virtual machine instances.
Move the data to a Compute Engine persistent disk, take a snapshot, create multiple disks from the snapshot, and attach each disk to its own instance.

questions.explanation:
A Compute Engine persistent disk can be attached simultaneously to multiple VM instances in read-only mode, allowing all instances to read the same filesystem data without maintaining a separate copy per instance. Google Cloud documents that read-only disk sharing is less expensive than copies on multiple disks and does not add sharing charges; it also preserves disk-backed access rather than requiring startup-time data copies.

**Learn more:** [Share disks between instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/sharing-disks-between-vms?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You developed a Python script that retrieves information from files uploaded to Cloud Storage and writes that information to Bigtable. You completed testing in your local environment and created the `python-script` service account with the Bigtable User IAM role. You want to deploy the code with appropriate authentication while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Deploy your code to Cloud Functions. Create a Cloud Storage trigger.2. Configure IAM binding for authentication.
1. Deploy your code to Cloud Functions. Create a Cloud Storage trigger.2. Create a service account key for authentication
1. Deploy your image to Cloud Run. Create a trigger in Cloud Scheduler that triggers the service every minute.2. Configure IAM binding for authentication.
1. Deploy your image to Cloud Run. Create a trigger in Cloud Scheduler that triggers the service every minute.2. Create a service account key for authentication.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Storage-triggered Cloud Function runs automatically for file-upload events and can be configured to run as the `python-script` user-managed service account. Its IAM role authorizes Bigtable access through Google-managed, short-lived credentials, avoiding user-managed service account keys, which Google recommends using only when no viable alternative exists.

**Learn more:** [Function Identity](https://docs.cloud.google.com/functions/docs/securing/function-identity?hl=en) · [Best practices for using service accounts securely](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has built an application hosted on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You need to connect the application to a legacy REST service deployed across two GKE clusters in two separate regions. You want the application’s connection to the target service to be resilient. You also need to run health checks against the legacy service on a separate port. How should you configure the connection? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Traffic Director with a sidecar proxy to connect the application to the service.
Use a proxyless Traffic Director configuration to connect the application to the service.
Configure the legacy service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the proxy.
Configure the legacy service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the application.
Configure the legacy service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the Traffic Director control plane.

questions.explanation: An Envoy sidecar proxy configured by Traffic Director routes HTTP/REST traffic across healthy regional backends, providing built-in failover and resilience. Envoy performs its own health checks on a separate port; the firewall must allow health-check traffic from the proxy IP addresses. Proxyless Traffic Director applies to gRPC clients only, not legacy REST services.

You are a lead developer building a new retail system that runs on Cloud Run and Firestore. A web UI requirement is that users can browse all products. A few months after go-live, you observe that Cloud Run instances are terminated with `HTTP 500: Container instances are exceeding memory limits` errors during busy periods. This error coincides with spikes in the number of Firestore queries.  
  
You need to stop Cloud Run from crashing and reduce the number of Firestore queries. You want to use a solution that optimizes system performance. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the query that returns the product list using cursors with limits.
Create a custom index over the products.
Modify the query that returns the product list using integer offsets.
Modify the Cloud Run configuration to increase the memory limits.

questions.explanation:
Cursor-based pagination with a query limit returns products in bounded batches instead of loading an entire product list into an application instance. This reduces per-request memory use and supports efficient browsing across pages. Firestore recommends cursors rather than offsets because offset queries still retrieve and bill for skipped documents internally.

**Learn more:** [Paginate data with query cursors](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/query-data/query-cursors) · [Understand Cloud Firestore billing](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/pricing)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work on a web development team at a small startup. The team is building a Node.js application with Google Cloud services, including Cloud Storage and Cloud Build, and uses a Git repository for version control.  
  
Over the weekend, your manager asks you to make an emergency change to one of the company’s websites. You are the only developer available and must access Google Cloud to make the change, but you do not have your work laptop. You may not store source code locally on a non-corporate computer. How should you configure your development environment?

options.text: Use a text editor and the Git command line to send your source code updates as pull requests from a public computer.
Use a text editor and the Git command line to send your source code updates as pull requests from a virtual machine running on a public computer.
Use Cloud Shell and the built-in code editor for development. Send your source code updates as pull requests.

Use a Cloud Storage bucket to store the source code that you need to edit. Mount the bucket to a public computer as a drive, and use a code editor to update the code. Turn on versioning for the bucket, and point it to the team's Git repository.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Shell supplies a Google-hosted development environment that is accessed from a browser, with a built-in code editor and Git version-control support. The repository can be edited and committed in Cloud Shell, then the changes can be submitted as a pull request, without storing the source code on the public computer.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Shell Editor interface overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/shell/docs/editor-overview) · [Use version control with Cloud Shell Editor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/shell/docs/version-control)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must load-test a group of REST API endpoints deployed to Cloud Run. The API responds to HTTP POST requests. Your load tests must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- Load is generated from multiple parallel threads.  
- API user traffic comes from multiple source IP addresses.  
- Load can scale up through additional test instances.  
  
You want to use Google-recommended best practices. How should you configure the load test?

options.text: Create an image that has cURL installed, and configure cURL to run a test plan. Deploy the image in a managed instance group, and run one instance of the image for each VM.
Create an image that has cURL installed, and configure cURL to run a test plan. Deploy the image in an unmanaged instance group, and run one instance of the image for each VM.
Deploy a distributed load testing framework on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Deploy additional Pods as needed to initiate more traffic and support the number of concurrent users.
Download the container image of a distributed load testing framework on Cloud Shell. Sequentially start several instances of the container on Cloud Shell to increase the load on the API.

questions.explanation:
A distributed load-testing framework on GKE can run concurrent test workers in multiple Pods and scale the test generator horizontally by adding Pods. This provides controlled concurrent traffic and multiple load-generator sources. Google Cloud recommends using a controlled test harness, such as JMeter, for Cloud Run load testing and increasing load through thread groups and request timing.

**Learn more:** [Load testing best practices | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-load-testing)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application that lets clients download a file from your website during a specified time period. How should you design the application to accomplish this task while following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Configure the application to send the file to the client as an email attachment.
Generate and assign a Cloud Storage-signed URL for the file. Make the URL available for the client to download.
Create a temporary Cloud Storage bucket with time expiration specified, and give download permissions to the bucket. Copy the file, and send it to the client.
Generate the HTTP cookies with time expiration specified. If the time is valid, copy the file from the Cloud Storage bucket, and make the file available for the client to download.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage signed URLs provide time-limited access to a specific object and are commonly used for downloads. The application can generate a signed URL with the required expiration time and provide it to the client, allowing direct download without granting broad bucket permissions or copying the file.

**Learn more:** [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls) · [V4 signing process with Cloud Storage tools | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signing-urls-with-helpers)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a CI/CD pipeline consisting of a version control system, Cloud Build, and Container Registry. Whenever a new tag is pushed to the repository, a Cloud Build job is triggered that runs unit tests on the new code, builds a new Docker container image, and pushes it to Container Registry. The final step of the pipeline must deploy the new container to your production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster.  
  
You need to choose a tool and deployment strategy that meet the following requirements:  
  
- No downtime is incurred.  
- Testing is fully automated.  
- Testing is possible before rollout to users.  
- Rollback can occur quickly if necessary.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Trigger a Spinnaker pipeline configured as an A/B test of your new code and, if it is successful, deploy the container to production.
Trigger a Spinnaker pipeline configured as a canary test of your new code and, if it is successful, deploy the container to production.
Trigger another Cloud Build job that uses the Kubernetes CLI tools to deploy your new container to your GKE cluster, where you can perform a canary test.
Trigger another Cloud Build job that uses the Kubernetes CLI tools to deploy your new container to your GKE cluster, where you can perform a shadow test.

questions.explanation:
A Spinnaker canary pipeline progressively exposes the new version to only a subset of users while the existing production version continues serving traffic. Its automated canary analysis evaluates configured metrics and can promote a successful release or trigger rollback on failure, providing automated pre-full-rollout validation and rapid recovery. [Google Cloud: Introducing Kayenta](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/introducing-kayenta-an-open-automated-canary-analysis-tool-from-google-and-netflix)

**Learn more:** [Introducing Kayenta: An open automated canary analysis tool from Google and Netflix](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/introducing-kayenta-an-open-automated-canary-analysis-tool-from-google-and-netflix) · [Use a canary deployment strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your service adds text to images it reads from Cloud Storage. During peak periods of the year, Cloud Storage requests fail with an HTTP 429 “Too Many Requests” status code.  
  
How should this error be handled?

options.text: Add a cache-control header to the objects.
Request a quota increase from the GCP Console.
Retry the request with a truncated exponential backoff strategy.
Change the storage class of the Cloud Storage bucket to Multi-regional.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage treats HTTP 429 as a request-rate-limit error. The appropriate response is to retry using truncated exponential backoff, which progressively delays retries and avoids increasing load during a traffic spike. [Cloud Storage HTTP status and error codes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/status-codes)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage HTTP status and error codes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/status-codes) · [Cloud Storage retry strategy](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/retry-strategy)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Python application running in production on Cloud Run. The application must read and write data stored in a Cloud Storage bucket within the same project. You want to grant the application access according to the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Create a user-managed service account with a custom Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
Create a user-managed service account with the Storage Admin Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
Create a user-managed service account with the Project Editor Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
Use the default service account linked to the Cloud Run revision in production.

questions.explanation:
A dedicated user-managed service account lets the Cloud Run workload have only the permissions required to read and write the relevant Cloud Storage data. A custom IAM role can be limited to those necessary permissions and granted at the bucket scope. Storage Admin and Project Editor provide broader administrative access than needed, while the default service account is not the recommended dedicated identity for a minimally permissioned production workload.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to service identity | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/service-identity) · [Overview of access control | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage security for internal applications in your company. The applications run on Cloud Run and use Secret Manager to store passwords required to access internal databases. Each application can cache secrets for up to 15 minutes. You need to decide how to rotate the secrets while avoiding application downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Store the new username and password in the secret. Reference the latest version of any secret required, and cache the secret for 15 minutes.
Design the applications to retrieve the Latest secret payload on application startup, and continue to use the secret for the duration of the application run.
Store the new password in the secret. Reference the latest version of any secret required, and cache the secret for 15 minutes.

Store the new password in the secret. Design the applications to reference a specific secret version. Change the code to reference the new version, and schedule the deployment of the application during a maintenance window.

questions.explanation:
A zero-downtime credential rotation requires the newly issued database credential to coexist with the old credential until every application instance has refreshed its cache. Storing a new username and password as a new secret version, having applications use the `latest` version, and allowing the existing 15-minute cache interval lets instances transition without invalidating those still using the old credentials. Google Cloud’s rotation guidance likewise requires that creating a new external-system secret not invalidate existing secrets used by current workloads.

**Learn more:** [About secret rotation | Secret Manager | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/regional-secrets/about-rotation-schedules-rs)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: You are building a new public-facing application that must retrieve particular properties from the metadata of users’ objects in their respective Cloud Storage buckets. Because of privacy and data-residency requirements, you must retrieve metadata only, not object data. You want to maximize retrieval performance. How should you retrieve the metadata?

options.text: Use the patch method.
Use the compose method.
Use the copy method.
Use the fields request parameter.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud Storage JSON API `fields` request parameter requests a partial response containing only the specified metadata properties, reducing response payload and improving retrieval performance without returning object data.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage JSON API overview — Partial response](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api) · [HTTP headers and common query string parameters for JSON](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/parameters)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: You are building a new public-facing application that must retrieve particular properties from the metadata of users’ objects in their respective Cloud Storage buckets. Because of privacy and data-residency requirements, you must retrieve metadata only, not object data. You want to maximize retrieval performance. How should you retrieve the metadata?

options.text: Assign the Apigee Analytics Viewer IAM role to the operations team for both environments. Use Cloud Monitoring to review traffic patterns.
Assign the Apigee Analytics Viewer IAM role to the operations team for both environments. Use Apigee API Analytics to review traffic patterns.
Assign the Apigee API Reader IAM role to each user of the operations team for both environments. Use Cloud Monitoring to review traffic patterns.
Assign the Apigee API Reader IAM role to each user of the operations team for both environments. Use Apigee API Analytics to review traffic patterns.

questions.explanation:
The Apigee Analytics Viewer role is designed to view an Apigee organization’s analytics data and retrieve environment statistics, providing the least privilege needed for traffic analysis. Granting that role to the operations team as a group follows IAM best practice, and Apigee API Analytics provides the API traffic-pattern analysis capability. The Apigee API Reader role is broader because it grants read-only access to many non-analytics Apigee resources.

**Learn more:** [Apigee roles](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/system-administration/apigee-roles) · [Apigee API Analytics overview](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/analytics/analytics-services-overview)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for developing a new ecommerce application running on Cloud Run. You need to connect the application to a Cloud SQL database in a separate project. That project uses an isolated network dedicated to multiple databases and has no public IP address. You need to connect the application to this database. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Private Service Connect endpoint on your network. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector on your project. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to create an internal connection.
Configure VPC Network Peering between both networks. In Cloud Run, create a Cloud SQL connection that uses the internal IP. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to interact with the database.
Configure private services access on your project. In Cloud Run, create a Cloud SQL connection. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to interact with the database.

Create a subnet on your VPC. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector on your project using the new subnet. In Cloud Run, create a Cloud SQL connection. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to interact with the database.

questions.explanation:
Private Service Connect enables private Cloud SQL access from VPC networks in different projects. A Private Service Connect endpoint supplies an internal address in the consumer VPC, while a Serverless VPC Access connector routes Cloud Run traffic into that VPC. Cloud SQL Language Connectors support Private Service Connect connections but do not themselves create the network path. [Connect to an instance using Private Service Connect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/configure-private-service-connect)

**Learn more:** [Connect to an instance using Private Service Connect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/configure-private-service-connect) · [Cloud SQL Language Connectors overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/language-connectors)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
For this question, use the HipLocal case study.  
  
Which Google Cloud product meets HipLocal’s business requirements for service-level indicators and objectives?

options.text: Cloud Profiler
Cloud Monitoring
Cloud Trace
Cloud Logging

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring provides SLO monitoring, including the ability to define service-level indicators (SLIs) and service-level objectives (SLOs), measure service performance, and alert on SLO violations.\
\
**Learn more:** [Service monitoring | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/slo-monitoring) · [Cloud Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications

options.text: Use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to run the application as a microservice. Run the MySQL database on a dedicated GKE node.

Use multiple Compute Engine instances to run MySQL to store state information. Use a Google Cloud-managed load balancer to distribute the load between instances. Use managed instance groups for scaling.

Use Memorystore to store session information and CloudSQL to store state information. Use a Google Cloud-managed load balancer to distribute the load between instances. Use managed instance groups for scaling.
Use a Cloud Storage bucket to serve the application as a static website, and use another Cloud Storage bucket to store user state information.

questions.explanation:
Memorystore can hold shared session information so application instances remain stateless, while Cloud SQL provides a managed relational database for durable application state. A Google Cloud managed load balancer distributes requests across Compute Engine instances, and managed instance groups can automatically add or remove instances as demand changes. This combination supports horizontal application scaling while reducing infrastructure-management overhead.

**Learn more:** [Load balancing and scaling | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/load-balancing-and-autoscaling) · [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview)

You are developing a single-page web application whose user interface uses `XMLHttpRequest` to communicate with a third-party API for content. The data the API returns and displays in the UI is less critical than other data shown on the same web page, so some requests may not display the API data in the UI. However, API calls must not delay rendering of other user-interface components. You want the application to perform well when the API response is an error or times out.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set the asynchronous option for your requests to the API to false and omit the widget displaying the API results when a timeout or error is encountered.
Set the asynchronous option for your request to the API to true and omit the widget displaying the API results when a timeout or error is encountered.
Catch timeout or error exceptions from the API call and keep trying with exponential backoff until the API response is successful.
Catch timeout or error exceptions from the API call and display the error response in the UI widget.

questions.explanation:
Asynchronous `XMLHttpRequest` calls allow the browser to continue rendering and processing the rest of the interface while the request is pending. If the noncritical API request errors or times out, omitting its widget avoids blocking or degrading the rest of the page. Synchronous XHR can block the main interface and should be avoided.

**Learn more:** [MDN: Synchronous and asynchronous requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Synchronous_and_Asynchronous_Requests) · [MDN: XMLHttpRequest open()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest/open)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running in a production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You use Cloud Deploy to automatically deploy the application to your production GKE cluster. As part of your development process, you plan to make frequent changes to the application's source code and must choose tools to test those changes before pushing them to your remote source code repository. Your toolset must meet these requirements:  
  
- Automatically test frequent local changes.  
- Local deployment emulates the production deployment.  
  
Which tools should you use to test building and running a container on your laptop while using minimal resources?

options.text: Docker Compose and dockerd
Terraform and kubeadm
Minikube and Skaffold
kaniko and Tekton

questions.explanation:
Minikube provides a lightweight local Kubernetes cluster, enabling local deployments that follow the Kubernetes deployment model used by GKE. Skaffold runs a continuous development loop: in `dev` mode it watches source changes, rebuilds images, retests, and redeploys to a local Minikube cluster. Skaffold is also the tool Cloud Deploy uses for rendering and deployment operations.

**Learn more:** [Get Started with Skaffold in Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/using-skaffold/getting-started-skaffold) · [Use Skaffold with Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/using-skaffold)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are monitoring a Go web application deployed in Google Kubernetes Engine. You observe increased CPU and memory utilization. You need to identify which source code consumes the most CPU and memory resources. What should you do?

options.text: Download, install, and start the Snapshot Debugger agent in your VM. Take debug snapshots of the functions that take the longest time. Review the call stack frame, and identify the local variables at that level in the stack.
Import the Cloud Profiler package into your application, and initialize the Profiler agent. Review the generated flame graph in the Google Cloud console to identify time-intensive functions.

Import OpenTelemetry and Trace export packages into your application, and create the trace provider.Review the latency data for your application on the Trace overview page, and identify where bottlenecks are occurring.

Create a Cloud Logging query that gathers the web application's logs. Write a Python script that calculates the difference between the timestamps from the beginning and the end of the application's longest functions to identity time-intensive functions.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Profiler supports Go workloads running on Google Kubernetes Engine and collects CPU-time and heap/allocation profiles that are attributed to source-code functions. Its console flame graphs show each function’s relative resource consumption, allowing CPU-intensive and memory-consuming functions to be identified.

**Learn more:** [Profiling Go applications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/profiling-go) · [Cloud Profiler documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application with distinct microservices that must stay internal to the cluster. You need to configure each microservice with a particular replica count. You also need to address a particular microservice uniformly from any other microservice, independent of how many replicas that microservice scales to. You plan to implement this solution on Google Kubernetes Engine. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy each microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment in the cluster using a Service, and use the Service DNS name to address it from other microservices within the cluster.
Deploy each microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment in the cluster using an Ingress, and use the Ingress IP address to address the Deployment from other microservices within the cluster.
Deploy each microservice as a Pod. Expose the Pod in the cluster using a Service, and use the Service DNS name to address the microservice from other microservices within the cluster.
Deploy each microservice as a Pod. Expose the Pod in the cluster using an Ingress, and use the Ingress IP address to address the Pod from other microservices within the cluster.

questions.explanation:
A Kubernetes Deployment manages a stateless workload and its desired number of Pod replicas. A Service provides a stable in-cluster network endpoint for the Pods selected by its labels and receives a DNS name, allowing other microservices to use the same name while the replica count and individual Pod identities change.

**Learn more:** [Kubernetes Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) · [Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)

You are creating a new application with these design requirements:  
  
- Application-infrastructure creation and modifications must be versioned and auditable.  
- The application and its deployment infrastructure must use Google-managed services wherever possible.  
- The application must run on a serverless compute platform.  
  
How should you design the application's architecture?

options.text: 1. Store the application and infrastructure source code in a Git repository. 2. Use Cloud Build to deploy the application infrastructure with Terraform. 3. Deploy the application to a Cloud Function as a pipeline step.

1. Deploy Jenkins from the Google Cloud Marketplace, and define a continuous integration pipeline in Jenkins. 2. Configure a pipeline step to pull the application source code from a Git repository. 3. Deploy the application source code to App Engine as a pipeline step.

1. Create a continuous integration pipeline on Cloud Build, and configure the pipeline to deploy the application infrastructure using Deployment Manager templates. 2. Configure a pipeline step to create a container with the latest application source code. 3. Deploy the container to a Compute Engine instance as a pipeline step.

1. Deploy the application infrastructure using gcloud commands. 2. Use Cloud Build to define a continuous integration pipeline for changes to the application source code. 3. Configure a pipeline step to pull the application source code from a Git repository, and create a containerized application. 4. Deploy the new container on Cloud Run as a pipeline step.

questions.explanation:
Store application code and infrastructure-as-code definitions in Git so infrastructure changes have a versioned, auditable history. Use the managed Cloud Build service to execute Terraform deployments, and deploy the application to Cloud Functions, a serverless compute platform. This meets the managed-services preference without requiring self-managed CI infrastructure or virtual machines.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [Deployment Manager deprecation](https://cloud.google.com/deployment-manager/docs/deprecations)

You are deploying new workloads on a GKE cluster in Autopilot mode. You must ensure that Pods are scheduled on nodes using Arm-architecture CPUs. The cluster currently has no Arm-based CPUs. You want to minimize cluster operations. How should you ensure that workloads on the GKE cluster use Arm-based CPU nodes?

options.text: Apply Pod tolerations to request GKE to avoid scheduling Pods on nodes that do not have Arm-based CPUs.
Apply node taints on node pools to tell GKE to only schedule your workloads on Arm-based CPU nodes.
Deploy a new cluster in GKE Standard mode, and set up a node pool with Arm-based CPU nodes. Use nodeSelector in your manifest to ensure that Pods are scheduled in this node pool.
Request the Scale-out compute class and the arm64 architecture in your manifest.

questions.explanation:
GKE Autopilot can automatically provision nodes for a requested ComputeClass and CPU architecture. The Scale-Out ComputeClass supports both amd64 and arm64; requesting Scale-Out together with arm64 in the workload manifest causes Autopilot to provision Arm-based nodes for those Pods, avoiding node-pool or cluster administration.

**Learn more:** [Deploy Autopilot workloads on Arm architecture](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/autopilot-arm-workloads) · [About Balanced and Scale-Out ComputeClasses in Autopilot clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/balanced-scale-out-autopilot)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a JPEG image-resizing API that is hosted on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Service callers will be within the same GKE cluster. You want clients to be able to obtain the service IP address.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Define a GKE Service. Clients should use the name of the A record in Cloud DNS to find the service's cluster IP address.
Define a GKE Service. Clients should use the service name in the URL to connect to the service.
Define a GKE Endpoint. Clients should get the endpoint name from the appropriate environment variable in the client container.
Define a GKE Endpoint. Clients should get the endpoint name from Cloud DNS.

questions.explanation:
A GKE Kubernetes Service provides a stable virtual IP address (ClusterIP) and an automatically generated DNS service name. Workloads in the same cluster can use the Service name in their URL; cluster DNS resolves that name to the Service IP address. Endpoints identify the backing workloads and are not the normal client discovery interface.

**Learn more:** [Service discovery and DNS](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/service-discovery) · [About Cloud DNS for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-cloud-dns)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],HipLocal wants to decrease the number of on-call engineers and remove manual scaling.  
  
Which two services should they select? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Google App Engine services.
Use serverless Google Cloud Functions.
Use Knative to build and deploy serverless applications.
Use Google Kubernetes Engine for automated deployments.
Use a large Google Compute Engine cluster for deployments.

questions.explanation:
Google App Engine is a fully managed application platform that automatically scales application instances with demand, reducing infrastructure operations. Google Cloud Functions provides serverless compute that automatically manages and scales its underlying infrastructure, which is appropriate for elastic, event-driven backend functionality. Together, these services satisfy the serverless, automatic-scaling, and reduced-operations requirements.

**Learn more:** [How instances are managed | App Engine standard environment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/how-instances-are-managed?hl=en) · [Cloud Run functions](https://cloud.google.com/functions)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Users report that your website hosted on Cloud Run responds too slowly during traffic spikes. You want to deliver a better user experience at traffic peaks. What should you do?

options.text: Read application configuration and static data from the database on application startup.
Package application configuration and static data into the application image during build time.
Perform as much work as possible in the background after the response has been returned to the user.
Ensure that timeout exceptions and errors cause the Cloud Run instance to exit quickly so a replacement instance can be started.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run can create new instances as traffic increases, and requests can wait while those instances start. Keeping immutable application configuration and static data in the application image avoids database access during startup, reducing startup-path latency. Cloud Run guidance also advises handling exceptions rather than crashing instances, because replacement startup can delay queued traffic.

**Learn more:** [General development tips for Cloud Run services](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/tips/general)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s new security initiative requires every item of data stored in Google Cloud to be encrypted with customer-managed encryption keys. You intend to use Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) to configure key access. You must follow the separation-of-duties principle and Google-recommended best practices. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Provision Cloud KMS in its own project.
Do not assign an owner to the Cloud KMS project.
Provision Cloud KMS in the project where the keys are being used.
Grant the roles/cloudkms.admin role to the owner of the project where the keys from Cloud KMS are being used.
Grant an owner role for the Cloud KMS project to a different user than the owner of the project where the keys from Cloud KMS are being used.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud recommends hosting Cloud KMS resources in a separate, dedicated key project to isolate key material from the projects containing protected data. Avoiding the basic Owner role in that key project preserves separation of duties because Owner grants both key-management and cryptographic-operation permissions.

**Learn more:** [Separation of duties | Cloud Key Management Service](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/separation-of-duties) · [Permissions and roles | Cloud Key Management Service](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/reference/permissions-and-roles)

questions.question: You are preparing to add unit tests to your application. You must be able to verify that your subscriber processes published Pub/Sub messages in order. You want the unit tests to remain cost-effective and reliable. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a mocking framework.
Create a topic and subscription for each tester.
Add a filter by tester to the subscription.
Use the Pub/Sub emulator.

questions.explanation:
The Pub/Sub emulator provides a local emulation of the Pub/Sub service for application development and testing. It supports publishing, subscribing, and message ordering, allowing tests to exercise ordered subscriber processing without creating and operating production Pub/Sub resources.\
\
**Learn more:** [Testing apps locally with the emulator | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator?hl=en)

questions.question: You are preparing to add unit tests to your application. You must be able to verify that your subscriber processes published Pub/Sub messages in order. You want the unit tests to remain cost-effective and reliable. What should you do?

options.text: Replace the current service with the new revision. Deploy the new revision with no traffic allocated. After the deployment, split the traffic between the previous service and the new revision.
Update the current service with the new changes. Deploy the new revision. After the deployment, split the traffic between the current service and the new revision.
Update the current service with the new changes. Deploy the new revision with no traffic allocated. Split the traffic between the current service and the new revision.
Replace the current service with the new revision. Deploy the new revision. Create a load balancer to split the traffic between the previous service and the new revision.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run supports gradual rollouts by updating an existing service to create a new revision, deploying that revision with no traffic, and then splitting service traffic between the old and new revisions. Assigning 10% to the new revision preserves the earlier revision for the remaining clients, supporting backward compatibility without an external load balancer.

**Learn more:** [Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

Your team uses Cloud Storage for a video and image application that was recently migrated to Google Cloud. After a viral surge, users report application instability that coincides with a 10x increase in HTTP 429 error codes from the Cloud Storage APIs. You need to resolve the errors and put a long-term solution in place. You want to ensure the application stays stable if load increases again in the future. What should you do?

options.text: Optimize the application code to reduce unnecessary calls to Cloud Storage APIs to prevent HTTP 429 errors.

Compress the video and images files to reduce their size, and minimize storage costs and bandwidth usage. Implement a custom throttling mechanism in the application that limits the number of concurrent API calls.
Migrate all image and video data to Firestore. Replace the Cloud Storage APIs in the application code with the new Firestore database.
Implement a retry strategy with exponential backoff for requests that encounter HTTP 429 errors.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage treats HTTP 429 responses as retryable transient errors and recommends retrying them with truncated exponential backoff, preferably with jitter. Increasing delays prevent repeated retry bursts from worsening rate limiting and make the application more resilient during future traffic spikes.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage retry strategy](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/retry-strategy) · [Cloud Storage JSON API HTTP status and error codes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/status-codes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an environmental agency in a large city. You are building a new monitoring platform that will collect air-quality readings from thousands of locations across the city. You want the air-quality reading devices to send and receive their data payloads to the newly created RESTful backend systems every minute by using a `curl` command. The backend systems run in a single cloud region and use Premium Tier networking. You must connect the devices to the backend while minimizing daily average latency, measured by Time to First Byte (TTFB). How should you build this service?

options.text: 1. Run the air quality devices’ backends on Compute Engine VMs.2. Create a weighted round robin routing policy on Cloud DNS.3. Configure the air quality devices to connect by using this DNS.

1. Run the air quality devices’ backends on Compute Engine VMs.2. Create a round robin routing policy on Cloud DNS for these Compute Engine VMs.3. Configure the air quality devices to connect by using this DNS.

1. Run the air quality devices' backends in a managed instance group.2. Create an external passthrough Network Load Balancer to connect to the managed instance group.3. Configure a connection between the air quality devices and the Network Load Balancer.

1 Run the air quality devices' backends in a managed instance group.2. Create an external Application Load Balancer, and connect it to the managed instance group.3. Configure a connection between the air quality devices and the Application Load Balancer.

questions.explanation:
An external Application Load Balancer is a proxy-based Layer 7 load balancer for HTTP and HTTPS traffic and supports instance-group backends. In Premium Tier, its global frontend is advertised from Google points of presence and terminates HTTP(S) traffic as close as possible to users, which minimizes network delay to the first response byte for RESTful requests. A managed instance group supplies scalable, healthy backends.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [Network Service Tiers overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-tiers/docs/overview)
