lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],For this question, use the HipLocal case study.  
  
A recent security audit found that HipLocal’s database credentials for its Compute Engine-hosted MySQL databases are kept in plaintext on persistent disks. HipLocal must reduce the risk that these credentials could be stolen. What should it do?

options.text: Create a service account and download its key. Use the key to authenticate to Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) to obtain the database credentials.
Create a service account and download its key. Use the key to authenticate to Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) to obtain a key used to decrypt the database credentials.
Create a service account and grant it the roles/iam.serviceAccountUser role. Impersonate as this account and authenticate using the Cloud SQL Proxy.
Grant the roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor role to the Compute Engine service account. Store and access the database credentials with the Secret Manager API.

questions.explanation:
Secret Manager is designed to store sensitive values such as database credentials. Granting the Compute Engine service account the Secret Manager Secret Accessor role lets the workload retrieve only the required secret through the API using its attached identity, rather than storing credentials on persistent disks or exporting a service-account key. Google Cloud recommends attached workload identities over exported service-account credentials and supports granting Secret Accessor at the individual-secret level for least-privilege access.

**Learn more:** [Secret Manager best practices](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/best-practices) · [Secret Manager access control with IAM](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/access-control)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an application running on a Compute Engine instance. You also have multiple backend services running in standalone Docker containers on Compute Engine instances. The Compute Engine instances that support the backend services are scaled by managed instance groups across multiple regions.  
  
You want the calling application to be loosely coupled. You need to invoke separate service implementations selected according to the value of an HTTP header in the request. Which Google Cloud feature should you use to invoke the backend services?

options.text: Traffic Director
Service Directory
Anthos Service Mesh
Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancing

questions.explanation:
Traffic Director provides service-mesh traffic management for Compute Engine workloads. Its HTTP routing rules can match request headers and route traffic to the appropriate backend service, while allowing the client application to call a service abstraction instead of selecting specific service endpoints or implementations. It supports backend selection across managed instance groups in multiple regions.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Service Mesh overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/overview) · [Advanced traffic management overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/service-routing/advanced-traffic-management)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must deploy a new European version of a website hosted on Google Kubernetes Engine. The existing and new websites must be reachable through the same HTTP(S) load balancer external IP address, while using different domain names. What should you do?

options.text: Define a new Ingress resource with a host rule matching the new domain
Modify the existing Ingress resource with a host rule matching the new domain
Create a new Service of type LoadBalancer specifying the existing IP address as the loadBalancerIP
Generate a new Ingress resource and specify the existing IP address as the kubernetes.io/ingress.global-static-ip-name annotation value

questions.explanation:
A GKE Ingress uses a single URL map for its HTTP(S) load balancer and supports hostname-based routing to different backend Services. Adding a host rule for the new domain to the existing Ingress updates that same load balancer configuration while preserving its external IP address.

**Learn more:** [About GKE Ingress routing and security](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ingress-routing-security) · [GKE Ingress for Application Load Balancers](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ingress)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application runs in a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. When a new application version is released, the CI/CD tool changes `spec.template.spec.containers[0].image` to point to the Docker image for that new version. When the Deployment applies this change, deploy at least one replica of the new version while keeping the existing replicas until that new replica is healthy.  
  
Which change should be made to the GKE Deployment object shown below?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783706112539-fy4eo77d.jpg)

options.text: Set the Deployment strategy to RollingUpdate with maxSurge set to 0, maxUnavailable set to 1.
Set the Deployment strategy to RollingUpdate with maxSurge set to 1, maxUnavailable set to 0.
Set the Deployment strategy to Recreate with maxSurge set to 0, maxUnavailable set to 1.
Set the Deployment strategy to Recreate with maxSurge set to 1, maxUnavailable set to 0.

questions.explanation:
A `RollingUpdate` rollout with `maxSurge: 1` can create one new Pod above the desired replica count, and `maxUnavailable: 0` prevents the Deployment from making any desired replica unavailable during the update. This keeps the existing replicas available until the new Pod is ready; `Recreate` instead terminates existing Pods before creating replacements.

**Learn more:** [Kubernetes Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer your company's ecommerce platform payment system, which runs on Google Cloud. The company must keep user logs for 1 year for internal auditing and for 3 years to satisfy compliance requirements. You need to store new user logs on Google Cloud to reduce on-premises storage use and make sure they can be searched easily. You want to minimize effort while ensuring the logs are stored properly. What should you do?

options.text: Store the logs in a Cloud Storage bucket with bucket lock turned on.
Store the logs in a Cloud Storage bucket with a 3-year retention period.
Store the logs in Cloud Logging as custom logs with a custom retention period.
Store the logs in a Cloud Storage bucket with a 1-year retention period. After 1 year, move the logs to another bucket with a 2-year retention period.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging is a fully managed service for storing and searching log data, including user-written custom logs. Project-level custom log buckets support configurable retention from 1 to 3,650 days, so setting a 3-year retention period satisfies both the 3-year compliance requirement and the shorter 1-year audit requirement without managing Cloud Storage lifecycle transitions.

**Learn more:** [Store log entries](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/store-log-entries) · [Configure log buckets](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an analytics application that uses the BigQuery API to run hundreds of queries every few minutes. You want to determine how long these queries take to execute.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Stackdriver Monitoring to plot slot usage.
Use Stackdriver Trace to plot API execution time.
Use Stackdriver Trace to plot query execution time.
Use Stackdriver Monitoring to plot query execution times.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring exposes the BigQuery **Query execution times** metric (`query/execution_times`), which reports the distribution of execution durations for successfully completed queries. It can be plotted to observe query execution time; Cloud Trace instead measures traced application or API-call latency.

**Learn more:** [Create dashboards, charts, and alerts | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/monitoring-dashboard) · [Google Cloud metrics: A or B | Cloud Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_gcp_a_b)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an online chat application in which users can upload profile pictures. Uploaded profile pictures must meet content-policy requirements. You need to automatically detect and label inappropriate images as they are uploaded. In the future, this process must be expanded to include additional processing tasks, such as watermarking and image compression.  
  
You want to simplify orchestration and minimize the operational overhead of the image-scanning and labeling steps, while ensuring that extra steps can be added or removed easily later. What should you do?

options.text: Save user-uploaded images to a temporary Cloud Storage bucket. Implement code on the backend server to retrieve the image content and call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure a Cloud Function that is triggered when a new image is uploaded and calls one or more Cloud Run services. Create additional Cloud Run services that call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure a Cloud Function that is triggered when a new image is uploaded and publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic. Deploy microservices in GKE that subscribe to the Pub/Sub topic and call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Create an Eventarc trigger that connects the bucket to the Workflows event receiver when a new image is uploaded. Create a workflow in Workflows with multiple Cloud Functions that call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

questions.explanation:
Eventarc can route Cloud Storage object-upload events to a Workflows event receiver. Workflows is a fully managed, serverless orchestration platform that defines and executes ordered steps, and it can combine Cloud Functions with Google Cloud services such as Cloud Vision AI. Defining image scanning, labeling, watermarking, and compression as workflow steps provides low-operational-overhead orchestration and allows the processing sequence to be changed without operating servers or a GKE cluster.

**Learn more:** [Workflows overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/overview) · [Trigger Workflows with direct events from Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/eventarc/standard/docs/workflows/quickstart-storage)

You have deployed a Java application on Cloud Run. The application needs access to a database hosted on Cloud SQL. Because of regulatory requirements, the connection to the Cloud SQL instance must use its internal IP address. How should you configure connectivity while following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Configure your Cloud Run service with a Cloud SQL connection.
Configure your Cloud Run service to use a Serverless VPC Access connector.
Configure your application to use the Cloud SQL Java connector.
Configure your application to connect to an instance of the Cloud SQL Auth proxy.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run must be connected to the VPC that contains the Cloud SQL private-IP endpoint. A Serverless VPC Access connector routes the service’s private-address egress through that VPC, allowing a direct TCP connection to the Cloud SQL instance’s internal IP. For private-IP paths, Cloud SQL documents direct VPC connectivity rather than use of the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.

**Learn more:** [Connect from Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/connect-run) · [VPC with connectors](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/vpc-connectors)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a web application that publishes messages to Pub/Sub. You plan to build new versions of the application locally and want to rapidly test Pub/Sub integration for each new build. How should you set up local testing?

options.text: Install Cloud Code on the integrated development environment (IDE). Navigate to Cloud APIs, and enable Pub/Sub against a valid Google Project ID. When developing locally, configure your application to call pubsub.googleapis.com.

questions.explanation:
The Pub/Sub emulator provides a local emulation of the production Pub/Sub service. After starting it, configure the application to connect to the emulator by exporting `PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST` to the emulator endpoint, rather than calling `pubsub.googleapis.com`.

**Learn more:** [Testing apps locally with the Pub/Sub emulator](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator)

questions.question: You want to move an on-premises container running in Knative to Google Cloud. You need to ensure that the migration does not affect your application's deployment strategy, and you want to use a fully managed service. Which Google Cloud service should you use to deploy the container?

options.text: Cloud Run
Compute Engine
Google Kubernetes Engine
App Engine flexible environment

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that implements the Knative Serving API specification and is designed to maximize portability with Knative Serving. It therefore supports migrating a Knative container workload while preserving its serverless deployment approach.\
\
**Learn more:** [Migrate a Knative Serving service to Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/enterprise/knative-serving/docs/migrate/cloud-run) · [What is Cloud Run?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications

options.text: Reboot the machine.
Enable and check the serial port output.
Delete the machine and create a new one.
Take a snapshot of the disk and attach it to a new machine.

questions.explanation:
Serial port output exposes boot and system-level diagnostic messages and remains useful when SSH or network access to a Compute Engine instance is unavailable. Reviewing it first helps identify the cause of the instance failure without prematurely rebooting, deleting, or replacing the VM.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting SSH errors | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/troubleshooting-ssh-errors?hl=en) · [Viewing serial port output | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/viewing-serial-port-output?hl=en)

Your development team has created several Cloud Functions in Java, along with corresponding integration and service tests. You use Cloud Build to build and deploy the functions and to run the tests. Your Cloud Build job reports deployment failures immediately after code validation succeeds. What should you do?

options.text: Check the maximum number of Cloud Function instances.
Verify that your Cloud Build trigger has the correct build parameters.
Retry the tests using the truncated exponential backoff polling strategy.
Verify that the Cloud Build service account is assigned the Cloud Functions Developer role.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Build service account must have the Cloud Functions Developer role (`roles/cloudfunctions.developer`) to deploy and manage Cloud Functions. Missing that IAM role can cause deployment to fail after successful code validation.

**Learn more:** [Deploying to Cloud Run functions](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/deploying-builds/deploy-functions) · [Cloud Functions IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/reference/iam/roles)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are preparing to deploy an application hosted on a Windows Compute Engine instance that uses Cloud SQL. You plan to use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to connect to the Cloud SQL instance and to follow Google-recommended practices and the principle of least privilege. You have already created a custom service account. What should you do next?

options.text: Create and assign a custom role with the cloudsql.instances.connect permission to the custom service account. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to specify your instance connection name.
Grant the custom service account the roles/cloudsql.client role. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to use the --unix-socket CLI option.
Grant the custom service account the roles/cloudsql.editor role.
Grant the custom service account the roles/cloudsql.viewer role. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to specify your instance connection name.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy needs the `cloudsql.instances.connect` permission to connect to an instance. Granting that permission through a narrowly scoped custom role implements least privilege, and the proxy is started by supplying the instance connection name. Windows does not support Unix sockets for the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.

**Learn more:** [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/sql-proxy) · [Cloud SQL roles and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/roles-and-permissions)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that will be deployed to Compute Engine instances across multiple distinct projects, each representing an environment in your software-development process (development, QA, staging, and production). The instances in every project use the same application code but different configuration. During deployment, each instance must receive the application configuration for the environment it serves. You want to minimize the number of steps required to configure this flow. What should you do?

options.text: When creating your instances, configure a startup script using the gcloud command to determine the project name that indicates the correct environment.

In each project, configure a metadata key ג€environmentג€ whose value is the environment it serves. Use your deployment tool to query the instance metadata and configure the application based on the ג€environmentג€ value.

Deploy your chosen deployment tool on an instance in each project. Use a deployment job to retrieve the appropriate configuration file from your version control system, and apply the configuration when deploying the application on each instance.

During each instance launch, configure an instance custom-metadata key named ג€environmentג€ whose value is the environment the instance serves. Use your deployment tool to query the instance metadata, and configure the application based on the ג€environmentג€ value.

questions.explanation:
Project metadata applies to every VM in a project, so a custom `environment` key can be set once for each environment-specific project and read by the deployment process to select the appropriate configuration. This avoids assigning the same metadata separately to every instance.

**Learn more:** [Set and remove custom metadata | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/metadata/setting-custom-metadata) · [About VM metadata | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/metadata/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer collaborating with the CI/CD team to troubleshoot a new feature introduced by your team. The CI/CD team used HashiCorp Packer to build a new Compute Engine image from your development branch. The image built successfully, but it does not boot.  
  
You need to investigate the issue with the CI/CD team. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new feature branch, and ask the build team to rebuild the image.
Shut down the deployed virtual machine, export the disk, and then mount the disk locally to access the boot logs.
Install Packer locally, build the Compute Engine image locally, and then run it in your personal Google Cloud project.
Check Compute Engine OS logs using the serial port, and check the Cloud Logging logs to confirm access to the serial port.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine writes BIOS, bootloader, kernel, and other system-level diagnostic output to virtual serial ports, making serial-port output the appropriate place to investigate failed boots. When serial-port output logging is enabled, Cloud Logging retains that output even if the VM is no longer running; relevant logs can also verify serial-console access.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting VM start up | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/vm-startup) · [Viewing serial port output | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/viewing-serial-port-output)

You intend to deploy a new application revision to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in production by using a Deployment resource. The container might not function correctly. You want to reduce risk if problems occur after the revision is deployed and follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget of 80%.
Perform a rolling update with a HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale-down policy value of 0.
Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet, and perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget of 80%.
Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet, and perform a rolling update with a HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale-down policy value of 0.

questions.explanation:
A Deployment rolling update progressively replaces the existing Pods with Pods for the new revision, avoiding the all-at-once interruption of a recreate-style rollout. A PodDisruptionBudget that preserves 80% availability helps maintain sufficient running replicas during voluntary disruptions. HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale-down behavior does not make a revision rollout safer, and a StatefulSet is intended for workloads that need stable identities, ordered deployment, or persistent storage semantics.

**Learn more:** [Ensure workloads are disruption-ready | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-disruption-readiness) · [Update a Deployment Without Downtime | Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/update-deployment-rolling/)

You use Cloud Build to build and test container images before deploying them to Cloud Run. Your images are stored in Artifact Registry. You need to ensure that only container images that passed testing are deployed, while minimizing operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a new revision to a Cloud Run service. Assign a tag that allows access to the revision at a specific URL without serving traffic. Test that revision again. Migrate the traffic to the Cloud Run service after you confirm that the new revision is performing as expected.

Enable Binary Authorization on your Cloud Run service. Create an attestation if the container image has passed all tests. Configure Binary Authorization to allow only images with appropriate attestation to be deployed to the Cloud Run service.
Create a GKE cluster. Verify that all tests have passed, and then deploy the image to the GKE cluster.
Configure build provenance on your Cloud Build pipeline. Verify that all the tests have passed, and then deploy the image to a Cloud Run service.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces a deployment policy for Cloud Run. A test pipeline can create an attestation for an image only after it passes all required tests, and the policy can require that attestation. At deployment time, Binary Authorization verifies the attestation and blocks images that do not meet the policy.

**Learn more:** [Create attestations | Binary Authorization | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/making-attestations) · [Set up overview for Cloud Run | Binary Authorization | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/run/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is building a new application with a PostgreSQL database and Cloud Run. You are responsible for ensuring that all traffic remains private on Google Cloud. You want to use managed services and follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Enable Cloud SQL and Cloud Run in the same project. 2. Configure a private IP address for Cloud SQL. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to Cloud SQL.

1. Install PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine virtual machine (VM), and enable Cloud Run in the same project. 2. Configure a private IP address for the VM. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to the VM hosting PostgreSQL.

1. Use Cloud SQL and Cloud Run in different projects. 2. Configure a private IP address for Cloud SQL. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Set up a VPN connection between the two projects. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to Cloud SQL.

1. Install PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine VM, and enable Cloud Run in different projects. 2. Configure a private IP address for the VM. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Set up a VPN connection between the two projects. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to access the VM hosting PostgreSQL

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL is Google Cloud’s managed PostgreSQL offering. Configuring its private IP requires private services access, which provides private connectivity between the VPC network and the Cloud SQL service-producer network. A Serverless VPC Access connector lets Cloud Run send traffic to private VPC addresses, including the Cloud SQL private IP, without using the public internet.

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to build and deploy, in C++, a microservice for an application hosted on Google Cloud. The code must be containerized and use several custom software libraries developed by your team. You want to minimize maintenance of the application’s underlying infrastructure. How should you deploy the microservice?

options.text: Use Cloud Run functions to deploy the microservice.
Use Cloud Build to create the container, and deploy it on Cloud Run.
Use Cloud Shell to containerize your microservice, and deploy it on GKE Standard.
Use Cloud Shell to containerize your microservice, and deploy it on a Container-Optimized OS Compute Engine instance.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can build the custom container image that includes the C++ application and its team-built libraries. Cloud Run deploys compatible container images on fully managed, scalable infrastructure, avoiding the cluster or virtual-machine administration required by GKE Standard or Compute Engine.

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has deployed a new API to a Compute Engine instance. During testing, the API is not operating as expected. You want to monitor the application for 12 hours to diagnose an issue within the application code without redeploying the application. Which tool should you use?

options.text: Cloud Trace
Cloud Monitoring
Cloud Debugger logpoints
Cloud Debugger snapshots

questions.explanation:
Cloud Debugger logpoints dynamically add log statements to a running application without a rebuild or redeployment. They can remain active for up to 24 hours, so they support a 12-hour diagnostic monitoring period. Snapshots capture application state at a specific point in time rather than continuously emitting diagnostic log entries.

**Learn more:** [Add log statements to your application on the fly with Stackdriver Debugger Logpoints](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/add-log-statements-to-your-application-on-the-fly-with-stackdriver-debugger-logpoints)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently deployed an application to GKE in which Pods write files to a Compute Engine persistent disk. You created a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) and a PersistentVolume (PV) Kubernetes object for the disk, and reference the PVC in the deployment manifest file.  
  
You recently increased the persistent disk's size because the application has consumed almost all available disk space. After logging in to one of the Pods, you find that the disk expansion is not visible in the container file system. What should you do?

options.text: Set the spec.capacity.storage value of the PV object to match the size of the persistent disk. Apply the updated configuration by using kubectl.

Recreate the application Pods by running the kubectl delete deployment DEPLOYMENT_NAME && kubectl apply deployment.yaml command, where the DEPLOYMENT_NAME parameter is the name of your deployment and deployment.yaml is its manifest file.
Set the spec.resources.requests.storage value of the PVC object to match the size of the persistent disk. Apply the updated configuration by using kubectl.
In the Pod, resize the disk partition to the maximum value by using the fdisk or parted utility.

questions.explanation:
GKE volume expansion is initiated by increasing the PVC’s `spec.resources.requests.storage` value. This lets Kubernetes update the volume state and lets kubelet resize the filesystem exposed to the container. Directly editing a PV’s capacity can prevent expansion and leave the container filesystem at its former size.

**Learn more:** [Using volume expansion | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/persistent-volumes/volume-expansion) · [Troubleshooting storage in GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/storage)

You work for an organization that operates an online ecommerce website. Your company plans to expand globally; however, the estore currently serves a single specific region. You need to choose a SQL database and configure a schema that will scale as the organization grows. You want to create a table to store all customer transactions and ensure that both the customer (`CustomerId`) and the transaction (`TransactionId`) are unique. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use an incremental number for the TransactionId.
Create a Cloud SQL table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use a random string (UUID) for the Transactionid.
Create a Cloud Spanner table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use a random string (UUID) for the TransactionId.
Create a Cloud Spanner table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use an incremental number for the TransactionId.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database designed to scale across regions. Spanner distributes data by primary-key ranges, so an incrementing `TransactionId` can concentrate inserts into one range and create a write hotspot. A random UUID transaction identifier is effectively unique and spreads writes more uniformly across the key space, supporting scalable transaction ingestion.

**Learn more:** [Schema design best practices | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-design) · [Primary key migration overview | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/primary-keys-overview)

questions.question: You are writing to a Cloud Spanner database from a Go application. You want to optimize your application's performance by following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Write to Cloud Spanner using Cloud Client Libraries.
Write to Cloud Spanner using Google API Client Libraries
Write to Cloud Spanner using a custom gRPC client library.
Write to Cloud Spanner using a third-party HTTP client library.

questions.explanation:

\

questions.question: You are writing to a Cloud Spanner database from a Go application. You want to optimize your application's performance by following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the Cloud Run service to use HTTP/2. Implement gRPC for communication between the microservices. Use streaming gRPCs when a large amount of data has to be sent.
Implement the microservices with the REST API communication protocol. Use Apigee with rate-limiting to provide the best QoS for high-priority services.
Use SOAP to build the microservices API, and use XML as the data format for communication across the microservices. Define SOAP data contracts for each microservice.
Use HTTP REST to communicate across the microservices. Implement pagination and add indexing to your database.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run supports gRPC for high-performance, low-latency communication between internal microservices. gRPC uses HTTP/2 and efficient Protocol Buffers serialization, and streaming gRPC is appropriate for transferring large volumes of data. Cloud Run recommends HTTP/2 configuration when using gRPC, particularly because streaming requires HTTP/2.

**Learn more:** [Using gRPC | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/triggering/grpc) · [Use HTTP/2 for services | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/http2)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application currently uses a logging library and writes to standard output. You need to export its logs to Cloud Logging, and the logs must include metadata for every request. You want to use the simplest approach. What should you do?

options.text: Change your application’s logging library to the Cloud Logging library, and configure your application to export logs to Cloud Logging.
Update your application to output logs in JSON format, and add the necessary metadata to the JSON.
Update your application to output logs in CSV format, and add the necessary metadata to the CSV.
Install the Fluent Bit agent on each of your GKE nodes, and have the agent export all logs from /var/log.

questions.explanation:
GKE’s managed logging agent automatically collects container output written to standard output and sends it to Cloud Logging. When that output is a serialized JSON object, GKE stores it as a structured log entry, allowing request metadata to be included as queryable JSON fields.

**Learn more:** [About GKE logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs) · [Structured logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/structured-logging)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to deploy your application to a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. The application provides an HTTP-based health check at `/healthz`. You want to use that health-check endpoint to decide whether the load balancer should route traffic to the Pod.  
  
Which code snippet should be included in the Pod configuration?

options.text: ![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785597205861-wuly5y9m.jpg)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785597208113-wn9e7nze.jpg)

questions.explanation:
A `readinessProbe` determines whether a container is ready to receive traffic. When its HTTP GET check to `/healthz` on port `80` fails, Kubernetes marks the Pod unready and removes it from matching Service endpoints, so load balancers do not route normal traffic to it. A liveness probe is for detecting containers that should be restarted, not for traffic eligibility.

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a regulated financial company and lead a risk-calculation application running on Cloud Run. Binary Authorization for Cloud Run is enabled through an organization policy, and one attestor exists. Every application in the company is attested. Each application image is deployed through a CI/CD pipeline during a 1-hour change window at 11 PM local time. A new security issue requires deployment of a critical fix before the next change window. You created a new image containing the fix, and your manager approved the image in an email. What should you do?

options.text: Add the image to the exempt image patterns in the Binary Authorization policy.
Sign the image with your private key and ask the project admin to change the public key in the attestor.
Change the organization policy to temporarily disable Binary Authorization, and deploy the image.
Use the breakglass approach to deploy the image.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run breakglass is the emergency override for deploying or serving a container image that violates the Binary Authorization policy. It bypasses enforcement for that deployment while recording the breakglass justification and event in Cloud Audit Logs, preserving an auditable exception rather than changing the organization policy, exemption patterns, or attestor configuration.

**Learn more:** [Use breakglass (Cloud Run)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/run/using-breakglass-cloud-run) · [Set up overview for Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/run/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a business-critical production application deployed on Cloud Run. The application is reporting HTTP 500 errors that are affecting its usability. You want to receive an alert when errors exceed 15% of requests within a specified time window. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Function that consumes the Cloud Monitoring API. Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger the Cloud Function daily and alert you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.

Navigate to the Cloud Run page in the Google Cloud console, and select the service from the services list. Use the Metrics tab to visualize the number of errors for that revision, and refresh the page daily.
Create an alerting policy in Cloud Monitoring that alerts you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.
Create a Cloud Function that consumes the Cloud Monitoring API. Use Cloud Composer to trigger the Cloud Function daily and alert you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Monitoring alerting policy can continuously evaluate a metric condition, including a ratio of HTTP error responses to total HTTP responses, against a threshold over a configured evaluation window and send a notification when the threshold is breached.

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new Python 3 API that must be deployed to Cloud Run. Your Cloud Run service is behind an Apigee proxy. You need to make sure that the Cloud Run service runs with the already deployed Apigee proxy. You want to perform this testing as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Store the service code as a zip file in a Cloud Storage bucket. Deploy your application by using the gcloud run deploy --source command, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.
Use the Cloud Run emulator to test your application locally. Test the integration by pointing Apigee to your local Cloud Run emulator.
Build a container image locally, and push the image to Artifact Registry. Deploy the Image to Cloud Run, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.
Deploy your application directly from the current directory by using the gcloud run deploy --source command, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run can deploy directly from a local source directory using `gcloud run deploy --source .`; Cloud Build and buildpacks build the container image automatically, eliminating the separate local container-build and Artifact Registry push steps. The deployed Cloud Run endpoint can then be used by the existing Apigee proxy for integration testing.

**Learn more:** [Deploy services from source code | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/deploying-source-code) · [gcloud run deploy reference](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/run/deploy)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a large organization. Your team uses Git for source code management (SCM). You want to make sure the team follows Google-recommended best practices for managing code to achieve higher software-delivery rates. Which SCM process should the team use?

options.text: Each developer commits their code to the main branch before each product release, conducts testing, and rolls back if integration issues are detected.
Each group of developers copies the repository, commits their changes to their repository, and merges their code into the main repository before each product release.
Each developer creates a branch for their own work, commits their changes to their branch, and merges their code into the main branch daily.
Each group of developers creates a feature branch from the main branch for their work, commits their changes to their branch, and merges their code into the main branch before each major release.

questions.explanation:
Trunk-based development relies on short-lived branches and frequent integration into the main branch, commonly at least once per day. This keeps changes small, provides rapid integration feedback, and avoids the merge conflicts and delayed integration associated with release-based or long-lived group branches. Google Cloud’s DORA guidance identifies trunk-based development as a capability for improving software delivery performance.

**Learn more:** [DevOps capabilities | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/devops)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a continuous-integration pipeline with Cloud Build to automate deployment of new container images to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The pipeline builds the application from source code, runs unit and integration tests as separate steps, and pushes the container to Container Registry. The application runs on a Python web server.  
  
The Dockerfile is:  
  
```dockerfile  
FROM python:3.7-alpine -  
  
COPY . /app -  
  
WORKDIR /app -  
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  
CMD [ "gunicorn", "-w 4", "main:app" ]  
```  
  
You observe that Cloud Build runs take longer than expected to finish. You want to reduce the build time. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Select a virtual machine (VM) size with higher CPU for Cloud Build runs.
Deploy a Container Registry on a Compute Engine VM in a VPC, and use it to store the final images.
Cache the Docker image for subsequent builds using the -- cache-from argument in your build config file.
Change the base image in the Dockerfile to ubuntu:latest, and install Python 3.7 using a package manager utility.
Store application source code on Cloud Storage, and configure the pipeline to use gsutil to download the source code.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can use a higher-vCPU VM machine type to increase build speed, subject to potential startup-time tradeoffs. For Docker builds, a previously built image can be pulled and supplied through `--cache-from`, allowing unchanged image layers to be reused instead of rebuilt. These measures directly reduce Cloud Build execution time.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for speeding up builds](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/speeding-up-builds) · [Increase vCPU for builds](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/increase-vcpu-for-builds)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a company that runs an ecommerce website. The website stores customer order data in a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database. Data scientists on the marketing team access this data to run reports. Whenever they run these reports, the website’s performance is adversely affected. You want to give them access to up-to-date customer order datasets without affecting the website. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud Scheduler to run an hourly Cloud Function that exports the data from the Cloud SQL database into CSV format and sends the data to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Set up a Bigtable table for the data science team. Configure the application to perform dual writes to both Cloud SQL and Bigtable simultaneously.
Set up a BigQuery dataset for the data science team. Configure Datastream to replicate the relevant Cloud SQL tables in BigQuery.
Create a clone of the PostgreSQL database instance for the data science team. Schedule a job to create a new clone every 15 minutes.

questions.explanation:
Datastream provides change data capture and replication from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL into BigQuery. BigQuery is a separate analytics platform, so data scientists can run reporting queries against replicated, up-to-date order tables without placing that reporting workload on the transactional Cloud SQL database.

**Learn more:** [Stream data from PostgreSQL databases | Datastream](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/sources-postgresql) · [Configure a BigQuery destination | Datastream](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/configure-bigquery-destination?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is developing a backend application that implements the business logic for an interactive voice response (IVR) system supporting a payroll application. The IVR system has these technical characteristics:  
  
- Each customer phone call is linked to a unique IVR session.  
- The IVR system establishes a separate persistent gRPC connection to the backend for every session.  
- If a connection is interrupted, the IVR system creates a new connection, introducing slight latency for that call.  
  
You need to decide which compute environment to use for deploying the backend application. From current call data, you determine the following:  
  
- Call duration varies from 1 to 30 minutes.  
- Calls are generally placed during business hours.  
- Significant call spikes occur around certain known dates (for example, pay days) or when large payroll changes take place.  
  
You want to minimize cost, effort, and operational overhead. Where should you deploy the backend application?

options.text: Compute Engine
Google Kubernetes Engine cluster in Standard mode
Cloud Functions
Cloud Run

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run supports gRPC, including streaming gRPC when HTTP/2 is configured. A service request timeout can be configured up to 60 minutes, which accommodates sessions lasting as long as 30 minutes. Its managed, request-based autoscaling can add capacity for predictable call spikes and remove idle capacity as demand falls, minimizing infrastructure management and operational overhead.

**Learn more:** [Using gRPC | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/triggering/grpc) · [Configure request timeout for services | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/request-timeout)

You recently instrumented a new application with OpenTelemetry and want to check the latency of your application requests in Trace. You need to ensure that a particular request is always traced. What should you do?

options.text: Wait 10 minutes, then verify that Trace captures those types of requests automatically.
Write a custom script that sends this type of request repeatedly from your dev project.
Use the Trace API to apply custom attributes to the trace.
Add the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header to the request with the appropriate parameters.

questions.explanation:
The `X-Cloud-Trace-Context` header carries trace context including an options field that can mark the parent request as sampled. Setting the appropriate sampled parameter requests that downstream tracing components sample the request, whereas trace attributes and repeated requests do not control the sampling decision.

**Learn more:** [Instrument for Cloud Trace](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/setup?hl=en) · [Trace context](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/trace-context?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are monitoring a web application written in Go and deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine. You observe increased CPU and memory utilization. You need to identify which function consumes the most CPU and memory resources. What should you do?

options.text: Add print commands to the application source code to log when each function is called, and redeploy the application.

Create a Cloud Logging query that gathers the web application s logs. Write a Python script that calculates the difference between the timestamps from the beginning and the end of the application's longest functions to identify time-intensive functions.

Import OpenTelemetry and Trace export packages into your application, and create the trace provider. Review the latency data for your application on the Trace overview page, and identify which functions cause the most latency.
Import the Cloud Profiler package into your application, and initialize the Profiler agent. Review the generated flame graph in the Google Cloud console to identify time-intensive functions.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Profiler continuously collects low-overhead CPU-usage and memory-allocation data and attributes it to application source code. For Go applications on GKE, initializing the Profiler agent and examining its flame graph identifies the functions responsible for the greatest CPU time or memory consumption.

**Learn more:** [Profiling Go applications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/profiling-go) · [Cloud Profiler documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has a data warehouse that stores application information in BigQuery. The BigQuery data warehouse contains 2 PBs of user data. Recently, your company expanded its user base to include EU users and must comply with these requirements:  
  
- Your company must be able to delete all user account information when a user requests it.  
- All EU user data must be stored in one region specifically for EU users.  
  
Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use BigQuery federated queries to query data from Cloud Storage.
Create a dataset in the EU region that will keep information about EU users only.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket in the EU region to store information for EU users only.
Re-upload your data using to a Cloud Dataflow pipeline by filtering your user records out.
Use DML statements in BigQuery to update/delete user records based on their requests.

questions.explanation:
A BigQuery dataset can be created with the `EU` location so that its Core BigQuery Customer Data resides in the EU. BigQuery DML includes conditional `DELETE` and `UPDATE` operations, enabling removal of records associated with a particular user request.

**Learn more:** [Create datasets | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/datasets) · [Transform data with data manipulation language (DML) | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/data-manipulation-language)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an application that subscribes to and receives messages from a single Pub/Sub topic, then inserts corresponding rows into a database. The application runs on Linux and uses preemptible virtual machines to reduce costs. You must create a shutdown script that initiates a graceful shutdown.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Write a shutdown script that uses inter-process signals to notify the application process to disconnect from the database.
Write a shutdown script that broadcasts a message to all signed-in users that the Compute Engine instance is going down and instructs them to save current work and sign out.
Write a shutdown script that writes a file in a location that is being polled by the application once every five minutes. After the file is read, the application disconnects from the database.
Write a shutdown script that publishes a message to the Pub/Sub topic announcing that a shutdown is in progress. After the application reads the message, it disconnects from the database.

questions.explanation:
A Linux shutdown script can signal the local application process directly, allowing it to stop work and disconnect from the database during the limited preemption shutdown period. Compute Engine documents using a shutdown script to gracefully stop a running process before the operating system terminates remaining processes; preemptible VM shutdown handling is best-effort and limited to up to 30 seconds.

**Learn more:** [Create and use preemptible VMs](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/create-use-preemptible) · [Preemptible VM instances](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/preemptible)

You are a developer at an ecommerce company. You are responsible for developing a globally consistent shopping cart for logged-in users across both mobile and desktop clients. You must configure how items added to users’ carts are stored. How should you configure this cart service?

options.text: Store the carts in a separate Memorystore for Redis instance, and configure each user's IP address as the key.
Store the carts in a separate Firestore document, and configure each user ID as the document's key.
Insert the carts in a separate Spanner table, and configure each user's encrypted password as the primary key.
Create and store the carts in the shopping-cart HTTP cookie.

questions.explanation:
Firestore stores application data as documents and supports document names based on application-defined keys such as user IDs. A cart document keyed by the authenticated user ID gives the same user a durable shared cart across mobile and desktop clients, and Firestore supports real-time synchronization across client applications.

**Learn more:** [Firestore overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/overview) · [Firestore data model](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/data-model)

Your team has detected an error spike in an application running on Cloud Run in your production project. The application is configured to read messages from Pub/Sub topic A, process those messages, and write them to topic B. You want to run tests to identify the cause of the errors. You can use a set of mock messages for testing. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators on your local machine. Deploy the application locally, and change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO. Write mock messages to topic A, and then analyze the logs.
Use the gcloud CLI to write mock messages to topic A. Change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO, and then analyze the logs.
Deploy the Pub/Sub emulator on your local machine. Point the production application to your local Pub/Sub topics. Write mock messages to topic A, and then analyze the logs.
Use the Google Cloud console to write mock messages to topic A. Change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO, and then analyze the logs.

questions.explanation:
A local Pub/Sub emulator can provide a local stand-in for Pub/Sub, and the application must be configured to communicate with that emulator rather than the production Pub/Sub service. Running the application locally in a Cloud Run-compatible development environment allows mock messages to be processed and debug or informational logs to be analyzed without injecting test traffic into production or changing the production application to use a local endpoint.

**Learn more:** [Test a Cloud Run service locally](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/testing/local) · [Testing apps locally with the Pub/Sub emulator](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a Workflow to handle complex data analytics for your application. You intend to use the Workflow to run a Cloud Run job while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub topic, and subscribe the Cloud Run job to the topic.
Configure an Eventarc trigger to invoke the Cloud Run job, and include the trigger in a step of the Workflow.
Use the Cloud Run Admin API connector to execute the Cloud Run job within the Workflow.
Determine the entry point of the Cloud Run job, and send an HTTP request from the Workflow.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run jobs do not listen for or serve HTTP requests. Workflows should execute them through the Cloud Run Admin API connector, whose job `run` method triggers a new job execution.

**Learn more:** [Invoke Cloud Run functions or Cloud Run — Workflows](https://cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/calling-run-functions) · [Execute a Cloud Run job using Workflows](https://cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/tutorials/execute-cloud-run-jobs)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the lead developer at a company that offers a financial risk-calculation API. The API runs on Cloud Run and exposes a gRPC interface. You regularly develop optimizations for the risk calculators. You want to enable these optimizations for selected customers who registered to test them before rolling the optimization out to all customers. Your CI/CD pipeline has built a new image and stored it in Artifact Registry.  
  
Which rollout strategy should you use?

options.text: Migrate the traffic to the new service by setting Cloud Run’s traffic split based on the percentage of registered customers.
Migrate the traffic to the new service by using a blue/green deployment approach.
Migrate the traffic to the new service by using a feature flag for registered customers.
Migrate the traffic to the new service and enable session affinity for Cloud Run.

questions.explanation:
A feature flag supports targeted activation based on an application-level customer attribute, such as whether a customer registered for the optimization trial. Cloud Run revision traffic splitting routes a percentage of requests to revisions, not a specified set of customers, while session affinity only provides best-effort routing continuity and does not implement customer-based eligibility.

**Learn more:** [Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration) · [Set session affinity for services | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/session-affinity)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently developed an application that monitors a large number of stock prices. You need to configure Pub/Sub to receive messages and update the current stock price in an in-memory database. A downstream service needs the most current prices in the in-memory database to perform stock-trading transactions. Each message contains three pieces of information:  
  
- Stock symbol  
- Stock price  
- Timestamp for the update  
  
How should you configure your Pub/Sub subscription?

options.text: Create a push subscription with exactly-once delivery enabled.
Create a pull subscription with both ordering and exactly-once delivery turned off.
Create a pull subscription with ordering enabled, using the stock symbol as the ordering key.
Create a push subscription with both ordering and exactly-once delivery turned off.

questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub message ordering preserves the published order only for messages sharing an ordering key. Using the stock symbol as that key ensures that updates for each stock are processed in sequence, preventing an earlier update from overwriting a later price in the in-memory database. A pull subscription supports ordered delivery. Exactly-once delivery is not necessary for maintaining the latest value when processing is made idempotent.

**Learn more:** [Order messages | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/ordering) · [Pull subscriptions | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/pull)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an event-driven application and have created a topic to receive messages sent to Pub/Sub. You want the messages processed in real time. The application must be independent of any other system and incur costs only when new messages arrive. How should you configure the architecture?

options.text: Deploy the application on Compute Engine. Use a Pub/Sub push subscription to process new messages in the topic.
Deploy your code on Cloud Functions. Use a Pub/Sub trigger to invoke the Cloud Function. Use the Pub/Sub API to create a pull subscription to the Pub/Sub topic and read messages from it.
Deploy the application on Google Kubernetes Engine. Use the Pub/Sub API to create a pull subscription to the Pub/Sub topic and read messages from it.
Deploy your code on Cloud Functions. Use a Pub/Sub trigger to handle new messages in the topic.

questions.explanation:
A Pub/Sub-triggered Cloud Function is invoked in response to messages published to its configured Pub/Sub topic, providing event-driven processing without continuously running Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine resources. The trigger manages message delivery, so an additional manually created pull subscription is not required.

**Learn more:** [Configure a Cloud Run functions trigger with Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/use-with-cloud-function-triggers) · [Write Cloud Run functions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/write-functions)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that will store frequently accessed data in a Memorystore for Redis Cluster instance. You want to make the application resilient to network problems. You need to ensure the application gracefully handles client disconnections from a Redis instance to minimize disruption and maintain application stability. What should you do?

options.text: Immediately terminate the application instance upon detecting a Redis disconnection to force a restart, and wait for clients to reconnect to the cache as soon as the application becomes available.
Configure the Redis client to reconnect after a fixed delay of 60 seconds.
Use Memorystore’s automatic failover mechanisms to make the Redis cache available in a secondary zone.
Implement exponential backoff with a jitter when reconnecting after a disconnection. Configure client-side caching to serve data during brief outages.

questions.explanation:
Exponential backoff with jitter spaces reconnection attempts and randomizes their timing, avoiding a synchronized retry surge that can overload Redis after a disconnect. Client-side caching can supply already cached data through a brief cache outage, reducing disruption while the connection is restored.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for Memorystore for Redis Cluster](https://cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/cluster/general-best-practices)

questions.question:
You need to view the memory usage of an application deployed on Compute Engine.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Install the Stackdriver Client Library.
Install the Stackdriver Monitoring Agent.
Use the Stackdriver Metrics Explorer.
Use the Google Cloud Platform Console.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine does not provide guest memory utilization as a default metric. Installing the Stackdriver Monitoring Agent on the VM collects memory metrics and sends them to Cloud Monitoring for viewing. The current replacement for this legacy agent is the Google Cloud Ops Agent.\
\
**Learn more:** [Monitoring agent overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/agent/monitoring) · [Observe and monitor VMs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/observe-monitor-vms)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
You need to view the memory usage of an application deployed on Compute Engine.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the appropriate service accounts, and use Workload Identity to run the pods.
Store the application credentials as Kubernetes Secrets, and expose them as environment variables.
Configure the appropriate routing rules, and use a VPC-native cluster to directly connect to the database.
Store the application credentials using Cloud Key Management Service, and retrieve them whenever a database connection is made.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets Pods use a Kubernetes service account with IAM permissions for Spanner and provides short-lived Application Default Credentials. This avoids storing static service-account credentials in Kubernetes Secrets or retrieving them from another service, while allowing standard Spanner client libraries to authenticate with minimal code changes.

**Learn more:** [Connect Spanner with a GKE cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/connect-gke-cluster) · [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an online gaming platform as a microservices application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Social-media users are reporting long load times for particular URL requests to the application. You need to investigate application performance bottlenecks and determine which HTTP requests have a significantly high-latency span in user requests. What should you do?

options.text: Configure GKE workload metrics using kubectl. Select all Pods to send their metrics to Cloud Monitoring. Create a custom dashboard of application metrics in Cloud Monitoring to determine performance bottlenecks of your GKE cluster.

Update your microservices to log HTTP request methods and URL paths to STDOUT. Use the logs router to send container logs to Cloud Logging. Create filters in Cloud Logging to evaluate the latency of user requests across different methods and URL paths.

Instrument your microservices by installing the OpenTelemetry tracing package. Update your application code to send traces to Trace for inspection and analysis. Create an analysis report on Trace to analyze user requests.

Install tcpdump on your GKE nodes. Run tcpdump to capture network traffic over an extended period of time to collect data. Analyze the data files using Wireshark to determine the cause of high latency.

questions.explanation:
OpenTelemetry instrumentation creates distributed traces that follow an HTTP request through the microservices and record timing for each span. Cloud Trace can inspect individual traces and aggregate span latency, enabling identification of the operations responsible for slow user requests.

**Learn more:** [Instrument for Cloud Trace](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/setup?hl=en) · [Traces and spans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/traces-and-spans)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a microservices application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that broadcasts livestreams. You anticipate unpredictable traffic patterns and significant variation in the number of concurrent users. Your application must meet these requirements:  
  
- Automatically scale during popular events while maintaining high availability.  
- Remain resilient if hardware failures occur.  
  
How should you configure the deployment parameters? (Choose two.)

options.text: Distribute your workload evenly using a multi-zonal node pool.
Distribute your workload evenly using multiple zonal node pools.
Use cluster autoscaler to resize the number of nodes in the node pool, and use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale the workload.
Create a managed instance group for Compute Engine with the cluster nodes. Configure autoscaling rules for the managed instance group.

Create alerting policies in Cloud Monitoring based on GKE CPU and memory utilization. Ask an on-duty engineer to scale the workload by executing a script when CPU and memory usage exceed predefined thresholds.

questions.explanation:
A multi-zonal node pool spreads worker nodes across multiple zones, improving availability and resilience to a zone or underlying hardware failure. The GKE cluster autoscaler automatically resizes node pools within configured limits as capacity is needed, while a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically increases or decreases workload Pods based on resource utilization or other metrics. Together, these mechanisms provide both resilient node placement and automatic workload and node-capacity scaling.

**Learn more:** [About GKE cluster autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-autoscaler) · [Horizontal Pod autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/horizontalpodautoscaler)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using the Cloud Client Library to upload an image from your application to Cloud Storage. Application users report that the upload occasionally fails to finish and that the client library returns an HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout error. You want to make the application more resilient to errors. What changes should you make to the application?

options.text: Write an exponential backoff process around the client library call.
Write a one-second wait time backoff process around the client library call.
Design a retry button in the application and ask users to click if the error occurs.
Create a queue for the object and inform the users that the application will try again in 10 minutes.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage identifies HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout as a transient failure that should be retried using truncated exponential backoff. Increasing the delay between retries helps prevent retry traffic from compounding a temporary service problem.

**Learn more:** [Retry strategy | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/retry-strategy) · [HTTP status and error codes for JSON | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/json_api/v1/status-codes)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently migrated an on-premises monolithic application to a microservices application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application depends on backend services that remain on-premises, including a CRM system and a MySQL database containing personally identifiable information (PII). The backend services must stay on-premises to satisfy regulatory requirements.  
  
You established a Cloud VPN connection between your on-premises data center and Google Cloud. Some requests from the GKE microservices application to the backend services are failing because latency is caused by fluctuating bandwidth, resulting in application crashes. How should you resolve the latency issues?

options.text: Use Memorystore to cache frequently accessed PII data from the on-premises MySQL database
Use Istio to create a service mesh that includes the microservices on GKE and the on-premises services
Increase the number of Cloud VPN tunnels for the connection between Google Cloud and the on-premises services
Decrease the network layer packet size by decreasing the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) value from its default value on Cloud VPN

questions.explanation:
Adding Cloud VPN tunnels distributes traffic across tunnels and can increase aggregate bandwidth between Google Cloud and the on-premises environment, reducing latency caused by an overloaded or variable-bandwidth tunnel. Google Cloud documents multiple tunnels as the approach for increasing Cloud VPN throughput.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies to increase bandwidth](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies-increase-bandwidth) · [Cloud VPN overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your infrastructure team is responsible for creating and managing Compute Engine VMs. The team uses the Google Cloud console and the gcloud CLI to provision resources in the development environment.  
  
You must ensure that every Compute Engine VM is labeled correctly for compliance reasons. When labels are missing, you need to implement corrective actions so the labels are configured appropriately without changing the existing deployment process. You want the most scalable approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use a Cloud Audit Logs trigger to invoke a Cloud Function when a Compute Engine VM is created. Check for missing labels and assign them if necessary.
Deploy resources with Terraform. Use the gcloud terraform vet command with a policy to ensure that every Compute Engine VM that is provisioned by Terraform has labels set.
Write a script to check all Compute Engine VMs for missing labels regularly by using Cloud Scheduler. Use the script to assign the labels.
Check all Compute Engine VMs for missing labels regularly. Use the console to assign the labels.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Audit Logs–based event trigger can invoke a function for each Compute Engine VM creation event. The function can validate the VM labels and update the instance when required, providing automatic, event-driven remediation that applies regardless of whether the VM was created through the console or gcloud CLI. Eventarc supports delivering matching Cloud Audit Logs events to Cloud Run functions, and Compute Engine audit-log triggers are supported.

**Learn more:** [Create a trigger for Cloud Run functions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/eventarc/standard/docs/functions/create-triggers) · [Known issues for Eventarc Standard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/eventarc/docs/issues)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building and running containers in different Google Cloud projects. The application you are developing must access Google Cloud services from within Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). What should you do?

options.text: Assign a Google service account to the GKE nodes.
Use a Google service account to run the Pod with Workload Identity.
Store the Google service account credentials as a Kubernetes Secret.
Use a Google service account with GKE role-based access control (RBAC).

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets a Pod use a Kubernetes service account mapped to a Google Cloud IAM service account or granted direct IAM access, providing short-lived, least-privilege credentials for calling Google Cloud services. It avoids sharing node credentials and avoids storing service-account keys in Kubernetes Secrets.

**Learn more:** [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity) · [Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your ecommerce application’s user base is growing rapidly, and excessive requests to your backend API are causing performance problems. Your team develops and manages this API. The Cloud SQL backend database is struggling with the heavy demand, resulting in latency and timeouts. You need to implement a solution that optimizes API performance and enhances the user experience. What should you do?

options.text: Use Apigee to expose your API. Use Memorystore for Redis to cache frequently accessed data. Implement exponential backoff in the application to retry failed requests.
Use Apigee to expose your API. Implement rate limiting and access control policies in Apigee to control API traffic. Use Pub/Sub to queue requests to prevent database overload.
Use Cloud Load Balancing to expose your API. Use Cloud CDN in front of the load balancer to cache responses. Implement exponential backoff to retry failed requests.

Use Cloud Load Balancing to expose your API. Increase the memory for the database instances to handle more concurrent requests. Implement a custom rate-limiting mechanism in your application code to control API requests.

questions.explanation:
Memorystore for Redis provides low-latency, high-throughput caching for heavily accessed data, including frequently accessed queries and pages. Serving cache hits from Redis reduces repeated Cloud SQL reads, relieving database pressure and lowering API latency. Apigee is suitable for exposing and managing the API, while exponential backoff avoids an immediate flood of retries when transient failures occur. [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview)

**Learn more:** [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview) · [Apigee rate limiting](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/develop/rate-limiting)
