questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work on an application that uses Cloud Spanner as its primary datastore. New application features have sometimes introduced performance regressions. You want to prevent performance problems by running an automated Cloud Build performance test for every commit. If several commits occur at the same time, the tests could run concurrently. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new project with a random name for every build. Load the required data. Delete the project after the test is run.
Create a new Cloud Spanner instance for every build. Load the required data. Delete the Cloud Spanner instance after the test is run.
Create a project with a Cloud Spanner instance and the required data. Adjust the Cloud Build build file to automatically restore the data to its previous state after the test is run.
Start the Cloud Spanner emulator locally. Load the required data. Shut down the emulator after the test is run.

questions.explanation:
Each concurrent performance test needs its own Cloud Spanner instance so that its workload, compute capacity, and test data are isolated from other builds. This produces reliable performance measurements; the temporary instance can be deleted after the test completes. The Spanner emulator is unsuitable because its performance and scalability are not comparable to the production service.

**Learn more:** [Performance overview | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/performance) · [Emulate Spanner locally | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/emulator?hl=en)

questions.question: An application runs on hundreds of Compute Engine instances in a managed instance group (MIG) across multiple zones. A new instance template must be deployed immediately to remediate a critical vulnerability, without affecting the service. Which MIG setting should be configured after updating the instance template?

options.text: Set the Max Surge to 100%.
Set the Update mode to Opportunistic.
Set the Maximum Unavailable to 100%.
Set the Minimum Wait time to 0 seconds.

questions.explanation:
`maxSurge` controls how many additional VMs a MIG can create above its target size during an automated update. Setting it to 100% permits replacement capacity to be created rapidly while the existing instances continue serving traffic, minimizing service disruption during the rollout.\
\
**Learn more:** [Automatically apply VM configuration updates in a MIG](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/rolling-out-updates-to-managed-instance-groups)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: An application runs on hundreds of Compute Engine instances in a managed instance group (MIG) across multiple zones. A new instance template must be deployed immediately to remediate a critical vulnerability, without affecting the service. Which MIG setting should be configured after updating the instance template?

options.text: Perform a rolling deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is complete.
Perform A/B testing, and test your application periodically after the new tests are implemented.
Perform a blue/green deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is. complete.
Perform a canary deployment, and test your new application periodically after the new version is deployed.

questions.explanation:
A blue/green deployment keeps the previous (blue) version available while the new (green) version is deployed and validated. If the new version fails, traffic can be rapidly switched back to the existing blue version. Google Cloud describes blue-green strategies as maintaining original and new environments concurrently and enabling a quick rollback to the existing environment when needed.

**Learn more:** [Standard cluster upgrades | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-upgrades)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises containerized service, written in the current stable version of Python 3, that is available only to users in the United States. The service receives high traffic during the day and no traffic at night. You need to migrate this application to Google Cloud and track error logs in Error Reporting after migration. You want to minimize the cost and effort required for these tasks. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the code on Cloud Run. Configure your code to write errors to standard error.
Deploy the code on Cloud Run. Configure your code to stream errors to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Deploy the code on a GKE Autopilot cluster. Configure your code to write error logs to standard error.
Deploy the code on a GKE Autopilot cluster. Configure your code to write error logs to a Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run runs containerized services with automatic scaling and can scale to zero when there are no requests, reducing idle-time cost. Container logs written to standard error are automatically sent to Cloud Logging, and exceptions with stack traces are captured by Error Reporting; this avoids Kubernetes management and custom log export handling.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [Logging and viewing logs in Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/logging)

options.text: Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API for redaction of the review dataset.
Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API for de-identification of the review dataset.
Use the Cloud Natural Language Processing API for redaction of the review dataset.
Use the Cloud Natural Language Processing API for de-identification of the review dataset.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Data Loss Prevention can detect personally identifiable information in review text and de-identify it through transformations such as masking, tokenization, or removal. This preserves data for analysis while helping meet privacy requirements such as GDPR. Cloud Natural Language Processing performs language analysis, not data de-identification.

**Learn more:** [De-identifying sensitive data | Sensitive Data Protection | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-sensitive-data)

You are pushing container images to Artifact Registry and deploying a containerized microservices application to GKE. After deployment, you find that the services are not behaving as expected. You run `kubectl get pods` to inspect the application Pods and discover that one Pod is in a `CrashLoopBackoff` state. How should you troubleshoot the Pod?

options.text: Connect to the problematic Pod by running the kubectl exec -it POD_NAME - /bin/bash command where the POD_NAME parameter is the name of the problematic Pod. Inspect the logs in the /var/log/messages folder to determine the root cause.

Execute the gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID command where the PROJECT_ID parameter is the name of the project where your Artifact Registry resides. Inspect the IAM bindings of the node pool s service account. Validate if the service account has the roles/artifactregistry.reader role.

Run the kubectl logs POD_NAME command where the POD_NAME parameter is the name of the problematic Pod. Analyze the logs of the Pod from previous runs to determine the root cause of failed start attempts of the Pod.

In the Google Cloud console, navigate to Cloud Logging in the project of the cluster’s VPC. Enter a filter to show denied egress traffic to the Private Google Access CIDR range. Validate if egress traffic is denied from your GKE cluster to the Private Google Access CIDR range.

questions.explanation:
A `CrashLoopBackOff` occurs when a container repeatedly fails and is restarted with an increasing delay. Inspecting the container logs exposes the application startup error that caused the failed attempts. For a prior crashed container instance, Kubernetes provides `kubectl logs POD_NAME --previous` (and `-c CONTAINER_NAME` when needed).

**Learn more:** [Debug Running Pods](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-running-pod/) · [kubectl logs reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_logs/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a Compute Engine-hosted application in project A that must securely authenticate to a Cloud Pub/Sub topic in project B.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the instances with a service account owned by project B. Add the service account as a Cloud Pub/Sub publisher to project A.
Configure the instances with a service account owned by project A. Add the service account as a publisher on the topic.
Configure Application Default Credentials to use the private key of a service account owned by project B. Add the service account as a Cloud Pub/Sub publisher to project A.
Configure Application Default Credentials to use the private key of a service account owned by project A. Add the service account as a publisher on the topic

questions.explanation:
A workload running on Compute Engine should use the credentials of its attached service account. Granting that project A service account the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic in project B authorizes it to publish cross-project without managing a private service-account key.

**Learn more:** [Authenticate to Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/authentication) · [Publish messages to topics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/publisher)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a marquee stateless web application that will run on Google Cloud. Incoming user-traffic rates are expected to be unpredictable, with no traffic on certain days and large spikes on others. You need the application to automatically scale up and down while minimizing the cost of running it. What should you do?

options.text: Build the application in Python with Firestore as the database. Deploy the application to Cloud Run.
Build the application in C# with Firestore as the database. Deploy the application to App Engine flexible environment.
Build the application in Python with CloudSQL as the database. Deploy the application to App Engine standard environment.
Build the application in Python with Firestore as the database. Deploy the application to a Compute Engine managed instance group with autoscaling.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run automatically adds instances to meet demand and removes idle instances, including scaling to zero when there is no traffic. Its default request-based billing charges for request processing rather than idle runtime. Firestore is a serverless database with usage-based charges, so the combination supports unpredictable spikes without requiring continuously running compute or database capacity.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [Cloud Run billing settings for services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/billing-settings)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You migrated your applications to Google Cloud Platform while retaining your existing monitoring platform. You now determine that your notification system is too slow for time-critical problems.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Replace your entire monitoring platform with Stackdriver.
Install the Stackdriver agents on your Compute Engine instances.
Use Stackdriver to capture and alert on logs, then ship them to your existing platform.
Migrate some traffic back to your old platform and perform AB testing on the two platforms concurrently.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging can collect Google Cloud log data and use log-based alerting policies to notify on specified events or messages, providing cloud-native alerting for time-critical conditions. Log entries can also be routed to an existing monitoring platform, allowing that platform to remain in use while alerting is handled in Google Cloud.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Logging overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/overview?hl=en) · [Configure log-based alerting policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/alerting/log-based-alerts)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: Which service should HipLocal use for its public APIs?

options.text: Cloud Armor
Cloud Functions
Cloud Endpoints
Shielded Virtual Machines

questions.explanation:
Cloud Endpoints is an API-management service that secures and manages APIs. Its Extensible Service Proxy validates incoming requests and supports authentication, logging, monitoring, and metrics, aligning with the requirements for strongly authenticated public APIs and API usage monitoring.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Endpoints documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs) · [Architectural overview of Cloud Endpoints](https://docs.cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/grpc/architecture-overview)

questions.question: Which service should HipLocal use for its public APIs?

options.text: Enable Binary Authorization, and configure it to attest that no vulnerabilities exist in a container image.
Upload the built container images to your Docker Hub instance, and scan them for vulnerabilities.
Enable the Container Scanning API in Artifact Registry, and scan the built container images for vulnerabilities.
Add Artifact Registry to your Aqua Security instance, and scan the built container images for vulnerabilities.

questions.explanation:
The Container Scanning API integrates with Artifact Registry to automatically scan container images pushed to the registry for vulnerabilities. The resulting vulnerability metadata is available in Google Cloud, so the deployment pipeline can consume it without changing the existing image destination or adding an external scanning system.

**Learn more:** [Enable or disable automatic scanning | Artifact Analysis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/enable-automatic-scanning) · [Container scanning overview | Artifact Analysis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/container-scanning-overview)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an application consisting of several microservices. Each microservice has its own RESTful API and will be deployed as an individual Kubernetes Service. You want to ensure that consumers of these APIs are not affected when an API changes, while also ensuring that third-party systems are not interrupted when new API versions are released. How should you configure the connection to the application according to Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Use an Ingress that uses the API's URL to route requests to the appropriate backend.
Leverage a Service Discovery system, and connect to the backend specified by the request.
Use multiple clusters, and use DNS entries to route requests to separate versioned backends.
Combine multiple versions in the same service, and then specify the API version in the POST request.

questions.explanation:
Major API versions should be exposed through distinct URL paths so existing clients can keep calling their current version while newer versions are introduced. An Ingress provides host- and path-based HTTP routing to the appropriate Kubernetes Service backend, allowing versioned API URLs to be routed independently without disrupting existing consumers. Google Cloud Endpoints likewise recommends including the major version in the base path and routing requests based on that path.

**Learn more:** [API lifecycle management](https://docs.cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/lifecycle-management)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have created a Cloud Function that accesses other Google Cloud resources. You want to secure the environment according to the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new service account that has Editor authority to access the resources. The deployer is given permission to get the access token.
Create a new service account that has a custom IAM role to access the resources. The deployer is given permission to get the access token.
Create a new service account that has Editor authority to access the resources. The deployer is given permission to act as the new service account.
Create a new service account that has a custom IAM role to access the resources. The deployer is given permission to act as the new service account.

questions.explanation:
A dedicated service account should receive a custom IAM role containing only the permissions the Cloud Function needs. The deployer must have permission to act as that service account in order to attach it as the function’s runtime identity; this requires `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`, commonly granted through the Service Account User role. Editor is overly broad, and `getAccessToken` is for service-account impersonation rather than attaching the runtime service account.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run functions IAM roles](https://docs.cloud.google.com/functions/docs/reference/iam/roles) · [Roles for service account authentication](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-permissions)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a flower-ordering application. At present, it has three microservices:  
  
- Order Service (receives orders)  
- Order Fulfillment Service (processes orders)  
- Notification Service (notifies the customer when an order is filled)  
  
You need to decide how these services will communicate. Incoming orders must be processed quickly, and you need to gather order information for fulfillment. You also need to ensure that orders are not lost between services and that the services can communicate asynchronously. How should the requests be processed?

options.text: ![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600316923-st0x7ey7.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600319741-yotmzsuy.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600322740-rpevw4nj.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600325186-o4qrw9rj.png)

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Pub/Sub is an asynchronous messaging service that decouples producers from consumers. Publishing each order to Pub/Sub lets the Order Service accept requests promptly while the Order Fulfillment Service processes them independently. Pub/Sub retains and redelivers unacknowledged messages, preventing a transient processing failure from losing an order. Firestore provides durable storage for the fulfillment information, and a second Pub/Sub event can asynchronously trigger the Notification Service after fulfillment.

**Learn more:** [What is Pub/Sub?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview) · [Overview of the Pub/Sub service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/pubsub-basics)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your operations team has requested that you create a script to list the Cloud Bigtable, Memorystore, and Cloud SQL databases operating within a project. The script must let users provide a filter expression to restrict the displayed results. How should you retrieve the data?

options.text: Use the HBase API, Redis API, and MySQL connection to retrieve database lists. Combine the results, and then apply the filter to display the results
Use the HBase API, Redis API, and MySQL connection to retrieve database lists. Filter the results individually, and then combine them to display the results
Run gcloud bigtable instances list, gcloud redis instances list, and gcloud sql databases list. Use a filter within the application, and then display the results
Run gcloud bigtable instances list, gcloud redis instances list, and gcloud sql databases list. Use --filter flag with each command, and then display the results

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud CLI list commands support the `--filter` flag, which applies a Boolean filter expression to each resource item before it is listed. Using the service-specific `gcloud ... list` commands with `--filter` provides inventory retrieval and filtering without using database data-plane connections.

**Learn more:** [gcloud topic filters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/topic/filters) · [gcloud bigtable instances list](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/bigtable/instances/list)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a corporate tool on Compute Engine for the finance department that must authenticate users and confirm that they belong to the finance department. All company employees use G Suite.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy on the HTTP(s) load balancer and restrict access to a Google Group containing users in the finance department. Verify the provided JSON Web Token within the application.

Enable Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy on the HTTP(s) load balancer and restrict access to a Google Group containing users in the finance department. Issue client-side certificates to everybody in the finance team and verify the certificates in the application.
Configure Cloud Armor Security Policies to restrict access to only corporate IP address ranges. Verify the provided JSON Web Token within the application.

Configure Cloud Armor Security Policies to restrict access to only corporate IP address ranges. Issue client side certificates to everybody in the finance team and verify the certificates in the application.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy authenticates users with their Google accounts and supports group-based access control, allowing access to be limited to a Google Group for the finance department. A Compute Engine application protected by IAP should validate the signed JWT assertion received from IAP to ensure requests were authorized by IAP.

**Learn more:** [Identity-Aware Proxy overview](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview) · [Securing your app with signed headers](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/signed-headers-howto)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that uses a distributed microservices architecture. You need to measure performance and system-resource utilization in one Java-written microservice. What should you do?

options.text: Instrument the service with Cloud Profiler to measure CPU utilization and method-level execution times in the service.
Instrument the service with Debugger to investigate service errors.
Instrument the service with Cloud Trace to measure request latency.
Instrument the service with OpenCensus to measure service latency, and write custom metrics to Cloud Monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Profiler continuously collects CPU-usage and memory-allocation profiling data from production applications and attributes it to source code. Java profiling supports CPU-time profiles, enabling analysis of resource consumption and execution time at the function or method level.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Profiler overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler) · [Profiling Java applications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/profiling-java)

You have a GKE cluster with three TPU nodes. An ML training job is running on the cluster, and you notice Cloud Logging entries similar to the following. To determine the root cause of a performance problem, you need to view all stdout logs from containers running on the TPU nodes. What should you do?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783714805360-qepfr9pu.png)

options.text: ![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783714809612-ik82yv3e.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783714811736-eoj9pmct.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783714813763-nz1lxa3h.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783714815874-0vkx85f1.png)

questions.explanation:
Container stdout output is recorded under resource.type="k8s_container" (not k8s_node, which covers node-level system logs), so the query must use that resource type together with log_id("stdout"). Matching labels."compute.googleapis.com/resource_name" against the shared node-name prefix with a regular expression (=~ "gke-tpu-9243ec28.*") returns stdout entries from every TPU node in the pool rather than being scoped to a single training job's pods.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot TPUs in GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/tpus)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
HipLocal's .NET-based authentication service intermittently fails under load.  
  
What should the company do?

options.text: Use App Engine for autoscaling.
Use Cloud Functions for autoscaling.
Use a Compute Engine cluster for the service.
Use a dedicated Compute Engine virtual machine instance for the service.

questions.explanation:
App Engine provides a managed platform for .NET web applications and automatically scales application instances based on incoming load, improving availability during intermittent demand without requiring management of a Compute Engine cluster or individual VM.\
\
**Learn more:** [App Engine flexible environment overview](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/flexible/overview) · [The .NET runtime for App Engine flexible environment](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/flexible/dotnet/runtime)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
HipLocal's .NET-based authentication service intermittently fails under load.  
  
What should the company do?

options.text: Reserve a static external IP address and assign it to an HTTP(S) load balancing service's forwarding rule. Clients should use this IP address to connect to the service.

Reserve a static external IP address and assign it to an HTTP(S) load balancing service's forwarding rule. Then, define an A record in Cloud DNS. Clients should use the name of the A record to connect to the service.
Ensure that clients use Compute Engine internal DNS by connecting to the instance name with the url https://[INSTANCE_NAME].[ZONE].c. [PROJECT_ID].internal/.
Ensure that clients use Compute Engine internal DNS by connecting to the instance name with the url https://[API_NAME]/[API_VERSION]/.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine internal DNS automatically creates an A record for a VM’s primary internal IPv4 address. Clients in the same VPC can use the zonal internal FQDN `INSTANCE_NAME.ZONE.c.PROJECT_ID.internal` to resolve and connect to that internal address.

**Learn more:** [Access VMs using internal DNS | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/networking/using-internal-dns) · [Overview of internal DNS | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/internal-dns)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application runs as a container in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. You need to add a secret to the application by using a secure method. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Kubernetes Secret, and pass the Secret as an environment variable to the container.
Enable Application-layer Secret Encryption on the cluster using a Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) key.

Store the credential in Cloud KMS. Create a Google service account (GSA) to read the credential from Cloud KMS. Export the GSA as a .json file, and pass the .json file to the container as a volume which can read the credential from Cloud KMS.

Store the credential in Secret Manager. Create a Google service account (GSA) to read the credential from Secret Manager. Create a Kubernetes service account (KSA) to run the container. Use Workload Identity to configure your KSA to act as a GSA.

questions.explanation:
Store the credential in Secret Manager and grant the workload only the required access through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. This lets the Pod’s Kubernetes service account use a Google service account identity without distributing a long-lived service-account JSON key, while keeping secret material outside in-cluster Kubernetes Secret storage. Google recommends Workload Identity Federation for GKE to securely access Google Cloud services and Secret Manager from GKE workloads.

**Learn more:** [Access secrets stored outside GKE clusters using client libraries](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/workload-identity-secrets) · [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer working for a local concert venue. Customers use your company’s website to buy tickets for events. You must give customers immediate confirmation when their chosen seat has been reserved. How should you design the ticket-ordering process?

options.text: Add the seat reservation to a Cloud Tasks queue, which triggers Workflows to process the seat reservation.
Publish the seat reservation to a Pub/Sub topic. Configure the backend service to use Eventarc to process the seat reservation on GKE.
Upload the seat reservation to a Cloud Storage bucket, which triggers an event to a Cloud Run service that processes the orders.

Submit the seat reservation in an HTTP POST request to an Application Load Balancer. Configure the Application Load Balancer to distribute the request to a Compute Engine managed instance group that processes the reservation.

questions.explanation:
A synchronous HTTP request can be routed by an Application Load Balancer to backend Compute Engine instances in a managed instance group. The reservation service can complete the seat-reservation transaction and return a success or failure response in that same request, providing immediate confirmation. Cloud Tasks, Pub/Sub, Eventarc, and Cloud Storage event triggers are asynchronous mechanisms and do not provide completion confirmation in the original customer request.

**Learn more:** [Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/application-load-balancer) · [Backend services overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-service)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application consists of a collection of loosely coupled services orchestrated by code running on Compute Engine. You want the application to be able to easily start new Compute Engine instances that locate and use a particular version of a service. How should this be configured?

options.text: Define your service endpoint information as metadata that is retrieved at runtime and used to connect to the desired service.
Define your service endpoint information as label data that is retrieved at runtime and used to connect to the desired service.
Define your service endpoint information to be retrieved from an environment variable at runtime and used to connect to the desired service.
Define your service to use a fixed hostname and port to connect to the desired service. Replace the service at the endpoint with your new version.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine custom metadata can hold service endpoint configuration that an instance retrieves at runtime through the metadata server. This allows newly started instances to discover the endpoint for the required service version without hard-coding that information into the instance or application deployment.

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a web application that publishes messages to Pub/Sub. You plan to build new application versions locally and must quickly test Pub/Sub integration for every new build. How should you configure local testing?

options.text: In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the API Library, and enable the Pub/Sub API. When developing locally configure your application to call pubsub.googleapis.com.

Install the Pub/Sub emulator using gcloud, and start the emulator with a valid Google Project ID. When developing locally, configure your applicat.cn to use the local emulator by exporting the PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST variable.
Run the gcloud config set api_endpoint_overrides/pubsub https://pubsubemulator.googleapis.com.com/ command to change the Pub/Sub endpoint prior to starting the application.

Install Cloud Code on the integrated development environment (IDE). Navigate to Cloud APIs, and enable Pub/Sub against a valid Google Project IWhen developing locally, configure your application to call pubsub.googleapis.com.

questions.explanation:
The Pub/Sub emulator provides a local emulation of the production Pub/Sub service for development and testing. Install and start it with the Google Cloud CLI, then set `PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST` so the application’s Pub/Sub client connects to the local emulator instead of the production service.

**Learn more:** [Testing apps locally with the Pub/Sub emulator](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a microservice-based ecommerce platform on Google Cloud that uses a Cloud Function to send confirmation emails to a third-party email service provider. Your company has just launched a marketing campaign, and some customers report not receiving order-confirmation emails. You find that the services invoking the Cloud Function receive HTTP 500 errors. You need to change how emails are handled to minimize email loss. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the Cloud Function's timeout to nine minutes.
Configure the sender application to publish the outgoing emails in a message to a Pub/Sub topic. Update the Cloud Function configuration to consume the Pub/Sub queue.

Configure the sender application to write emails to Memorystore and then trigger the Cloud Function. When the function is triggered, it reads the email details from Memorystore and sends them to the email service.
Configure the sender application to retry the execution of the Cloud Function every one second if a request fails.

questions.explanation:
Publishing outgoing-email details to Pub/Sub creates a durable asynchronous boundary between the sender and the email-delivery function. Event-driven functions can retry failed invocations, and Pub/Sub supports at-least-once delivery, so a transient function or third-party email-service failure is less likely to cause the email request to be lost. The email-processing function must be idempotent because a message can be delivered more than once.

**Learn more:** [Configure event-driven function retries](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/tips/function-retries) · [Event-driven architecture with Pub/Sub](https://cloud.google.com/solutions/event-driven-architecture-pubsub)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A new version of your containerized application has been tested and is ready for production deployment on Google Kubernetes Engine. You could not fully load-test the new version in pre-production environments, and you must ensure it has no performance issues after deployment. The deployment must be automated. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Load Balancing to slowly ramp up traffic between versions. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues.
Deploy the application via a continuous delivery pipeline using canary deployments. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues. and ramp up traffic as the metrics support it.
Deploy the application via a continuous delivery pipeline using blue/green deployments. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues, and launch fully when the metrics support it.

Deploy the application using kubectl and set the spec.updateStrategv.type to RollingUpdate. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues, and run the kubectl rollback command if there are any issues.

questions.explanation:
A canary deployment in a continuous delivery pipeline progressively releases the new application version to a subset of production traffic while monitoring its performance. Traffic can be increased only as the observed metrics support the rollout, limiting the impact of any performance regression. Cloud Deploy supports automated canary progression and can use Google Cloud Observability metrics for rollout analysis.

**Learn more:** [Use a canary deployment strategy](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary) · [Canary deployments to GKE using service-based networking](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary/gke/service-networking)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have containerized a legacy application that keeps its configuration on an NFS share. You need to deploy this application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and do not want it to serve traffic until the configuration has been retrieved. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gsutil utility to copy files from within the Docker container at startup, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
Create a PersistentVolumeClaim on the GKE cluster. Access the configuration files from the volume, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
Use the COPY statement in the Dockerfile to load the configuration into the container image. Verify that the configuration is available, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
Add a startup script to the GKE instance group to mount the NFS share at node startup. Copy the configuration files into the container, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.

questions.explanation:
A PersistentVolumeClaim provides Kubernetes-managed storage to the Pod and mounts the bound volume for the workload. NFS-backed storage can be exposed through a PersistentVolume/PersistentVolumeClaim, allowing the container ENTRYPOINT to access the configuration before it starts the service. This keeps configuration external to the container image and avoids node-specific mount scripts.

**Learn more:** [GKE persistent volumes and provisioning](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/persistent-volumes) · [Access Filestore instances with the Filestore CSI driver](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/persistent-volumes/filestore-csi-driver)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an ecommerce web application that uses the App Engine standard environment and Memorystore for Redis. When a user signs in to the app, the application caches that user's information (for example, session, name, address, and preferences) for fast retrieval during checkout.  
  
While testing the application in a browser, you receive a 502 Bad Gateway error. You have determined that the application is not connecting to Memorystore. What is causing this error?

options.text: Your Memorystore for Redis instance was deployed without a public IP address.
You configured your Serverless VPC Access connector in a different region than your App Engine instance.
The firewall rule allowing a connection between App Engine and Memorystore was removed during an infrastructure update by the DevOps team.
You configured your application to use a Serverless VPC Access connector on a different subnet in a different availability zone than your App Engine instance.

questions.explanation:
App Engine standard environment reaches Memorystore for Redis through a Serverless VPC Access connector. The connector must be in the same region as the App Engine application and attached to the Redis instance's authorized VPC network; a connector in another region prevents the required connection. Memorystore for Redis uses internal IP addresses rather than a public IP address.

**Learn more:** [Connect to a Redis instance from an App Engine standard environment application](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/connect-redis-instance-standard) · [Networking — Memorystore for Redis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/networking)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Cloud Run to host a global ecommerce web application. Your company’s design team is developing a new color scheme for the web app. You have been asked to determine whether the new color scheme will increase sales. You want to test it using live production traffic. How should you design the study?

options.text: Use an external HTTP(S) load balancer to route a predetermined percentage of traffic to two different color schemes of your application. Analyze the results to determine whether there is a statistically significant difference in sales.

Use an external HTTP(S) load balancer to route traffic to the original color scheme while the new deployment is created and tested. After testing is complete, reroute all traffic to the new color scheme. Analyze the results to determine whether there is a statistically significant difference in sales.
Use an external HTTP(S) load balancer to mirror traffic to the new version of your application. Analyze the results to determine whether there is a statistically significant difference in sales.
Enable a feature flag that displays the new color scheme to half of all users. Monitor sales to see whether they increase for this group of users.

questions.explanation:
Splitting live production traffic between the two color-scheme revisions with a percentage-based rule on an external HTTP(S) load balancer, then comparing sales for statistically significant difference, is a properly controlled concurrent A/B test that isolates the color-scheme variable from time-based confounders. A sequential full cutover (option B) or traffic mirroring without measuring the mirrored responses (option C) cannot produce a valid causal comparison, and Cloud Run/Firebase feature flags are not a built-in traffic-splitting or statistical-analysis mechanism for this setup.

**Learn more:** [Traffic migration for Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

questions.domain: Deploying applications

options.text: Use Cloud Armor in front of Cloud Run to protect the container image from threats.
Use Artifact Analysis to scan the image for vulnerabilities. Use Cloud Key Management Service to encrypt the image to be deployed to production.
Use Secret Manager to store the encrypted image. Deploy this image to production.
Use Binary Authorization to enforce a policy that only allows images that have been signed with a trusted key to be deployed to production.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization is a deploy-time security control for Cloud Run that enforces policies on container images. A policy can require an attestation signed by a trusted authority/key, blocking deployment of images that lack the required trusted signature.

**Learn more:** [Use Binary Authorization for Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/binary-authorization) · [Binary Authorization attestations overview](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations)

You have two Google Cloud projects: Project A and Project B. You need to create a Cloud Function in Project A that saves its output to a Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. You want to follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a Google service account in Project B.2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the service account in Project A.3. Assign this service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

1. Create a Google service account in Project A2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the service account in Project A.3. Assign this service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

1. Determine the default App Engine service account ([email protected]) in Project A.2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the default App Engine service account in Project A.3. Assign the default App Engine service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

1. Determine the default App Engine service account ([email protected]) in Project B.2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the default App Engine service account in Project A.3. Assign the default App Engine service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

questions.explanation:
Use a dedicated runtime service account for the Cloud Function in Project A and grant that principal `roles/storage.objectCreator` on the specific Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. Cloud Functions can run with a user-managed service account, and Storage Object Creator grants object-creation capability without permissions to view, delete, or overwrite objects; granting it at the bucket level limits access to that bucket.

**Learn more:** [Function Identity](https://docs.cloud.google.com/functions/docs/securing/function-identity?hl=en) · [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],For this question, refer to the HipLocal case study.  
  
How can HipLocal accelerate API development while continuing to provide the QA team with a stable testing environment that fulfills feature requirements?

options.text: Include unit tests in their code, and prevent deployments to QA until all tests have a passing status.
Include performance tests in their code, and prevent deployments to QA until all tests have a passing status.
Create health checks for the QA environment, and redeploy the APIs at a later time if the environment is unhealthy.
Redeploy the APIs to App Engine using Traffic Splitting. Do not move QA traffic to the new versions if errors are found.

questions.explanation: The HipLocal case study notes that release cycles include development freezes to allow for QA testing and that HipLocal needs faster, more accurate validation of new features. Gating deployments on unit tests (failing the build and blocking promotion to QA whenever a test fails) lets developers commit and iterate continuously while guaranteeing that only functionally correct code ever reaches the QA environment, so QA always has a stable build that reflects the intended feature set. Performance tests, environment health checks, and App Engine traffic splitting address non-functional or rollout concerns, not whether the code deployed to QA actually implements the required features correctly.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An HTTP(S) Load Balancer has been deployed using the following `gcloud` commands:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783706328833-rjmq64wh.jpg)  
  
Health checks on port 80 for the Compute Engine virtual machine instance are failing, so no traffic is being sent to the instances. You want to fix this issue.  
  
Which commands should you run?
questions.explanation:
Google Cloud health-check and Google Front End traffic must be allowed to reach the backend VM through an ingress firewall rule. Allowing TCP traffic from `130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16` on the load balancer VPC permits those probes and proxy connections; assigning an external IP or creating an egress rule does not allow inbound health checks.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Load Balancing firewall rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/firewall-rules)

HipLocal has linked its Hadoop infrastructure to GCP through Cloud Interconnect to query data held on persistent disks.  
  
Which IP strategy should it use?

options.text: Create manual subnets.
Create an auto mode subnet.
Create multiple peered VPCs.
Provision a single instance for NAT.

questions.explanation:
A custom-mode VPC with manually created subnets provides control over CIDR allocation, helping prevent overlap with on-premises address ranges connected through Cloud Interconnect. Google Cloud recommends custom-mode VPC networks for most production environments because they enable deliberate subnet and IP-range planning.\
\
**Learn more:** [Subnets | Virtual Private Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/subnets) · [VPC networks | Virtual Private Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc)

questions.question:
HipLocal has linked its Hadoop infrastructure to GCP through Cloud Interconnect to query data held on persistent disks.  
  
Which IP strategy should it use?

options.text: 1. Create a managed instance group. Replicate the static content across the virtual machines (VMs)2. Create an external HTTP(S) load balancer.3. Enable Cloud CDN, and send traffic to the managed instance group.
1. Create an unmanaged instance group. Replicate the static content across the VMs.2. Create an external HTTP(S) load balancer3. Enable Cloud CDN, and send traffic to the unmanaged instance group.

1. Create a Standard storage class, regional Cloud Storage bucket. Put the static content in the bucket2. Reserve an external IP address, and create an external HTTP(S) load balancer3. Enable Cloud CDN, and send traffic to your backend bucket

1. Create a Standard storage class, multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket. Put the static content in the bucket.2. Reserve an external IP address, and create an external HTTP(S) load balancer.3. Enable Cloud CDN, and send traffic to your backend bucket.

questions.explanation:
A Standard multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket provides automatically replicated static-content storage across multiple Google Cloud regions, improving availability and failure tolerance without managing VMs. Using that bucket as a backend bucket behind an external HTTP(S) load balancer with Cloud CDN delivers cached content from Google’s global edge network, reducing latency for users worldwide.

**Learn more:** [Set up a backend bucket](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/setting-up-cdn-with-bucket) · [Data availability and durability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/availability-durability)
