A teammate asks you to review the following code, which is intended to efficiently add a large number of small rows to a BigQuery table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783706322783-3jed6td2.jpg)  
  
What improvement should you recommend to your teammate?

options.text: Include multiple rows with each request.
Perform the inserts in parallel by creating multiple threads.
Write each row to a Cloud Storage object, then load into BigQuery.
Write each row to a Cloud Storage object in parallel, then load into BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
A legacy `tabledata.insertAll` request accepts an array of rows, so batching multiple small rows into each request reduces request overhead and improves throughput. BigQuery’s quota guidance explicitly notes that batching can increase streaming-insert performance and throughput.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery quotas and limits](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/quotas) · [tabledata.insertAll method reference](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/tabledata/insertAll)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Refer to the HipLocal case study for this question.  
  
HipLocal is expanding to new locations. It must capture additional data whenever the application is launched in a new European country. This is delaying the development process because of continual schema changes and insufficient environments for testing the application changes. How should they address the issue while meeting the business requirements?

options.text: Create new Cloud SQL instances in Europe and North America for testing and deployment. Provide developers with local MySQL instances to conduct testing on the application changes.
Migrate data to Bigtable. Instruct the development teams to use the Cloud SDK to emulate a local Bigtable development environment.

Move from Cloud SQL to MySQL hosted on Compute Engine. Replicate hosts across regions in the Americas and Europe. Provide developers with local MySQL instances to conduct testing on the application changes.

Migrate data to Firestore in Native mode and set up instances in Europe and North America. Instruct the development teams to use the Cloud SDK to emulate a local Firestore in Native mode development environment.

questions.explanation:
Firestore in Native mode provides a flexible document data model that can accommodate newly introduced fields without repeated relational schema migrations. Its location options support deployments in Europe and North America, and the Cloud Firestore emulator enables local development and testing without requiring separate provisioned database environments.

**Learn more:** [Firestore in Native mode locations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/locations) · [Connect your app to the Cloud Firestore Emulator](https://firebase.google.com/docs/emulator-suite/connect_firestore)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an ecommerce company and are developing a new application with these requirements:  
  
- The application must always be able to access the most up-to-date data.  
- Because of company policy, data that is older than 30 days must be deleted automatically.  
  
You need to decide which service should host the database and how to configure data deletion. You want the most efficient solution. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Spanner to host the database. Use Data Catalog to delete data older than 30 days.
Configure Spanner to host the database. Create a time-to-live policy that deletes data older than 30 days.
Configure Bigtable to host the database. Create a time-to-live policy that deletes data older than 30 days.
Configure Bigtable to host the database. Create a garbage collection policy in Bigtable that deletes data older than 30 days.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Bigtable provides low-latency access to operational data and supports age-based garbage-collection policies at the column-family level. Setting a maximum age of 30 days causes Bigtable to automatically expire data whose timestamps exceed that retention period, without requiring a separate deletion process. Data Catalog is for metadata management, not deleting stored data.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable garbage collection overview](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/garbage-collection) · [Configure garbage collection in Bigtable](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/configuring-garbage-collection)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a social media application and plan to add a feature that lets users upload images. These images will be 2 MB to 1 GB in size. You want to minimize infrastructure operations overhead for this feature.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Change the application to accept images directly and store them in the database that stores other user information.
Change the application to create signed URLs for Cloud Storage. Transfer these signed URLs to the client application to upload images to Cloud Storage.
Set up a web server on GCP to accept user images and create a file store to keep uploaded files. Change the application to retrieve images from the file store.

Create a separate bucket for each user in Cloud Storage. Assign a separate service account to allow write access on each bucket. Transfer service account credentials to the client application based on user information. The application uses this service account to upload images to Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage provides managed object storage for uploaded images, and signed URLs grant time-limited permission for a client to write a specific object directly. This avoids operating upload servers and avoids distributing service-account credentials to clients. Google Cloud documents signed URLs as a typical mechanism for uploads, where object data moves directly between the requester and Cloud Storage.

**Learn more:** [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Cloud Run service that uses the default Cloud SQL connection to connect to a Cloud SQL Enterprise edition database instance. You need to allow more than 100 connections per Cloud Run instance. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the queries per minute quota limit of the Cloud SQL Admin API.
Increase the max_connection flag in Cloud SQL for PostgresSQL.
Upgrade to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition.
Use Cloud SQL Auth Proxy in a sidecar.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run's built-in Cloud SQL connection support caps connections to a Cloud SQL instance at 100 per container instance. Running the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy manually as a sidecar container instead of using the built-in connector removes this cap, allowing more than 100 connections per Cloud Run instance. Upgrading the Cloud SQL edition or raising Cloud SQL Admin API quotas does not affect this Cloud Run-side connection limit.

**Learn more:** [Connect from Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/connect-run)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a secure document-sharing platform. The platform enables users to share documents with other users, who might be external to their organization. Access to these documents must be revoked after a configurable period of time. The documents are stored in Cloud Storage. How should Cloud Storage be configured to support this functionality?

options.text: Create signed policy documents on the Cloud Storage bucket.
Apply access control list (ACL) permissions to the Cloud Storage bucket.
Generate a signed URL for each document the user wants to share.
Grant the Storage Object Viewer IAM role to all authenticated users.

questions.explanation:
A signed URL grants time-limited access to a specific Cloud Storage object and includes an expiration time. It can be shared with external recipients without granting them ongoing bucket-level IAM or ACL permissions. Signed policy documents are intended to control uploads, not to provide time-limited access to existing documents.

**Learn more:** [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls?hl=en) · [Overview of access control | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: You recently built an application. You must call the Cloud Storage API from a Compute Engine instance that has no public IP address. What should you do?

options.text: Use Carrier Peering
Use VPC Network Peering
Use Shared VPC networks
Use Private Google Access

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access lets Compute Engine VMs that have only internal IP addresses reach Google APIs and services, including Cloud Storage, when it is enabled on the VM’s subnet.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access) · [Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-google-access)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: You recently built an application. You must call the Cloud Storage API from a Compute Engine instance that has no public IP address. What should you do?

options.text: Install the Stackdriver Logging Agent and configure it to send the application logs.
Use a Stackdriver Logging Library to log directly from the application to Stackdriver Logging.
Provide the log file folder path in the metadata of the instance to configure it to send the application logs.
Change the application to log to /var/log so that its logs are automatically sent to Stackdriver Logging.

questions.explanation:
The Stackdriver Logging Agent can be configured to read application log files stored on a Compute Engine VM and forward their records to Cloud Logging, without requiring changes to the application. The legacy Logging agent supports configuring additional file-based log inputs.

**Learn more:** [Configure the Logging agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/configuration) · [Which should you use: Logging agent or client library?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent-or-library)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a financial-services company that follows a container-first approach. Your team develops microservices applications. You have a Cloud Build pipeline that builds a container image, runs regression tests, and publishes the image to Artifact Registry. You need to ensure that only containers that passed the regression tests are deployed to GKE clusters. Binary Authorization is already enabled on the GKE clusters. What should you do next?

options.text: Deploy Voucher Server and Voucher Client components. After a container image has passed the regression tests, run Voucher Client as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.
Create an attestor and a policy. Run a vulnerability scan to create an attestation for the container image as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.
Create an attestor and a policy. Create an attestation for the container images that have passed the regression tests as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.
Set the Pod Security Standard level to Restricted for the relevant namespaces. Digitally sign the container images that have passed the regression tests as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization policies can require attestations from specified attestors before an image is deployed. An attestation created only after a container image passes regression testing provides the required verifiable evidence, and a policy that requires that attestor blocks images without it from deployment.

**Learn more:** [Attestations overview | Binary Authorization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations?hl=en) · [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a new image-processing application that must perform different tasks, including resizing, cropping, and watermarking images. You must also monitor the workflow and ensure it scales efficiently for large image volumes. You want to automate the image-processing tasks and workflow monitoring with the least effort. What should you do?

options.text: Employ Cloud Composer to manage the image processing workflows. Use Dataproc for workflow monitoring and analytics.
Use Cloud Run to deploy the image processing functions. Use Apigee to expose the API. Use Cloud Logging for workflow monitoring.
Implement Workflows to orchestrate the image processing tasks. Use Cloud Logging for workflow monitoring.
Use Cloud Build to trigger Cloud Functions for the image processing tasks. Use Cloud Monitoring for workflow monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Workflows is a fully managed, serverless orchestration service for executing defined sequences of service operations and can scale to a high number of concurrent executions. It automatically generates execution logs in Cloud Logging, providing a low-effort way to observe and troubleshoot workflow runs.

**Learn more:** [Workflows overview](https://cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/overview) · [Send execution logs to Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/log-workflow)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Refer to the HipLocal case study.  
  
HipLocal wants to lower service latency for users in global locations. It has created database read replicas in the locations where users live and configured the service to direct read traffic to those replicas. What should it do next to reduce latency for all database interactions with the least effort?

options.text: Migrate the database to Bigtable and use it to serve all global user traffic.
Migrate the database to Cloud Spanner and use it to serve all global user traffic.
Migrate the database to Firestore in Datastore mode and use it to serve all global user traffic.
Migrate the services to Google Kubernetes Engine and use a load balancer service to better scale the application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner provides a single, globally distributed relational database that can serve both read and write workloads across regions while maintaining strong consistency. Database read replicas improve read latency only; they do not eliminate the cross-region latency of writes to a single primary MySQL instance. Spanner is therefore the appropriate managed global-database migration for reducing latency across all interactions.

**Learn more:** [Geo-partitioning overview | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/geo-partitioning) · [Life of Spanner Reads & Writes | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/whitepapers/life-of-reads-and-writes)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The application named `ecom-web-app` is deployed across three GKE clusters: `ecom-web-app-dev`, `ecom-web-app-qa`, and `ecom-web-app-prod`. You must ensure that only trusted container images are deployed to the `ecom-web-app-prod` GKE cluster in the production environment, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Set up Binary Authorization, and define cluster-specific rules in clusterAdmissionRules nodes in the policy YAML file.
Set up Binary Authorization, and exempt any container images that are not deployed to the ecom-web-app-prod GKE cluster.
Set up an image verification process that scans the container images in Artifact Registry for vulnerabilities and tags the image versions that fail the scan as untrusted.

Set up an image verification process by using Cloud Functions where the function is invoked when a container image is built in Cloud Build and ensures that only trusted container images are stored in Artifact Registry.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces image trust at deployment time in GKE. A `clusterAdmissionRules` policy entry can apply an attestation-required rule specifically to the production cluster, preventing images without the required trusted attestation from being deployed there while allowing distinct rules for development and QA clusters.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization policy YAML reference](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/policy-yaml-reference) · [Binary Authorization example policies](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/example-policies)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is building a Google Cloud application that runs using user identities managed by Cloud Identity. Every application user will have an associated Pub/Sub topic where messages are published, plus a Pub/Sub subscription through which that same user retrieves published messages. You must ensure that only authorized users can publish to and subscribe from their own specific Pub/Sub topic and subscription. What should you do?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783707045775-hvhqv9gd.jpg)

options.text: Bind the user identity to the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles at the resource level.
Grant the user identity the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles at the project level.
Grant the user identity a custom role that contains the pubsub.topics.create and pubsub.subscriptions.create permissions.
Configure the application to run as a service account that has the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles.

questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub IAM policies can be applied to individual topics and subscriptions. Granting each user the Pub/Sub Publisher role on that user’s topic permits publishing only there, while granting the Pub/Sub Subscriber role on that user’s subscription permits consuming messages only from that subscription. This applies least privilege and prevents project-wide access to other users’ Pub/Sub resources.

**Learn more:** [Pub/Sub access control with IAM](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/access-control) · [Pub/Sub roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/pubsub)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
You want to use the Stackdriver Logging Agent to send an application’s log file from a Compute Engine virtual machine instance to Stackdriver.  
  
After you install the Stackdriver Logging Agent, what should you do first?

options.text: Enable the Error Reporting API on the project.
Grant the instance full access to all Cloud APIs.
Configure the application log file as a custom source.
Create a Stackdriver Logs Export Sink with a filter that matches the application's log entries.

questions.explanation:
The Logging Agent must be configured with an additional custom input source for an application log file. That configuration tells the agent which file to tail and stream to Cloud Logging; a log export sink only routes entries after they have been ingested.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure the Logging agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/configuration)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
You want to use the Stackdriver Logging Agent to send an application’s log file from a Compute Engine virtual machine instance to Stackdriver.  
  
After you install the Stackdriver Logging Agent, what should you do first?

options.text: Blue/green deployment
Canary deployment
Rolling deployment
Recreate deployment

questions.explanation:
A canary deployment progressively routes a small percentage of production traffic to the new version while the existing version continues serving the remaining users. Monitoring that limited release exposes production-only defects early and limits their impact before the rollout is expanded. [Google Cloud: Use a canary deployment strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary)

**Learn more:** [Use a canary deployment strategy | Cloud Deploy | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary) · [Architecture strategies for safe deployment practices | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/safe-deployments)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support an application that uses the Cloud Storage API. After reviewing the logs, you find multiple HTTP 503 Service Unavailable responses from the API. Your application records the error but takes no additional action. You want to implement Google-recommended retry logic to increase success rates.  
  
Which approach should you use?

options.text: Retry the failures in batch after a set number of failures is logged.
Retry each failure at a set time interval up to a maximum number of times.
Retry each failure at increasing time intervals up to a maximum number of tries.
Retry each failure at decreasing time intervals up to a maximum number of tries.

questions.explanation:
HTTP 503 Service Unavailable is a transient, retryable Cloud Storage response. Google Cloud recommends exponential backoff (normally with jitter and a retry limit), which increases the wait time between successive retry attempts to avoid overwhelming a temporarily unavailable service.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage retry strategy](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/retry-strategy)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a large organization. An application written in Go runs in a production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You need to add a feature that requires access to BigQuery. You want to grant the GKE cluster access to BigQuery by following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google service account with BigQuery access. Add the JSON key to Secret Manager, and use the Go client library to access the JSON key.
Create a Google service account with BigQuery access. Add the Google service account JSON key as a Kubernetes secret, and configure the application to use this secret.
Create a Google service account with BigQuery access. Add the Google service account JSON key to Secret Manager, and use an init container to access the secret for the application to use.
Create a Google service account and a Kubernetes service account. Configure Workload Identity on the GKE cluster, and reference the Kubernetes service account on the application Deployment.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE provides Kubernetes workloads with a managed identity for access to Google Cloud APIs, including BigQuery, without exporting or storing service-account JSON keys. An IAM service account can receive the necessary BigQuery role, while the Deployment runs under the corresponding Kubernetes service account.

**Learn more:** [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team intends to use AlloyDB as the database backend for an upcoming application release. The application is currently hosted in a different project and network from the AlloyDB instances. You must securely connect the application to the AlloyDB instance while keeping the projects isolated. You want to minimize additional operations and follow Google-recommended practices. How should you configure network connectivity for the database?

options.text: Provision a Shared VPC project where both the application project and the AlloyDB project are service projects.
Use AlloyDB Auth Proxy and configure the application project’s firewall to allow connections to port 5433.
Provision a service account from the AlloyDB project. Use this service account’s JSON key file as the --credentials-file to connect to the AlloyDB instance.
Ask the database team to provision AlloyDB databases in the same project and network as the application.

questions.explanation:
Shared VPC lets separate service projects use a common host-project VPC while retaining project-level isolation and centralized network controls. AlloyDB documentation specifies using Shared VPC to configure private services access when the VPC network is in a different project from the AlloyDB cluster. The AlloyDB Auth Proxy secures authentication and transport but does not itself establish the required network path.

**Learn more:** [Enable private services access — AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/configure-connectivity) · [Shared VPC overview — Virtual Private Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a web application that contains private images and videos in a Cloud Storage bucket. Your users are anonymous and do not have Google Accounts. You want application-specific logic to control access to the images and videos. How should access be configured?

options.text: Cache each web application user's IP address to create a named IP table using Google Cloud Armor. Create a Google Cloud Armor security policy that allows users to access the backend bucket.
Grant the Storage Object Viewer IAM role to allUsers. Allow users to access the bucket after authenticating through your web application.
Configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to authenticate users into the web application. Allow users to access the bucket after authenticating through IAP.
Generate a signed URL that grants read access to the bucket. Allow users to access the URL after authenticating through your web application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage signed URLs provide time-limited, scoped access to a resource for anyone who has the URL, including users without Google Accounts. The web application can enforce its own authentication and authorization logic before generating and returning a signed URL for read access, without making the bucket publicly readable.

**Learn more:** [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services

options.text: Create an object with the name of the subdirectory ending with a trailing slash ('/') that is zero bytes in length.
Create an object with the name of the subdirectory, and then immediately delete the object within that subdirectory.
Create an object with the name of the subdirectory that is zero bytes in length and has WRITER access control list permission.
Create an object with the name of the subdirectory that is zero bytes in length. Set the Content-Type metadata to CLOUDSTORAGE_FOLDER.

questions.explanation:
In a flat-namespace Cloud Storage bucket, folders are simulated rather than stored as directory resources. Creating an empty folder in the Cloud Storage console creates a zero-byte placeholder object named with the folder path followed by a trailing slash, such as `user-id/`.

**Learn more:** [About Cloud Storage objects](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/objects)

You are building a single-player mobile game backend with unpredictable traffic patterns as users interact with the game during the day and night. You want to optimize costs by ensuring sufficient resources are available to handle requests while minimizing over-provisioning. You also need the system to efficiently handle traffic spikes. Which compute platform should you use?

options.text: Cloud Run
Compute Engine with managed instance groups
Compute Engine with unmanaged instance groups
Google Kubernetes Engine using cluster autoscaling

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run automatically scales service instances in response to incoming request demand and removes idle instances when demand falls, including scaling to zero by default. Its request-based billing avoids charges for idle instances, making it well suited to unpredictable traffic and sudden request spikes while minimizing over-provisioning.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently developed a new application. You want to deploy it on Cloud Run without using a Dockerfile. Your organization requires that every container image be pushed to a centrally managed container repository. How should you build your container by using Google Cloud services? (Choose two.)

options.text: Push your source code to Artifact Registry.
Submit a Cloud Build job to push the image.
Use the pack build command with pack CLI.
Include the --source flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command.
Include the --platform=kubernetes flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run source deployment with `gcloud run deploy --source` uses Google Cloud buildpacks when no Dockerfile is present, invokes Cloud Build, and stores the built container image in Artifact Registry. Cloud Build can also build and push an image to Artifact Registry, which provides centrally managed container-image storage.

**Learn more:** [Deploy services from source code | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/deploying-source-code) · [gcloud run deploy reference](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/run/deploy)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application consisting of several microservices that run in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. One microservice must connect to a third-party database operating on-premises. You need to store the database credentials and ensure they can be rotated according to security best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Store the credentials in a sidecar container proxy, and use it to connect to the third-party database.
Configure a service mesh to allow or restrict traffic from the Pods in your microservice to the database.
Store the credentials in an encrypted volume mount, and associate a Persistent Volume Claim with the client Pod.
Store the credentials as a Kubernetes Secret, and use the Cloud Key Management Service plugin to handle encryption and decryption.

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes Secrets are the appropriate Kubernetes resource for storing sensitive database credentials. In GKE, application-layer Secrets encryption uses a customer-managed Cloud KMS key, providing envelope encryption and supporting Cloud KMS key-rotation practices for the Secret data stored by the cluster.

**Learn more:** [Encrypt secrets at the application layer | GKE security](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/encrypting-secrets)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a company that runs an ecommerce website. You are building a new integration that will manage every order-fulfillment step after orders are placed. You have created multiple Cloud Functions to process each order. You need to orchestrate function execution, using each function’s output to determine the flow. You want to minimize this process’s latency. What should you do?

options.text: Use Workflows to call the functions, and use callbacks to handle the execution logic.
Use Workflows to call the functions, and use conditional jumps to handle the execution logic.
Use Cloud Composer to call the functions, and use an Apache Airflow HTTP operator to handle the execution logic.
Use Cloud Composer to call the functions, and use an Apache Airflow operator to handle the execution logic.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Workflows provides low-latency orchestration for HTTP-based services, including Cloud Functions. Its conditional jumps use a `switch` block to select the next step according to a condition evaluated from a preceding step’s returned result. Cloud Composer is better suited to batch data workflows and has task-execution latency measured in seconds; callbacks are for pausing until an external process resumes the workflow.

**Learn more:** [Choose Workflows or Cloud Composer for service orchestration](https://cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/choose-orchestration) · [Control the order of execution in a workflow](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/controlling-execution-order)

Once the Cloud Function finishes, the collected data must be immediately available for ongoing, complex analytics by many users in parallel. How should you persist the submissions?

options.text: Directly persist each POST request's JSON data into Datastore.
Transform the POST request's JSON data, and stream it into BigQuery.
Transform the POST request's JSON data, and store it in a regional Cloud SQL cluster.

You have an application deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that reads and processes Pub/Sub messages. Each Pod processes a fixed number of messages per minute. The rate at which messages are published to the Pub/Sub topic varies significantly throughout the day and week, including occasional large batches published at a single time.  
  
You want to scale your GKE Deployment so it can process messages promptly. Which GKE feature should you use to automatically adapt your workload?

options.text: Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode
Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Recommendation mode
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on an external metric
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on resources utilization

questions.explanation:
A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler using an external metric can scale Deployment replica count from the Pub/Sub subscription backlog, such as the number of undelivered messages. This directly reflects incoming work and accommodates both fluctuating publish rates and sudden message batches. Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts Pod resource requests rather than the number of message-processing Pods.

**Learn more:** [Optimize Pod autoscaling based on metrics](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/autoscaling-metrics) · [About autoscaling workloads based on metrics](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/custom-and-external-metrics)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s corporate policy requires a copyright comment at the very start of every source file. You want to create a custom Cloud Build step that runs for each source commit. The trigger must verify that the source includes a copyright comment and add one for subsequent steps when it is absent. What should you do?

options.text: Build a new Docker container that examines the files in /workspace and then checks and adds a copyright for each source file. Changed files are explicitly committed back to the source repository.
Build a new Docker container that examines the files in /workspace and then checks and adds a copyright for each source file. Changed files do not need to be committed back to the source repository.
Build a new Docker container that examines the files in a Cloud Storage bucket and then checks and adds a copyright for each source file. Changed files are written back to the Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build extracts source code into `/workspace`, and files written there by one build step are available to subsequent steps. A custom Docker container can inspect and update the source files in `/workspace`; the changes need not be committed back to the source repository merely to make them available during the remaining build steps.

**Learn more:** [Passing data between build steps | Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/configuring-builds/pass-data-between-steps) · [Build configuration file schema | Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/build-config-file-schema)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your code runs on Cloud Functions in project A and is intended to write an object to a Cloud Storage bucket owned by project B. However, the write request fails with the error `403 Forbidden`.  
  
What should you do to fix the issue?

options.text: Grant your user account the roles/storage.objectCreator role for the Cloud Storage bucket.
Grant your user account the roles/iam.serviceAccountUser role for the [email protected] service account.
Grant the [email protected] service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role for the Cloud Storage bucket.
Enable the Cloud Storage API in project B.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Function accesses Google Cloud resources as its runtime service account. The destination bucket must grant that service account `storage.objects.create`; `roles/storage.objectCreator` includes this permission and can be assigned directly on the Cloud Storage bucket.

**Learn more:** [Access control with IAM — Cloud Run functions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/functions/docs/concepts/iam) · [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles?authuser=09)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are conducting load testing for your server application. In the first 30 seconds, you observe that a previously inactive Cloud Storage bucket is servicing 2000 write requests per second and 7500 read requests per second. As demand escalates, your application begins receiving intermittent 5xx and 429 HTTP responses from the Cloud Storage JSON API. You want to reduce failed responses from the Cloud Storage API.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Distribute the uploads across a large number of individual storage buckets.
Use the XML API instead of the JSON API for interfacing with Cloud Storage.
Pass the HTTP response codes back to clients that are invoking the uploads from your application.
Limit the upload rate from your application clients so that the dormant bucket's peak request rate is reached more gradually.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage buckets have approximate initial capacities of 1,000 object write requests per second and 5,000 object read requests per second, and autoscaling takes time to redistribute load. For a bucket that has not had a high request rate recently, traffic above those thresholds must be ramped up gradually; if latency or errors occur, temporarily reduce the request rate to allow the bucket to scale. The recommended maximum ramp is a doubling no faster than every 20 minutes.

**Learn more:** [Request rate and access distribution guidelines | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/request-rate)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a container-build pipeline for an application hosted on GKE. You have these requirements:  
  
- Only images produced through your build pipeline must be deployed to your GKE cluster.  
- All code and build artifacts must remain in your environment and be protected against data exfiltration.  
  
How should you build the pipeline?

options.text: 1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with the default worker pool.2. Deploy container images to a private container registry in your VPC.3. Create a VPC firewall policy in your project that denies all egress and ingress traffic to public networks.

1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with a private worker pool.2. Use VPC Service Controls to place all components and services in your CI/CD pipeline inside a security perimeter.3. Configure your GKE cluster to only allow container images signed by Binary Authorization.

1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with a private worker pool.2. Configure the CI/CD pipeline to build container images and store them in Artifact Registry.3. Configure Artifact Registry to encrypt container images by using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with the default worker pool.2. Configure the CI/CD pipeline to build container images and store them in Artifact Registry.3. Configure your GKE cluster to only allow container images signed by Binary Authorization.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization can enforce a policy requiring Cloud Build’s `built-by-cloud-build` attestation, so GKE deploys only images built by the trusted Cloud Build pipeline. VPC Service Controls establishes a service perimeter to mitigate data exfiltration, and Cloud Build support for VPC Service Controls requires private worker pools rather than default worker pools.

**Learn more:** [Deploy only images built by Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/deploy-cloud-build) · [Use VPC Service Controls with Cloud Build private pools](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/private-pools/using-vpc-service-controls)

Your team operates a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that runs an application. Another team plans to integrate with this application. Before they begin the integration, you must ensure that the other team cannot modify your application, while still allowing them to deploy the integration on GKE. What should you do?

options.text: Using Identity and Access Management (IAM), grant the Viewer IAM role on the cluster project to the other team.
Create a new GKE cluster. Using Identity and Access Management (IAM), grant the Editor role on the cluster project to the other team.
Create a new namespace in the existing cluster. Using Identity and Access Management (IAM), grant the Editor role on the cluster project to the other team.
Create a new namespace in the existing cluster. Using Kubernetes role-based access control (RBAC), grant the Admin role on the new namespace to the other team.

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes RBAC can grant permissions at the namespace level. Creating a separate namespace and granting the other team the Admin role only in that namespace allows them to deploy and manage their integration there without authorizing changes to workloads in the application’s namespace. IAM roles such as Editor operate at the Google Cloud project level and cannot be limited to a particular Kubernetes namespace.

**Learn more:** [GKE access control](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/access-control) · [Authorize actions in clusters using role-based access control](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/role-based-access-control)

questions.question: You are designing a chat-room application that will host multiple rooms and preserve the message history for each room. You have chosen Firestore as the database. How should the data be represented in Firestore?

![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783708348710-blcja39t.png)

questions.explanation:
Cloud Firestore recommends a `rooms` collection containing one document per chat room, with a `messages` subcollection under each room document and one document for each message. Messages can grow without enlarging the room document, while remaining queryable within their room.\
\

Which data structure should you use?

options.text: A linked list
A hash table
A two-dimensional array
A comma-delimited string

questions.explanation: A hash table stores each account number as a key and its cumulative transaction amount as the associated value, enabling efficient lookup and update while processing each log entry.

You are processing a log file with three columns: a timestamp, an account number (a string), and a transaction amount (a number). You need to efficiently calculate the total transaction amount for every unique account number.  
  
Which data structure should you use?

options.text: Configure an Apigee Quota policy with the Synchronous setting set to false. Reset the quota on every booking or when 24 hours have passed.

Store a query counter in a Firestore document that uses the customer ID as the key. Reset the counter to zero when a booking occurs or 24 hours have passed. Deny a search request if the user’s counter is over 1000.

Store a query counter in memory that counts the number of search requests by each customer. Reset the counter to zero when a booking occurs or 24 hours have passed. Deny a search request if the user’s counter is over 1000.

In BigQuery, store a table row for each search and booking request along with the customer ID and current time. Query the table for the number of prior search and booking requests made in the last 24 hours. Deny the search request if the number of prior search requests is 1000 times more than the number of prior booking requests.

questions.explanation:
An Apigee Quota policy can enforce a per-customer request allowance and can be reset when a booking succeeds or after a 24-hour interval. With `Synchronous` set to `false`, quota counters are updated asynchronously, avoiding the performance and throughput cost of synchronous updates. This can allow some requests above the limit, which is appropriate when speed is preferred over exact quota enforcement.

**Learn more:** [Apigee Quota policy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/policies/quota-policy)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a discussion portal on Cloud Run. Incoming external requests pass through a group of microservices before a response is returned. Some of these microservices connect to databases. You need to conduct a load test to identify any application bottlenecks while it is under load. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the response to include a time series that shows elapsed time per service. Use Log Analytics in Cloud Logging to create a heatmap that exposes any service that could be a bottleneck.
Configure Cloud Trace to capture the requests from the load testing clients. Review the timings in Cloud Trace.
Expose the latency metrics per service for each request. Configure Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, and use it to scrape and analyze the metrics.
Add log statements that capture elapsed time. Analyze the logs and metrics by using BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Trace provides distributed tracing and latency data for requests and their operations across a microservices architecture, enabling per-service timing analysis to locate slow components. Cloud Run automatically sends trace latency data for incoming and outgoing HTTP requests.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Trace overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview) · [View latency of app requests](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/trace-app-latency)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You migrated some applications to Google Cloud. You use a legacy monitoring platform deployed on-premises for both on-premises and cloud-deployed applications. You discover that the notification system responds slowly to time-critical issues in the cloud applications. What should you do?

options.text: Replace your monitoring platform with Cloud Monitoring.
Install the Cloud Monitoring agent on your Compute Engine instances.
Migrate some traffic back to your old platform. Perform A/B testing on the two platforms concurrently.
Use Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring to capture logs, monitor, and send alerts. Send them to your existing platform.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring natively collects Google Cloud service metrics and supports alerting policies with notification channels, allowing cloud incidents to be evaluated and notified within Google Cloud instead of depending on an on-premises monitoring platform. This removes the legacy platform from the time-critical cloud notification path.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Monitoring overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/docs/monitoring-overview) · [Alerting overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application to a Compute Engine virtual machine instance that has the Stackdriver Monitoring Agent installed. Your application is a Unix process on the instance. You want to receive an alert if the Unix process has not been running for at least 5 minutes. You cannot modify the application to generate metrics or logs.  
  
Which alert condition should you configure?

options.text: Uptime check
Process health
Metric absence
Metric threshold

questions.explanation:
A process-health alert condition counts VM processes that match a specified command-line pattern and can notify when the count drops below a threshold. Setting the threshold to fewer than one matching process with a 300-second duration detects that the process has stopped running for at least five minutes, without requiring the application to emit custom metrics or logs.

**Learn more:** [Monitor count of processes on a VM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/monitor-process-count) · [Sample policies in JSON](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/policies-in-json)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application runs in multiple Google Kubernetes Engine clusters and is managed by a Deployment in each cluster. Each Deployment has created multiple replicas of your Pod in its cluster. You want to view the stdout logs for every replica in your Deployment across all clusters.  
  
Which command should you use?

options.text: kubectl logs [PARAM]
gcloud logging read [PARAM]
kubectl exec ג€
gcloud compute ssh [PARAM] ג€

questions.explanation:
GKE collects workload container logs written to standard output and standard error in Cloud Logging as `k8s_container` log entries. `gcloud logging read` can query logs for clusters, pods, and containers with filters that span the relevant clusters, whereas `kubectl logs` operates against a Kubernetes cluster context and does not provide this cross-cluster aggregation.

**Learn more:** [View GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/view-logs) · [About GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application deployed in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to update the application so it can make authorized requests to Google Cloud managed services. You want this to be a one-time configuration and to follow security best practices for automatically rotating security keys and storing them in an encrypted store. You already created a service account with appropriate access to the Google Cloud service. What should you do next?

options.text: Assign the Google Cloud service account to your GKE Pod using Workload Identity.
Export the Google Cloud service account, and share it with the Pod as a Kubernetes Secret.
Export the Google Cloud service account, and embed it in the source code of the application.
Export the Google Cloud service account, and upload it to HashiCorp Vault to generate a dynamic service account for your application.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE associates a Pod’s Kubernetes service account with an IAM service account and supplies short-lived credentials for Google Cloud API access. It avoids exporting, distributing, or embedding long-lived service-account key files, which Google Cloud recommends avoiding whenever possible.

**Learn more:** [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity) · [Best practices for using service accounts securely](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to copy the `local-scripts` directory and all its contents from your local workstation to a Compute Engine virtual machine instance.  
  
Which command should you use?

options.text: gsutil cp --project ג€my-gcp-projectג€ -r ~/local-scripts/ gcp-instance-name:~/server-scripts/ --zone ג€us-east1-bג€
gsutil cp --project ג€my-gcp-projectג€ -R ~/local-scripts/ gcp-instance-name:~/server-scripts/ --zone ג€us-east1-bג€
gcloud compute scp --project ג€my-gcp-projectג€ --recurse ~/local-scripts/ gcp-instance-name:~/server-scripts/ --zone ג€us-east1-bג€
gcloud compute mv --project ג€my-gcp-projectג€ --recurse ~/local-scripts/ gcp-instance-name:~/server-scripts/ --zone ג€us-east1-bג€

questions.explanation:
`gcloud compute scp` copies files between a local machine and a Compute Engine VM. Its `--recurse` flag uploads an entire directory hierarchy, and the `INSTANCE:~/server-scripts/` destination identifies the VM and its remote path.

**Learn more:** [gcloud compute scp | Google Cloud SDK](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/scp)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a developer at a large corporation and manage three Google Kubernetes Engine clusters on Google Cloud. Your team’s developers must regularly switch between clusters without losing access to their preferred development tools. You want to configure access to these multiple clusters in accordance with Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the developers to use Cloud Shell and run gcloud container clusters get-credential to switch to another cluster.
In a configuration file, define the clusters, users, and contexts. Share the file with the developers and ask them to use kubect1 contig to add cluster, user, and context details.
Ask the developers to install the gcloud CLI on their workstation and run gcloud container clusters get-credentials to switch to another cluster.
Ask the developers to open three terminals on their workstation and use kubect1 config to configure access to each cluster.

questions.explanation:
Installing the gcloud CLI on each developer’s workstation and using `gcloud container clusters get-credentials` creates or updates that developer’s local kubeconfig entry for the selected GKE cluster. The command also changes kubectl’s current context, enabling developers to switch among clusters while continuing to use their local development tools.

**Learn more:** [Install kubectl and configure cluster access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/cluster-access-for-kubectl) · [gcloud container clusters get-credentials](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/container/clusters/get-credentials)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team operates a large Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Several application teams presently share one namespace while developing microservices for the cluster. Your organization intends to onboard more teams to build microservices. You need to configure multiple environments while maintaining the security and optimal performance of every team’s work. You want to minimize cost and adhere to Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create new role-based access controls (RBAC) for each team in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.
Create a new namespace for each environment in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.
Create a new GKE cluster for each team.
Create a new namespace for each team in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.

questions.explanation:
GKE multi-tenancy best practices use a separate namespace for each tenant team to provide logical isolation within a shared cluster. Applying resource quotas to each namespace prevents one team from consuming more than its assigned CPU, memory, or object capacity, supporting fair performance while retaining the lower cost and reduced operational overhead of a shared cluster.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for enterprise multi-tenancy | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/best-practices/enterprise-multitenancy) · [Cluster multi-tenancy | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/multitenancy-overview)

questions.question:
HipLocal is setting up its access controls.  
  
Which firewall configuration should it implement?

options.text: Block all traffic on port 443.
Allow all traffic into the network.
Allow traffic on port 443 for a specific tag.
Allow all traffic on port 443 into the network.

questions.explanation:
A firewall rule that allows TCP port 443 only for instances with a specified network tag limits HTTPS access to the intended workloads. Google Cloud VPC firewall rules support network tags as targets, whereas a rule without a target applies to all instances in the network. [Use VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)\
\
**Learn more:** [Use VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
HipLocal is setting up its access controls.  
  
Which firewall configuration should it implement?

options.text: Set up a backend with Compute Engine web server instances with a private IP address behind a TCP proxy load balancer.
Configure the firewall rules to allow all ingress traffic to connect to the Compute Engine web servers, with each server having a unique external IP address.
Configure Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy API for SSH access. Then configure the Compute Engine servers with private IP addresses behind an HTTP(s) load balancer for the application web traffic.

Set up a backend with Compute Engine web server instances with a private IP address behind an HTTP(S) load balancer. Set up a bastion host with a public IP address and open firewall ports. Connect to the web instances using the bastion host.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding provides authenticated and IAM-authorized SSH access to Compute Engine instances without external IP addresses. An external HTTP(S) load balancer is the appropriate frontend for web application HTTP and HTTPS traffic, while the Compute Engine backends can remain private.

**Learn more:** [Use IAP for TCP forwarding](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/using-tcp-forwarding) · [Best practices for controlling SSH network access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/ssh-best-practices/network-access)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a scalable web application for internal users. Your organization uses Google Workspace. You must configure user authentication for the application and then deploy it on Google Cloud. You intend to use cloud-native features and minimize infrastructure-management effort. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a Compute Engine VM, configure a web server, and deploy the application in a VPC.
Containerize the application, and deploy it as a Cloud Run service.
Configure Cloud SQL database with a table containing the users and password hashes. Add an authentication screen to ensure that only internal users can access the application.
Configure Identity Aware Proxy, and grant the roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor IAM role to the users that need to access the application.
Configure Identity Aware Proxy, and grant the roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor IAM role to the users that need to access the application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run is a fully managed, scalable platform for deploying containerized applications, so it minimizes infrastructure operations. Identity-Aware Proxy provides authentication and authorization for internal users, and granting `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor` gives users access to IAP-secured web applications. `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` is intended for IAP-secured VM tunnel access.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [Manage access to IAP-secured resources](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/managing-access)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an application deployed on GKE clusters in multiple environments. You use Cloud Build to run user acceptance testing (UAT) tests. You have integrated Cloud Build with Artifact Analysis and enabled the Binary Authorization API in every Google Cloud project that hosts your environments.  
  
You want only container images that have passed specified automated UAT tests to be deployed to the production environment. You have already created an attestor. What should you do next?

options.text: After the UAT phase, sign the attestation with a key stored as a Kubernetes secret. Add a GKE cluster-specific rule in Binary Authorization for the UAT Google Cloud project.
After the UAT phase, sign the attestation with a key stored as a Kubernetes secret. Add a GKE cluster-specific rule in Binary Authorization for the production Google Cloud project policy.
After the UAT phase, sign the attestation with a key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (KMS). Add a default rule in Binary Authorization for the UAT Google Cloud project.

After the UAT phase, sign the attestation with a key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (KMS). Add a GKE cluster-specific rule in Binary Authorization for the production Google Cloud project policy.

questions.explanation:
A successful UAT stage should create a signed attestation for the container image. Cloud Build’s Binary Authorization attestation workflow uses Cloud KMS to manage the signing key. A cluster-specific rule in the production project’s Binary Authorization policy can require that attestation for the production GKE cluster, preventing images without verified UAT approval from deploying there.

**Learn more:** [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build) · [Policy YAML reference — Binary Authorization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/policy-yaml-reference)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has recently deployed an application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You are monitoring the application and want to receive alerts when your containers’ average memory consumption is below 20% or above 80%. How should you configure the alerts?

options.text: Create a Cloud Function that consumes the Monitoring API. Create a schedule to trigger the Cloud Function hourly and alert you if the average memory consumption is outside the defined range.
In Cloud Monitoring, create an alerting policy to notify you if the average memory consumption is outside the defined range.
Create a Cloud Function that runs on a schedule, executes kubectl top on all the workloads on the cluster, and sends an email alert if the average memory consumption is outside the defined range.
Write a script that pulls the memory consumption of the instance at the OS level and sends an email alert if the average memory consumption is outside the defined range.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring can continuously evaluate GKE container memory-utilization metrics, aggregate the relevant time series by average, and send notifications through a metric-threshold alerting policy when the value is below 20% or above 80%.

**Learn more:** [Create metric-threshold alerting policies](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/using-alerting-ui) · [GKE system metrics](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_kubernetes)

Your team develops multiple microservices that run on Cloud Run and connect to a Cloud SQL instance. You normally test in a local environment before deploying new features. However, the external IP address was recently removed from the Cloud SQL instance, so you can no longer perform the tests.  
  
You need to connect to the database to test with the most current data and want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Export the data from the database to a Cloud Storage bucket. Create a database on your computer and import the data.
Create a Cloud VPN tunnel from your computer to your Google Cloud project, and connect to the Cloud SQL instance.
Add your IP as an authorized network on the Cloud SQL instance.
Create a VM in the same VPC as the Cloud SQL instance. Connect to the VM by using Identity-Aware Proxy for TCP forwarding. Install and configure the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.

questions.explanation:
For a Cloud SQL instance using private IP, the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy must run on a resource that has access to the same VPC network as the instance. A VM in that VPC provides that connectivity, while Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding permits secure access to the VM without exposing an external IP. The proxy uses IAM-based authorization and secure encrypted connections without requiring authorized networks.

**Learn more:** [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/sql-proxy) · [Configure private IP for Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/configure-private-ip?hl=en)

You recently developed a new service on Cloud Run. The service authenticates through a custom service and then writes transactional information to a Cloud Spanner database. You need to verify that the application supports up to 5,000 read and 1,000 write transactions per second, while identifying any bottlenecks that arise. Your test infrastructure must be able to autoscale. What should you do?

options.text: Build a test harness to generate requests and deploy it to Cloud Run. Analyze the VPC Flow Logs using Cloud Logging.
Create a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster running the Locust or JMeter images to dynamically generate load tests. Analyze the results using Cloud Trace.
Create a Cloud Task to generate a test load. Use Cloud Scheduler to run 60,000 Cloud Task transactions per minute for 10 minutes. Analyze the results using Cloud Monitoring.
Create a Compute Engine instance that uses a LAMP stack image from the Marketplace, and use Apache Bench to generate load tests against the service. Analyze the results using Cloud Trace.

questions.explanation:
Distributed JMeter or Locust load generators on GKE can scale the test environment while producing concurrent, representative read and write transactions. Cloud Trace provides distributed latency data for Cloud Run requests and can measure time spent in implementation layers such as database queries, enabling bottleneck analysis across authentication, service processing, and Cloud Spanner access.

**Learn more:** [Spanner proof of concept playbook](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/proof-of-concept-playbook) · [Using distributed tracing with Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/trace)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Cloud Logging to manage high volumes of log data. You need to create a real-time log-analysis architecture that sends logs to a third-party application for processing. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Logging log export to Pub/Sub.
Create a Cloud Logging log export to BigQuery.
Create a Cloud Logging log export to Cloud Storage.
Create a Cloud Function to read Cloud Logging log entries and send them to the third-party application.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Logging log export (sink) to a Pub/Sub topic routes incoming log entries for near-real-time delivery. A third-party application can subscribe to that topic to process the logs. Google Cloud specifically recommends Pub/Sub for integrating Cloud Logging with third-party software.

**Learn more:** [View logs routed to Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/pubsub?hl=en) · [Route log entries](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company plans to expand the user base of its popular application beyond the United States. It wants to ensure **99.999% database availability** for the application while minimizing read latency for users worldwide.  
  
Which two actions should it take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance with
Create a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance with
Create a cluster with at least 3 Spanner nodes.
Create a cluster with at least 1 Spanner node.
Create a minimum of two Cloud Spanner instances in separate regions with at least one node.
Create a Cloud Dataflow pipeline to replicate data across different databases.

questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner's multi-regional configuration spanning North America, Asia, and Europe (nam-asia-eur1) places read replicas near users worldwide, minimizing read latency. Achieving 99.999% availability requires Spanner's multi-region replication with strong consistency. A minimum of three Spanner nodes is required for multi-region configurations. Single-region configs or separate database instances do not provide native strong-consistency replication.

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the lead developer for a new retail system running on Cloud Run and Firestore in Datastore mode. A web UI requirement is that the system display a list of available products when users access it and allow users to browse through all products. During the minimum viable product (MVP) phase, you implemented this requirement by returning a list of every available product stored in Firestore.  
  
A few months after go-live, you notice that Cloud Run instances terminate with `HTTP 500: Container instances are exceeding memory limits` errors during busy periods. This error coincides with spikes in the number of Datastore entity reads. You need to prevent Cloud Run from crashing and reduce the number of Datastore entity reads. You want a solution that optimizes system performance. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the query that returns the product list using integer offsets.
Modify the query that returns the product list using limits.
Modify the Cloud Run configuration to increase the memory limits.
Modify the query that returns the product list using cursors.

questions.explanation:
Datastore query cursors support efficient pagination by resuming a query at the index position following the last result in the previous page. This avoids loading all product entities into a single container response and avoids the internal reads, latency, and billing incurred by integer offsets for skipped entities. Google Cloud recommends cursors rather than offsets for this reason.

**Learn more:** [Datastore queries — Cursors, limits, and offsets](https://cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/concepts/queries) · [Firestore in Datastore mode best practices](https://cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/best-practices)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is building a new application that is packaged as a container and stored in Artifact Registry. You are responsible for setting up the Cloud Build CI/CD pipelines. Containers can be pushed manually for local development or during an emergency. Each time a new container is pushed to Artifact Registry, you must trigger another Cloud Build pipeline to perform a vulnerability scan. You want to implement this requirement with the least effort. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Artifact Registry to publish a message to a Pub/Sub topic when a new image is pushed. Configure the vulnerability scan pipeline to be triggered by the Pub/Sub message.
Configure the Cloud Build Cl pipeline that publishes the new image to send a message to a Pub/Sub topic that triggers the vulnerability scan pipeline.
Configure Artifact Registry to publish a message to a Pub/Sub topic when a new image is pushed. Configure Pub/Sub to invoke a Cloud Function that triggers the vulnerability scan pipeline.
Use Cloud Scheduler to periodically check for new versions of the container in Artifact Registry and trigger the vulnerability scan pipeline.

questions.explanation:
Artifact Registry can publish Pub/Sub notifications for repository changes, including container image uploads and new tags. A Cloud Build Pub/Sub trigger can directly start a build from those messages, so it also covers images pushed manually or during emergencies without adding a Cloud Function or polling process.

**Learn more:** [Configure Pub/Sub notifications for Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/configure-notifications) · [Automate Cloud Build in response to Pub/Sub events](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/automate-builds-pubsub-events)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster administrator. Your organization’s clusters are enrolled in a release channel. You need to be notified about relevant events affecting your GKE clusters, such as available upgrades and security bulletins. What should you do?

options.text: Configure cluster notifications to be sent to a Pub/Sub topic.
Execute a scheduled query against the google_cloud_release_notes BigQuery dataset.
Query the GKE API for available versions.
Create an RSS subscription to receive a daily summary of the GKE release notes.

questions.explanation:
GKE cluster notifications can publish messages to a configured Pub/Sub topic for events relevant to a cluster. For release-channel clusters, these notifications include available-version upgrade events, and they also include security bulletins that affect the cluster.

**Learn more:** [Cluster notifications | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-notifications) · [Receive cluster notifications through Pub/Sub | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/cluster-notifications)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to use C++ to build and deploy a microservice for an application hosted on Google Cloud. The code must be containerized and use several custom software libraries developed by your team. You do not want to manage the application’s underlying infrastructure. How should the microservice be deployed?

options.text: Use Cloud Functions to deploy the microservice.
Use Cloud Build to create the container, and deploy it on Cloud Run.
Use Cloud Shell to containerize your microservice, and deploy it on a Container-Optimized OS Compute Engine instance.
Use Cloud Shell to containerize your microservice, and deploy it on standard Google Kubernetes Engine.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run is a fully managed platform for running containerized services, so it supports a C++ application and its custom dependencies when they are packaged in a container image. Cloud Build can create that image, while Cloud Run removes the need to operate virtual machines or Kubernetes infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [Build container images](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/building/build-containers)

Your company operates an application that records stock data in an internal database. You need to build an API that delivers real-time stock data to users. You want to return this data as fast as possible and require a highly scalable solution. What should you do?

options.text: Create a BigQuery dataset and table to act as the internal database. Query the table when user requests are received.
Create a Memorystore for Redis instance to store all stock market data. Query this database when user requests are received.
Create a Bigtable instance. Query the table when user requests are received. Configure a Pub/Sub topic to queue user requests that your API will respond to.

Create a Memorystore for Redis instance, and use this database to store the most accessed stock data. Query this instance first when user requests are received, and fall back to the internal database.

questions.explanation:
Memorystore for Redis provides low-latency, high-throughput in-memory caching for heavily accessed data. Checking Redis before the internal database minimizes latency and database load for common requests, while falling back to the internal database preserves availability and completeness on cache misses. [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview)

**Learn more:** [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview) · [Caching data with Memorystore](https://docs.cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/using-memorystore)
