questions.question:
You are developing a new API. You want to minimize image-storage costs and reduce the latency of serving images.  
  
Which architecture should you use?

options.text: App Engine backed by Cloud Storage
Compute Engine backed by Persistent Disk
Transfer Appliance backed by Cloud Filestore
Cloud Content Delivery Network (CDN) backed by Cloud Storage

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage is appropriate low-cost object storage for images, and Cloud CDN caches cacheable content near users. Serving cached images from edge locations reduces latency and reduces requests to the origin storage service.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud CDN overview](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/overview) · [Caching with Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/caching)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
You are developing a new API. You want to minimize image-storage costs and reduce the latency of serving images.  
  
Which architecture should you use?

options.text: Use the Bucket Lock feature to set the retention policy on the data.
Run a scheduled job to set the storage class to Coldline for objects older than 14 days.
Create a JSON Web Token (JWT) for users needing access to the Coldline storage buckets.
Create a lifecycle management policy to set the storage class to Coldline for objects older than 14 days.
Create a lifecycle management policy to set the storage class to Nearline for objects older than 14 days.

questions.explanation: Bucket Lock enforces the 7-year retention policy, preventing deletion or modification before the compliance deadline. Object Lifecycle Management automatically transitions logs older than the 14-day access window to Coldline, a storage class optimized for data accessed less than once yearly at minimal cost ($0.004/GB/month storage). Coldline provides the lowest cost tier suitable for annual auditor access while maintaining retention guarantees.

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
You need to notify on-call engineers about a production service degradation while minimizing development time.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Function to monitor resources and raise alerts.
Use Cloud Pub/Sub to monitor resources and raise alerts.
Use Stackdriver Error Reporting to capture errors and raise alerts.
Use Stackdriver Monitoring to monitor resources and raise alerts.

questions.explanation:
Stackdriver Monitoring provides built-in monitoring of resources and metrics, plus alerting policies and notification channels for on-call responders. This directly supports detecting service degradation without writing custom monitoring code.\
\
**Learn more:** [Alerting overview | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
You need to notify on-call engineers about a production service degradation while minimizing development time.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a service to publish messages, and deploy the Pub/Sub emulator. Generate random content in the publishing service, and publish to the emulator.
Create a service to publish messages to your application. Collect the messages from Pub/Sub in production, and replay them through the publishing service.
Create a service to publish messages, and deploy the Pub/Sub emulator. Collect the messages from Pub/Sub in production, and publish them to the emulator.
Create a service to publish messages, and deploy the Pub/Sub emulator. Publish a standard set of testing messages from the publishing service to the emulator.

questions.explanation:
The Pub/Sub emulator provides a local emulation of Pub/Sub for application testing, including publishing and subscribing. Integration tests involving credit card data should use a controlled, non-production set of test messages so that tests are repeatable and do not expose or copy sensitive production data.

**Learn more:** [Testing apps locally with the Pub/Sub emulator](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company recently modernized its monolithic ecommerce site into a microservices application on GKE. Your team uses Google Cloud's operations suite for monitoring and logging. You want to improve logging indexing and searchability in Cloud Logging across your microservices with the least effort. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the SRE team to enable Managed Service for Prometheus on your GKE cluster.
Reconfigure your applications to write logs to an emptyDir volume. Configure a sidecar agent to read the logs and send them to the Cloud Logging API.
Update your microservices code to emit logs in JSON format.
Instrument your microservices code with OpenTelemetry libraries.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging stores JSON-formatted application logs as structured `jsonPayload` data. Structured payload fields can be queried by JSON path and used as custom indexed fields, while unstructured text payload content cannot be indexed. Emitting JSON logs from microservices on GKE therefore improves searchability and supports indexing without adding collection infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Structured logging | Cloud Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/structured-logging) · [Improve query time with custom indexing | Cloud Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/custom-index)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You deployed a new application to Google Kubernetes Engine and are seeing some performance degradation. Your logs are written to Cloud Logging, and you use a Prometheus sidecar model to capture metrics. You need to correlate the metrics with data from the logs to troubleshoot the performance issue and send real-time alerts while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Create custom metrics from the Cloud Logging logs, and use Prometheus to import the results using the Cloud Monitoring REST API.
Export the Cloud Logging logs and the Prometheus metrics to Cloud Bigtable. Run a query to join the results, and analyze in Google Data Studio.
Export the Cloud Logging logs and stream the Prometheus metrics to BigQuery. Run a recurring query to join the results, and send notifications using Cloud Tasks.

Export the Prometheus metrics and use Cloud Monitoring to view them as external metrics. Configure Cloud Monitoring to create log-based metrics from the logs, and correlate them with the Prometheus data.

questions.explanation:
A Stackdriver Prometheus sidecar converts Prometheus metrics into Cloud Monitoring external metrics (`external.googleapis.com/prometheus`). Cloud Logging log-based metrics are ingested by Cloud Monitoring, where they can be charted, correlated with other metrics, and used in alerting policies. This avoids exporting and repeatedly joining telemetry in separate data stores, reducing operational complexity and cost.

**Learn more:** [External metrics list](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_other) · [Log-based metrics overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team develops stateless services running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to deploy a new service that will be accessed only by other services running in the GKE cluster. The service must scale as quickly as possible in response to changing load. What should you do?

options.text: Use a Vertical Pod Autoscaler to scale the containers, and expose them via a ClusterIP Service.
Use a Vertical Pod Autoscaler to scale the containers, and expose them via a NodePort Service.
Use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale the containers, and expose them via a ClusterIP Service.
Use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale the containers, and expose them via a NodePort Service.

questions.explanation:
A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts the number of workload Pod replicas according to observed metrics, allowing a stateless service to add capacity as load changes. A ClusterIP Service exposes the service on a cluster-internal IP, making it suitable for access solely by workloads within the cluster. A Vertical Pod Autoscaler changes CPU and memory resources assigned to Pods instead of increasing replica count, while a NodePort exposes the Service on every node’s network interface.

**Learn more:** [Horizontal Pod Autoscaling](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/) · [Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You maintain a popular mobile game that is deployed on Google Cloud services, including Firebase, Firestore, and Cloud Functions. Recently, the game had a surge in usage, and the application received HTTP 429 `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` errors while accessing the Firestore API. The application has since stabilized.  
  
You want to resolve this issue quickly because your company has a marketing campaign next week and you anticipate another usage surge. What should you do?

options.text: Request a quota increase, and modify the application code to retry the Firestore API call with fixed backoff.
Request a quota increase, and modify the application code to retry the Firestore API call with exponential backoff.
Optimize database queries to reduce read/write operations, and modify the application code to retry the Firestore API call with fixed backoff.
Optimize database queries to reduce read/write operations, and modify the application code to retry the Firestore API call with exponential backoff.

questions.explanation:
Firestore `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` indicates that a project quota has been exceeded or that regional capacity is constrained. A quota increase helps accommodate the anticipated higher request volume, while exponential backoff spaces retries progressively to avoid amplifying load during temporary capacity pressure. Fixed-delay retries can create synchronized retry bursts.

**Learn more:** [Use the Cloud Firestore REST API](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/use-rest-api)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You intend to make a simple HTML application accessible on the internet. The site stores FAQ information for your application. It is static and includes images, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. You want to publish this application on the internet using as few steps as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Upload your application to Cloud Storage.
Upload your application to an App Engine environment.
Create a Compute Engine instance with Apache web server installed. Configure Apache web server to host the application.
Containerize your application first. Deploy this container to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and assign an external IP address to the GKE pod hosting the application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage can host a static website and serve client-side HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and image assets directly. This is the simplest suitable managed option for a fully static application; App Engine, a Compute Engine web server, and GKE introduce unnecessary deployment or infrastructure management.

**Learn more:** [Host a static website | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/hosting-static-website)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application on a Compute Engine instance that communicates with Cloud SQL. You will use Cloud SQL Proxy to enable the application to communicate with the database through the service account associated with the application’s instance. You want to follow Google’s recommended best practice of granting the minimum access required for the role assigned to the service account. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the Project Editor role.
Assign the Project Owner role.
Assign the Cloud SQL Client role.
Assign the Cloud SQL Editor role.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud SQL Client role (`roles/cloudsql.client`) includes the `cloudsql.instances.connect` permission required for a service account to connect through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. It provides the necessary connection access without the broader resource-management privileges granted by Cloud SQL Editor or project-level Editor and Owner roles.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL roles and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/roles-and-permissions) · [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/sql-proxy)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is working to reduce cloud spend and wants to assess the costs of its GKE Autopilot cluster. While reviewing the manifests, you notice that resource requests are not currently specified. The application is stateless and fault-tolerant, with no particular node hardware or memory requirements. You want to modify the cluster as quickly as possible so that it is scalable and cost-effective while retaining sufficient computing resources. What should you do?

options.text: Request that your Pods run as Spot Pods, and use the cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true label in your YAML manifest.
Request the Balanced compute class in your YAML manifest.
In the YAML deployment configuration manifest, request and set the maximum CPU to 5 vCPU.
Set up Cloud Trace and Cloud Monitoring, identify the maximum memory used in the past 30 days, and set the YAML manifest to request that amount of memory.

questions.explanation:
GKE Autopilot Spot Pods are designed for fault-tolerant workloads at lower cost. A stateless, fault-tolerant application can tolerate Spot Pod interruptions, and the `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true` node-selector label in the Pod specification requests Spot Pods. This provides a direct cost reduction without requiring specialized hardware or manual resource-sizing analysis.

**Learn more:** [Run fault-tolerant workloads at lower costs in Spot Pods](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/autopilot-spot-pods)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: A container is deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine. Because the container can occasionally be slow to start, you implemented a liveness probe. You find that the liveness probe sometimes fails during launch. What should you do?

options.text: Add a startup probe.
Increase the initial delay for the liveness probe.
Increase the CPU limit for the container.
Add a readiness probe.

questions.explanation:
A startup probe allows time for a slow-starting container to finish initialization. Kubernetes does not run liveness or readiness probes until the startup probe succeeds, preventing premature liveness-probe failures and container restarts during startup.\
\
**Learn more:** [Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: A container is deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine. Because the container can occasionally be slow to start, you implemented a liveness probe. You find that the liveness probe sometimes fails during launch. What should you do?

options.text: Set the ACL permission on the Cloud Storage bucket. Set the permission of each text file to allUsers with READER access. Delete each text file 2 hours after itis created.
Set the permission on the Cloud Storage bucket with the text files to allUsers. Delete each text file 2 hours after itis created.
Create a new Cloud Storage bucket for each user. Grant the user access to the bucket with a conditional IAM role that expires after 2 hours.
Create a signed URL for each text file that expires after 2 hours.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Storage signed URL provides time-limited, narrowly scoped access to a specific object without making the bucket or object public or requiring the recipient to have a Google account. Creating a signed URL for the transcript with a two-hour expiration grants only the required temporary read access. Google recommends signed URLs for securely sharing content with users who do not have accounts while controlling the access duration.

**Learn more:** [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls?hl=en) · [Best practices for Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/best-practices)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team develops services running on Google Kubernetes Engine. The team’s code is stored in Cloud Source Repositories. You need to rapidly find code bugs before deployment to production, and you want to invest in automation to improve developer feedback and make the process as efficient as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Spinnaker to automate building container images from code based on Git tags.
Use Cloud Build to automate building container images from code based on Git tags.
Use Spinnaker to automate deploying container images to the production environment.
Use Cloud Build to automate building container images from code based on forked versions.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build provides automated continuous-integration builds triggered by source changes and can build container images. Running those builds against developers’ forked versions validates changes and exposes build or test failures before the code is promoted to production, giving rapid automated feedback.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Build triggers](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/triggers) · [Automating builds with Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/source-repositories/docs/integrating-with-cloud-build)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a financial services company that takes a container-first approach. Your team develops microservices applications. A Cloud Build pipeline builds the container image, runs regression tests, and publishes the image to Artifact Registry.  
  
You must ensure that only containers that have passed the regression tests are deployed to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters. Binary Authorization is already enabled on the GKE clusters. What should you do next?

options.text: Create an attestor and a policy. After a container image has successfully passed the regression tests, use Cloud Build to run Kritis Signer to create an attestation for the container image.
Deploy Voucher Server and Voucher Client components. After a container image has successfully passed the regression tests, run Voucher Client as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.
Set the Pod Security Standard level to Restricted for the relevant namespaces. Use Cloud Build to digitally sign the container images that have passed the regression tests.
Create an attestor and a policy. Create an attestation for the container images that have passed the regression tests as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.

questions.explanation:
With Binary Authorization already enabled, the remaining steps are to define an attestor and policy and then generate the attestation for each image directly as a step in the existing Cloud Build pipeline once regression tests pass. Google's current Cloud Build integration guidance creates the attestation with a build step (e.g., invoking the signing/attestation command against Cloud KMS) rather than through the separate, older Kritis Signer tool referenced in the other option.

**Learn more:** [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running on a GKE cluster. The application has a stateless web frontend and requires high availability. The cluster is configured for automatic upgrades, and some nodes must be drained. You need to ensure the application retains serving capacity for 10% of its Pods before the drain. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to increase the memory and CPU by 10% and set the updateMode to Auto.
Configure the Pod replica count to be 10% more than the current replica count.
Configure a Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) value to have a minAvailable value of 10%.
Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) maxReplicas value to 10% more than the current replica count.

questions.explanation:
A PodDisruptionBudget governs voluntary Pod evictions, including those performed while draining nodes for GKE upgrades. Its `minAvailable` field can be expressed as a percentage, so `minAvailable: 10%` requires that at least 10% of the selected Pods remain available while the disruption is processed.

**Learn more:** [Manually upgrade a cluster's control plane or node pools](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/upgrading-a-cluster) · [Deploy a Redis cluster on GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/upgrading-stateful-workload)

You operate a microservices application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with Istio. You protect the communication channels between your microservices by implementing an Istio AuthorizationPolicy, a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, and mTLS on the GKE cluster. You find that HTTP requests between two Pods to certain URLs fail, while requests to other URLs succeed. What is causing the connection issue?

options.text: A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resource is blocking HTTP traffic between the Pods.
The Pod initiating the HTTP requests is attempting to connect to the target Pod via an incorrect TCP port.
The Authorization Policy of your cluster is blocking HTTP requests for specific paths within your application.
The cluster has mTLS configured in permissive mode, but the Pod's sidecar proxy is sending unencrypted traffic in plain text.

questions.explanation:
Istio AuthorizationPolicy supports Layer 7 access controls, including HTTP request paths. A policy that denies, or does not allow, particular paths can therefore block only requests to those URLs. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy operates at the network and transport layers, controlling Pods, IP addresses, and ports rather than HTTP paths; port or mTLS configuration issues would not normally be URL-specific.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Service Mesh security best practices](https://cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/security/anthos-service-mesh-security-best-practices) · [Authorization policy overview](https://cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/security/authorization-policy-overview)

You introduced a typo into a low-level Linux configuration file that stops your Compute Engine instance from booting to its normal run level. You created the Compute Engine instance only today and have performed no maintenance on it besides modifying files. How should you fix this error?

options.text: Download the file using scp, change the file, and then upload the modified version
Configure and log in to the Compute Engine instance through SSH, and change the file
Configure and log in to the Compute Engine instance through the serial port, and change the file
Configure and log in to the Compute Engine instance using a remote desktop client, and change the file

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine’s interactive serial console can be used to troubleshoot a malfunctioning instance that is not fully booted or cannot be accessed through SSH. It provides text-mode command access independent of the instance’s normal network and SSH availability, so the erroneous Linux configuration file can be edited and the instance can then boot normally.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting using the serial console | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/troubleshooting-using-serial-console)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that must connect to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database by using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is hosted in a different Google Cloud VPC network. The Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance has both public and private IP addresses. You must use the private IP for security reasons. When you test the connection to the Cloud SQL instance, you can connect by using the public IP address, but cannot connect by using the private IP address. How should you resolve this issue?

options.text: Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a background service.
Add the --private-ip option when starting the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.
Set up VPC Network Peering between your VPC and the VPC where the Cloud SQL instance is deployed.
Grant yourself the IAM role that provides access to the Cloud SQL instance.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud SQL Auth Proxy running in a different VPC network has no route to the Cloud SQL instance's private IP address until private connectivity is established between that VPC and the network with private services access to the instance. VPC Network Peering between the two networks supplies the missing routing path, while the --private-ip flag and IAM role changes do nothing to fix a lack of network reachability.

**Learn more:** [Learn about using private IP](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/private-ip)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application writes logs to Stackdriver. You want to obtain the number of all requests across every `/api/alpha/*` endpoint.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Add a Stackdriver counter metric for path:/api/alpha/.
Add a Stackdriver counter metric for endpoint:/api/alpha/*.
Export the logs to Cloud Storage and count lines matching /api/alpha.
Export the logs to Cloud Pub/Sub and count lines matching /api/alpha.

questions.explanation:
A counter-type log-based metric counts every log entry that matches its filter. Filtering the `path` field for `/api/alpha/` counts requests to all paths under that prefix without exporting the logs for external line counting. [Configure counter metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/counter-metrics)

**Learn more:** [Configure counter metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/counter-metrics) · [Logging query language](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/view/logging-query-language)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has developed an application hosted on a Google Kubemetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You need to connect the application to a legacy REST service deployed across two GKE clusters in two separate regions. You want the connection to the legacy service to be resilient and to require the fewest steps. You also need to run probe-based health checks for the legacy service on a separate port. How should you configure the connection? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Traffic Director with a sidecar proxy to connect the application to the service.
Set up a proxyless Traffic Director configuration for the application.
Configure the legacy service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the sidecar proxy.
Configure the legacy service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the application.
Configure the legacy service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the Traffic Director control plane.

questions.explanation:
Traffic Director with an Envoy sidecar proxy supports HTTP/REST traffic and can route to healthy endpoints across regions for resilient failover. Proxyless Traffic Director is for xDS-enabled gRPC applications, not a general REST-client configuration. Traffic Director backend health checks use Google Cloud health-check probers and support an explicitly configured health-check port, so the legacy service must allow those control-plane-managed probes through its firewall.

**Learn more:** [Use health checks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-checks) · [Health checks overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-check-concepts)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question:
Your website is running on Compute Engine. Your marketing team wants to test conversion rates across 3 different website designs.  
  
Which approach should you choose?

options.text: Deploy the website on App Engine and use traffic splitting.
Deploy the website on App Engine as three separate services.
Deploy the website on Cloud Functions and use traffic splitting.
Deploy the website on Cloud Functions as three separate functions.

questions.explanation:
App Engine traffic splitting distributes a specified percentage of requests across two or more versions within a service and is designed for A/B testing. Deploying the three designs as versions and splitting traffic enables conversion-rate comparison.\
\
**Learn more:** [Splitting traffic | App Engine standard environment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/splitting-traffic)

Which approach should you choose?

options.text: Use Cloud Code to develop applications.
Use the Cloud Shell integrated Code Editor to edit code and configuration files.
Use a Cloud Notebook instance to ingest and process data and deploy models.
Use Cloud Shell to manage your infrastructure and applications from the command line.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Code provides integrated GKE development capabilities directly in VS Code and IntelliJ, including Kubernetes application creation, deployment, debugging, configuration authoring, and resource management. This aligns with a development environment that uses both IDEs and needs streamlined GKE adoption and integration.

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You observed that your application was forcibly shut down during a Deployment update in Google Kubernetes Engine. The application did not close its database connection before termination. You want to update the application so that it performs a graceful shutdown. What should you do?

options.text: Update your code to process a received SIGTERM signal to gracefully disconnect from the database.
Configure a PodDisruptionBudget to prevent the Pod from being forcefully shut down.
Increase the terminationGracePeriodSeconds for your application.
Configure a PreStop hook to shut down your application.

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes sends a SIGTERM signal to containers as part of graceful Pod termination. Application code should handle that signal by stopping work and releasing resources such as database connections before the termination grace period expires; otherwise Kubernetes can force termination with SIGKILL.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot GKE Standard node pools](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/node-pools)

You use Cloud Build to build and test application source code stored in Cloud Source Repositories. The build process needs a build tool that is unavailable in the Cloud Build environment.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Download the binary from the internet during the build process.
Build a custom cloud builder image and reference the image in your build steps.
Include the binary in your Cloud Source Repositories repository and reference it in your build scripts.
Ask to have the binary added to the Cloud Build environment by filing a feature request against the Cloud Build public Issue Tracker.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build supports custom builder images for tasks whose required capabilities or toolchains are not available in existing builder images. A custom builder packages the required binary or toolchain in a container image, which Cloud Build runs by referencing the image in a build step.

**Learn more:** [Using community-contributed builders and custom builders](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/configuring-builds/use-community-and-custom-builders)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A team maintains an application that aggregates news articles from many different sources. Its monitoring dashboard provides publicly accessible, real-time reports and runs as a web application on a Compute Engine instance. External stakeholders and analysts must access these reports through a secure channel without authentication. How should this secure channel be configured?

options.text: Add a public IP address to the instance. Use the service account key of the instance to encrypt the traffic.
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger Cloud Build every hour to create an export from the reports. Store the reports in a public Cloud Storage bucket.
Add an HTTP(S) load balancer in front of the monitoring dashboard. Configure Identity-Aware Proxy to secure the communication channel.
Add an HTTP(S) load balancer in front of the monitoring dashboard. Set up a Google-managed SSL certificate on the load balancer for traffic encryption.

questions.explanation:
An external HTTP(S) load balancer with a Google-managed SSL certificate provides HTTPS/TLS encryption between public clients and the dashboard without requiring users to authenticate. Identity-Aware Proxy is unsuitable because it verifies user identity and enforces authorization. Google Cloud documents that TLS encrypts information in transit between a client and a load balancer, and that Google-managed SSL certificates are supported by external Application Load Balancers.

**Learn more:** [SSL certificates overview | Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/ssl-certificates?hl=en) · [Use Google-managed SSL certificates | Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/ssl-certificates/google-managed-certs?hl=en)

questions.question:
You must build a public API that authenticates API callers, enforces quotas, and reports metrics. Which tool should you use to complete this architecture?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783709008589-bjzijhfi.png)

options.text: App Engine
Cloud Endpoints
Identity-Aware Proxy
GKE Ingress for HTTP(S) Load Balancing

questions.explanation:
Cloud Endpoints is an API management service that secures APIs, enforces caller quotas, and monitors API usage and metrics. It supports authentication configuration and API-key-based consumer identification for quota enforcement.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Endpoints documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs) · [Quickstart: Deploy an API managed by Cloud Endpoints](https://docs.cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/deploy-api)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
You have an application running in production. When you deploy a new version, you want to ensure that all production traffic is routed to the new version of the application. You also want to retain the previous version so you can revert to it if the new version has an issue.  
  
Which deployment strategy should you use?

options.text: Blue/green deployment
Canary deployment
Rolling deployment
Recreate deployment

questions.explanation:
Blue/green deployment maintains the current (blue) version alongside the new (green) version, shifts production traffic to the new version, and retains the previous version for rapid rollback if a problem is found.\
\
**Learn more:** [Blue/Green Deployments on AWS — Introduction](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/blue-green-deployments/introduction.html)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
You have an application running in production. When you deploy a new version, you want to ensure that all production traffic is routed to the new version of the application. You also want to retain the previous version so you can revert to it if the new version has an issue.  
  
Which deployment strategy should you use?

options.text: Manually trigger the build for new releases.
Create a build trigger on a Git tag pattern. Use a Git tag convention for new releases.
Create a build trigger on a Git branch name pattern. Use a Git branch naming convention for new releases.
Commit your source code to a second Cloud Source Repositories repository with a second Cloud Build trigger. Use this repository for new releases only.

questions.explanation:
A Git tag identifies a specific commit as a release. Cloud Build supports triggers for pushes of tags that match a configured tag pattern, so a release-tag convention can automatically invoke the release build for selected commits while ordinary commits to `master` continue through the normal build process.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application performs well in local testing, but runs substantially slower after deployment to a Compute Engine instance. You need to diagnose the issue. What should you do?  
  
What should you do?

options.text: File a ticket with Cloud Support indicating that the application performs faster locally.
Use Cloud Debugger snapshots to look at a point-in-time execution of the application.
Use Cloud Profiler to determine which functions within the application take the longest amount of time.
Add logging commands to the application and use Cloud Logging to check where the latency problem occurs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Profiler continuously collects low-overhead production performance data and attributes resource use to application source code. Its CPU-time and wall-time profiles identify functions that consume the most execution time, making it suitable for locating the cause of a slowdown on a Compute Engine instance.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Profiler overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler) · [Profiling concepts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/concepts-profiling)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an internal application that lets employees organize community events within your company. You deployed the application on a single Compute Engine instance. Your company uses Google Workspace (formerly G Suite), and you must ensure that company employees can authenticate to the application from anywhere. What should you do?

options.text: Add a public IP address to your instance, and restrict access to the instance using firewall rules. Allow your company's proxy as the only source IP address.
Add an HTTP(S) load balancer in front of the instance, and set up Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP). Configure the IAP settings to allow your company domain to access the website.

Set up a VPN tunnel between your company network and your instance's VPC location on Google Cloud. Configure the required firewall rules and routing information to both the on-premises and Google Cloud networks.

Add a public IP address to your instance, and allow traffic from the internet. Generate a random hash, and create a subdomain that includes this hash and points to your instance. Distribute this DNS address to your company's employees.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy authenticates users with Google identity and enforces authorization for applications served through an HTTP(S) load balancer. Granting access to the Google Workspace domain allows company employees to sign in from any location, while restricting the application to authorized identities rather than network location. IAP for Compute Engine requires the workload to be served by a load balancer, and a Google Workspace domain can be assigned access through the IAP-secured Web App User role.

**Learn more:** [Enable IAP for Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/enabling-compute-howto) · [Manage access to IAP-secured resources](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/managing-access)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has developed an application that uploads a report to a Cloud Storage bucket. When the report is uploaded to the bucket, you want to publish a message to a Cloud Pub/Sub topic. You want to implement a solution that requires little effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the Cloud Storage bucket to trigger Cloud Pub/Sub notifications when objects are modified.
Create an App Engine application to receive the file; when it is received, publish a message to the Cloud Pub/Sub topic.
Create a Cloud Function that is triggered by the Cloud Storage bucket. In the Cloud Function, publish a message to the Cloud Pub/Sub topic.
Create an application deployed in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster to receive the file; when it is received, publish a message to the Cloud Pub/Sub topic.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage can be configured with a Pub/Sub notification that sends messages to a chosen Pub/Sub topic when objects change. An upload successfully creating an object triggers the `OBJECT_FINALIZE` event, so this direct configuration meets the requirement with the least implementation work.

**Learn more:** [Pub/Sub notifications for Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/pubsub-notifications) · [Configure Pub/Sub notifications for Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/reporting-changes)

questions.domain: Designing scalable, available, and reliable cloud-native applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your development team has been tasked with refactoring an existing monolithic application into a collection of composable microservices. Which design aspects should be implemented for the new application? (Choose two.)

options.text: Develop the microservice code in the same programming language used by the microservice caller.
Create an API contract agreement between the microservice implementation and microservice caller.
Require asynchronous communications between all microservice implementations and microservice callers.
Ensure that sufficient instances of the microservice are running to accommodate the performance requirements.
Implement a versioning scheme to permit future changes that could be incompatible with the current interface.

questions.explanation:
Microservices should expose documented API contracts that define the agreement between service producers and consumers, allowing each side to evolve independently and use different technology stacks. API versioning enables incompatible interface changes while allowing existing consumers to remain on the current version until they can migrate.

**Learn more:** [AWS Well-Architected Framework: Provide service contracts per API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2024-06-27/framework/rel_service_architecture_api_contracts.html)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application accepts input from a user and publishes it to that user's contacts. The input is stored in a Cloud Spanner table. The application is more latency-sensitive and less consistency-sensitive.  
  
How should this application perform Cloud Spanner reads?

options.text: Perform Read-Only transactions.
Perform stale reads using single-read methods.
Perform strong reads using single-read methods.
Perform stale reads using read-write transactions.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner stale reads can be served from an earlier timestamp and provide latency benefits when an application can tolerate data that is not fully current. Single-read methods support stale reads and are suitable when a consistent view across multiple read operations is not required. [Reads outside of transactions](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reads)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner: Reads outside of transactions](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reads) · [Cloud Spanner: Timestamp bounds](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/timestamp-bounds)

questions.domain: Building and testing applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is building a Cloud Function that Cloud Storage events trigger. You want to speed up testing and development of the Cloud Function while following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new Cloud Function that is triggered when Cloud Audit Logs detects the cloudfunctions.functions.sourceCodeSet operation in the original Cloud Function. Send mock requests to the new function to evaluate the functionality.

Make a copy of the Cloud Function, and rewrite the code to be HTTP-triggered. Edit and test the new version by triggering the HTTP endpoint. Send mock requests to the new function to evaluate the functionality.
Install the Functions Frameworks library, and configure the Cloud Function on localhost. Make a copy of the function, and make edits to the new version. Test the new version using curl.

Make a copy of the Cloud Function in the Google Cloud console. Use the Cloud console's in-line editor to make source code changes to the new function. Modify your web application to call the new function, and test the new version in production

questions.explanation:
The Functions Framework enables local execution of event-driven functions on localhost, where simulated Cloud Storage events can be sent with `curl`. This supports rapid, isolated development and testing without changing production traffic or redeploying an HTTP-triggered variant.

**Learn more:** [Local functions development](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/local-dev-functions) · [Cloud Storage integration tests](https://docs.cloud.google.com/functions/docs/samples/functions-storage-integration-test)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question:
You are using a Cloud Build build to promote a Docker image through the Development, Test, and Production environments. You need to make sure that the identical Docker image is deployed to each of these environments.  
  
How should you identify the Docker image in your build?

options.text: Use the latest Docker image tag.
Use a unique Docker image name.
Use the digest of the Docker image.
Use a semantic version Docker image tag.

questions.explanation:
A Docker image manifest digest uniquely identifies a specific image version by its content. Tags can be mutable and can be moved to a different image, so a digest ensures that Development, Test, and Production all deploy the exact same image.\
\
**Learn more:** [Container concepts | Artifact Registry | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/container-concepts)

questions.domain: Deploying applications

options.text: Deploy the third-party solution as a DaemonSet
Modify your container image to include the monitoring software
Use SSH to connect to the GKE node, and install the software manually
Deploy the third-party solution using Terraform and deploy the logging Pod as a Kubernetes Deployment

questions.explanation:
A Kubernetes DaemonSet ensures that a copy of its Pod runs on every eligible cluster node and automatically deploys the Pod to nodes added later. It is therefore the appropriate workload for a node-level third-party logging agent in GKE.

**Learn more:** [About GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs) · [Automatically bootstrap GKE nodes with DaemonSets](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/automatically-bootstrapping-gke-nodes-with-daemonsets)

You are designing a schema for a table that will be migrated from MySQL to Cloud Bigtable. The MySQL table is as follows:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783706122818-hh1iuvp6.png)  
  
How should you design a Cloud Bigtable row key for this table?

options.text: Set Account_id as a key.
Set Account_id_Event_timestamp as a key.
Set Event_timestamp_Account_id as a key.
Set Event_timestamp as a key.

questions.explanation:
A composite row key of `Account_id_Event_timestamp` preserves uniqueness for multiple activities belonging to an account and keeps that account’s events together for efficient prefix and range reads. Bigtable advises designing keys around query patterns and not using a timestamp by itself or as the leading row-key segment, because timestamp-leading keys can create write hotspots.

**Learn more:** [Schema design best practices | Bigtable](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design) · [Schema design for time series data | Bigtable](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design-time-series)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Before releasing your new application code to production, you want to test it across a range of different users. Although the approach is risky, you want to test the new application version with production users and control which users are routed to that version according to their operating system. If bugs are found in the new version, you want to roll back the newly deployed application version as quickly as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy your application on Cloud Run. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the revision tag.
Deploy your application on Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the user-agent header.
Deploy your application on App Engine. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the IP address.
Deploy your application on Compute Engine. Use Traffic Director to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on predefined weights.

questions.explanation:
GKE with Anthos Service Mesh can use HTTP header matching, including the `User-Agent` header that identifies a client operating system, to route selected production traffic to a new service version. It also supports weighted traffic splitting for staged deployments; changing the routing configuration to send traffic back to the stable version provides a rapid rollback.

**Learn more:** [Advanced traffic management overview | Cloud Service Mesh](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/service-routing/advanced-traffic-management)

questions.domain: Deploying applications
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You intend to deploy a new Go application to Cloud Run. Its source code is stored in Cloud Source Repositories. You need to set up a fully managed, automated continuous-deployment pipeline that runs whenever a source-code commit is made. You want the simplest deployment solution. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a cron job on your workstations to periodically run gcloud run deploy --source in the working directory.
Configure a Jenkins trigger to run the container build and deploy process for each source code commit to Cloud Source Repositories.
Configure continuous deployment of new revisions from a source repository for Cloud Run using buildpacks.
Use Cloud Build with a trigger configured to run the container build and deploy process for each source code commit to Cloud Source Repositories.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run's built-in continuous deployment feature lets you connect a Cloud Source Repositories repo directly and build with Google Cloud buildpacks, so a new revision is built and deployed automatically on every commit without writing a Dockerfile or manually authoring a Cloud Build configuration or trigger. That is simpler than manually configuring a Cloud Build trigger (option D), which still requires you to define and maintain the build steps yourself, so it best satisfies the requirement for the simplest fully managed, automated solution.

**Learn more:** [Continuously deploy from a repository | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/continuous-deployment)

questions.domain: Integrating applications with Google Cloud services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application that will process requests from end users. You must secure a Cloud Function that the application calls so authorized end users can authenticate to the function through the application, while unauthorized users are denied access. You will integrate Google Sign-In into the solution and want to follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy from a source code repository and grant users the roles/cloudfunctions.viewer role.
Deploy from a source code repository and grant users the roles/cloudfunctions.invoker role
Deploy from your local machine using gcloud and grant users the roles/cloudfunctions.admin role
Deploy from your local machine using gcloud and grant users the roles/cloudfunctions.developer role

questions.explanation:
Google Sign-In supplies an authenticated end-user identity, and access to a restricted HTTP Cloud Function requires the appropriate invoker permission. The `roles/cloudfunctions.invoker` role grants the ability to invoke a first-generation HTTP function with restricted access, following least privilege. Viewer does not grant invocation, while Admin and Developer grant unnecessary function-management permissions.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Functions IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/reference/iam/roles) · [Authenticate for invocation](https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/securing/authenticating)

3d:[["$","p",null,{"children":"A deployed application in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) has intermittent performance problems. Your team uses a third-party logging solution and wants to install it on every node in the GKE cluster to view the logs. What should you do?"}],"
",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Deploy the third-party solution as a DaemonSet","B":"Modify your container image to include the monitoring software","C":"Use SSH to connect to the GKE node, and install the software manually","D":"Deploy the third-party solution using Terraform and deploy the logging Pod as a Kubernetes Deployment"},"correctAnswer":"A","explanation":"A Kubernetes DaemonSet ensures that a copy of its Pod runs on every eligible cluster node and automatically deploys the Pod to nodes added later. ",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Configure a cron job on your workstations to periodically run gcloud run deploy --source in the working directory.","B":"Configure a Jenkins trigger to run the container build and deploy process for each source code commit to Cloud Source Repositories.","C":"Configure continuous deployment of new revisions from a source repository for Cloud Run using buildpacks.","D":"Use Cloud Build with a trigger configured to run the container build and deploy process for each source code commit to Cloud Source Repositories."},"correctAnswer":"C","explanation":"Cloud Run's built-in continuous deployment feature lets you connect a Cloud Source Repositories repo directly and build with Google Cloud buildpacks, so a new revision is built and deployed automatically on every commit without writing a Dockerfile or manually authoring a Cloud Build configuration or trigger. You are responsible for enhancing the security of your Cloud Run services to protect them from supply-chain threats. You need to ensure adequate security controls, including SLSA Level 3 builds for container images and non-falsifiable provenance for container images, using Google Cloud tools. What should you do?

options.text: Ask developers to build container images locally and ensure strict version controls by using Container Registry.
Use Cloud Build to build container images. Configure a Binary Authorization policy on the Cloud Run job.
Use Cloud Deploy to generate authenticated and non-falsifiable build provenance for container images.
Use Cloud Build to build container images. Use Cloud Scheduler to automate delivery of your applications to a series of target environments in a defined sequence.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build provides SLSA Level 3 build assurance for container images and generates authenticated, non-falsifiable build provenance. Binary Authorization can enforce a deployment policy for Cloud Run services and jobs, allowing only images that meet the required trust policy to be deployed.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud: Software supply chain security overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/software-supply-chain-security/docs/overview) · [Google Cloud: Enable Binary Authorization for Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/run/enabling-binauthz-cloud-run)

Your security team is auditing every deployed application running on Google Kubernetes Engine. After the audit is complete, the team finds that some applications send traffic within the cluster in clear text. You must ensure that all application traffic is encrypted as quickly as possible, while minimizing changes to the applications and retaining Google support. What should you do?

options.text: Use Network Policies to block traffic between applications.
Install Istio, enable proxy injection on your application namespace, and then enable mTLS.
Define Trusted Network ranges within the application, and configure the applications to allow traffic only from those networks.
Use an automated process to request SSL Certificates for your applications from Let's Encrypt and add them to your applications.

questions.explanation:
A service mesh uses injected sidecar proxies to establish mutual TLS (mTLS) for service-to-service traffic, so the traffic can be encrypted without adding TLS logic to each application. Enforcing `STRICT` mTLS prevents workloads in the mesh from accepting plaintext traffic. Current Google guidance provides this supported model through managed Cloud Service Mesh, which uses standard Istio APIs.

**Learn more:** [Configure transport security | Cloud Service Mesh | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/security/configuring-mtls) · [Secure Kubernetes Services with Istio | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/secure-services-istio?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to create `fully baked`, or `golden`, Compute Engine images for your application. You need to bootstrap the application so that it connects to the appropriate database for the environment in which it runs (test, staging, production). What should you do?

options.text: Embed the appropriate database connection string in the image. Create a different image for each environment.

When creating the Compute Engine instance, add a tag with the name of the database to be connected. In your application, query the Compute Engine API to pull the tags for the current instance, and use the tag to construct the appropriate database connection string.

When creating the Compute Engine instance, create a metadata item with a key of ג€DATABASEג€ and a value for the appropriate database connection string. In your application, read the ג€DATABASEג€ environment variable, and use the value to connect to the appropriate database.

When creating the Compute Engine instance, create a metadata item with a key of ג€DATABASEג€ and a value for the appropriate database connection string. In your application, query the metadata server for the ג€DATABASEג€ value, and use the value to connect to the appropriate database.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine custom instance metadata can hold environment-specific key-value configuration when a VM is created. An application running on that VM can query the metadata server to retrieve the custom `DATABASE` value, allowing the same golden image to be used across test, staging, and production without embedding a different connection string in each image.

**Learn more:** [View and query VM metadata](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/metadata/querying-metadata?hl=en) · [Set and remove custom metadata](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/metadata/setting-custom-metadata?authuser=0000)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating an existing Apache/MySQL/PHP application stack from one machine to Google Kubernetes Engine. You must decide how to containerize the application. Your approach should follow Google-recommended best practices for availability.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Package each component in a separate container. Implement readiness and liveness probes.
Package the application in a single container. Use a process management tool to manage each component.
Package each component in a separate container. Use a script to orchestrate the launch of the components.
Package the application in a single container. Use a bash script as an entrypoint to the container, and then spawn each component as a background job.

questions.explanation:
Separating Apache, MySQL, and PHP into independently managed containers lets Kubernetes manage each component’s lifecycle and health separately. Readiness probes withhold traffic until a workload is ready to serve it, while liveness probes identify unhealthy workloads for restart; together they improve service availability and recovery.

**Learn more:** [Ensure workloads are disruption-ready](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-disruption-readiness) · [Kubernetes best practices: Setting up health checks with readiness and liveness probes](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/kubernetes-best-practices-setting-up-health-checks-with-readiness-and-liveness-probes)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a web application that will be deployed to production on Cloud Run. The application contains multiple microservices: some will be publicly available, while others will be accessible only after Google-identity authentication.  
  
You must ensure that only authenticated users can reach the restricted services while preserving unrestricted access to the application’s public services. You want the most secure approach with minimal management overhead and complexity. How should access be configured?

options.text: Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for all microservices. Develop a new microservice that checks the authentication requirements for each application and controls access to the respective services.
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for all microservices. Manage access control lists (ACLs) for the restricted services, and configure allAuthenticatedUsers access to the public services.
Use Cloud Endpoints with Firebase Authentication for all microservices. Configure Firebase rules to manage access control lists (ACLs) for each service, allowing access to the public services.

Configure separate Cloud Run services for the public and restricted microservices. Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) only for the restricted services, and configure the Cloud Run ingress settings to ‘Internal and Cloud Load Balancing’.

questions.explanation:
Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) enforces Google-identity authentication and access policy for the restricted Cloud Run services. Separating public and restricted microservices into distinct Cloud Run services lets the public services remain unauthenticated. Using the **Internal and Cloud Load Balancing** ingress setting for restricted services blocks direct internet access to their `run.app` URL and routes external traffic through the load balancer, where IAP is applied. This provides layered protection without a custom authentication service or per-service Firebase ACL design.

**Learn more:** [Configure IAP for Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/identity-aware-proxy-cloud-run) · [Restrict network endpoint ingress for Cloud Run services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/ingress)

You manage a CI/CD pipeline for an application that runs on GKE. Cloud Build creates container images and pushes them to Artifact Registry. Your pipeline uses the `latest` tag when building the image.  
  
You recently needed to roll back a deployment 24 hours after the rollout. The rollback was difficult because the `latest` tag had been overwritten. You need to avoid this issue in the future by using the most efficient approach. What should you do?

options.text: Rebuild the Docker image for each environment, and tag it with the specific environment name.
Build a separate Docker image for each new version of the application, and tag it with the version number.
Implement Helm charts to manage your container deployments.
Use a Docker registry to store the container images, and create separate repositories for each version of the application.

questions.explanation:
A unique version tag for each application release preserves a stable reference to the exact container image that was deployed, allowing a deployment to be rolled back to that version. In Artifact Registry, a mutable tag such as `latest` can be moved to a newer image version; Google recommends using tags other than `latest` for releases.

**Learn more:** [Container concepts — Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/container-concepts)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a custom job scheduler that requires a persistent cache containing every Compute Engine VM in a running state (not deleted, stopped, or suspended). The job scheduler checks this cache and sends jobs only to the available Compute Engine VMs it contains. You must ensure that the available Compute Engine instance cache does not become stale. What should you do?

options.text: Set up an organization-level Cloud Storage log sink with a filter to capture the audit log events for Compute Engine. Configure an Eventarc trigger that executes when the Cloud Storage bucket is updated and sends these events to the application to update the cache.

Set up a Cloud Asset Inventory real-time feed of insert and delete events with the asset types filter set to compute.googleapis.com/Instance. Configure an Eventarc trigger that sends these events to the application to update the cache.

Set up an organization-level Pub/Sub log sink with a filter to capture the audit log events for Compute Engine. Configure an Eventarc trigger that sends these events to the application to update the cache.
Set up an organization-level BigQuery log sink. Configure the application to query this BigQuery table every minute to retrieve the last minute’s events and update the cache.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine lifecycle operations are recorded in Cloud Audit Logs, so an organization-level log sink filtered for Compute Engine audit events can publish the relevant changes to Pub/Sub. Eventarc can trigger an application when a message is published to that Pub/Sub topic, enabling prompt cache updates for both instance creation/deletion and state transitions such as starting, stopping, suspending, and resuming.

**Learn more:** [Monitor asset changes with Pub/Sub](https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/monitor-asset-changes) · [Event routes](https://cloud.google.com/eventarc/standard/docs/run/event-routing-options)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s security team uses Identity and Access Management (IAM) to track which users can access which resources. You need to create a version-control system that integrates with your security team’s processes. You want the solution to support rapid release cycles and frequent merges to the main branch to minimize merge conflicts. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Source Repositories repository, and use trunk-based development.
Create a Cloud Source Repositories repository, and use feature-based development.
Create a GitHub repository, mirror it to a Cloud Source Repositories repository, and use trunk-based development.
Create a GitHub repository, mirror it to a Cloud Source Repositories repository, and use feature-based development.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Source Repositories supports IAM-based repository permissions, enabling access to be managed through the same IAM processes used for Google Cloud resources. Trunk-based development keeps changes small and merges them frequently into a shared main branch, supporting rapid releases while reducing the likelihood and scope of merge conflicts.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Source Repositories roles and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/source) · [Accelerate State of DevOps 2021](https://cloud.google.com/resources/state-of-devops)

Your team presently uses Bigtable as its database backend. In the application's app profile, you see that the connection to the Bigtable cluster is configured for single-cluster routing, and that the cluster connection logic performs manual failover if the cluster becomes unavailable. You want to optimize the application code for more efficient, highly available Bigtable connectivity. What should you do?

options.text: Set up Memcached so that queries hit the cache layer first and automatically get data from Bigtable in the event of a cache miss.
Increase the Bigtable client’s connection pool size.
Configure a Dataflow template, and use a Beam connector to stream data changes.
Configure the app profile to use multi-cluster routing.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable multi-cluster routing makes multiple clusters available for application requests and handles failovers automatically when a cluster is unavailable. Single-cluster routing directs requests to one cluster and requires a manual failover decision.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable routing options](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/routing) · [Bigtable failovers](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/failovers)
